q: You have never seen the word 'frunk'. Then you read: 'She poured the frunk into two glasses', 'a bottle of dry Franconian frunk', 'after the third frunk he sang'. You now have a decent guess what frunk is. Which principle did you just use, and word embeddings with you?
options: Compositionality: the meaning of a word is built from the meanings of its letters
The distributional hypothesis: words in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings
Zipf's law: a rare word is likely to mean something similar to a frequent word
The Markov assumption: a word's meaning depends only on the one word before it
explain: Poured, bottle, dry, sang: the company a word keeps narrows its meaning down. In Würzburg the answer would have been Silvaner.

q: A startup founder has a model head that emits exactly one label per input token, and nothing else. Which task fits this output format without any tricks?
options: Machine translation from English into German
Abstractive summarization of news articles
Topic classification of whole documents
Part-of-speech tagging of sentences
explain: POS tagging is token-level: n tokens in, n labels out. Translation and summarization need output of a different length, and topic classification needs one label for the whole text.

q: You count word types in a novel of 200,000 tokens. Which finding is typical of natural language text of this size?
options: Almost every word type occurs at least ten times
Word types are spread about evenly over all frequencies
Roughly half of the word types occur exactly once
Only about 1% of the word types occur exactly once
explain: The long Zipfian tail: around half of the types in a corpus are hapax legomena. Any model that needs many examples per word is out of luck for most of the vocabulary.

q: 'The trophy did not fit into the suitcase because it was too big.' A reader knows at once what 'it' is. What kind of problem is this for a machine?
options: A lexical ambiguity: 'fit' has two unrelated dictionary senses here
An attachment ambiguity: 'into the suitcase' has two possible heads
A segmentation problem: the word boundaries are not clear in English
A reference ambiguity that needs world knowledge about sizes to resolve
explain: Syntax allows 'it' to be either noun. Only knowing that big things do not fit into small ones settles it; swap 'big' for 'small' and the answer flips.

q: A student at 3 a.m. counts 'words' in a Chinese corpus by splitting on whitespace and gets about one word per sentence. What went wrong?
options: Chinese is written without spaces between words, so word segmentation is a task of its own
Chinese sentences usually consist of a single very long compound word
Chinese characters are not valid Unicode, so the split function silently skipped them
Chinese has no words at all, only characters, so word counts are undefined
explain: Whitespace tokenization is a convenience of some scripts, not a law of language. Chinese, Japanese and Thai need a segmenter, or a tokenizer that does not care about words.

q: Gold annotation for 'Angela Merkel visited the University of Würzburg': 'Angela Merkel' is a PER span and 'University of Würzburg' is an ORG span. In the BIO scheme, how many of the seven tokens get an I- tag?
options: Two
Three
Four
Five
explain: B-PER I-PER O O B-ORG I-ORG I-ORG. Each entity gets one B- tag, the remaining entity tokens get I-: one for Merkel, two for 'of Würzburg'.

q: A chatbot convinces 4 of 10 judges in five-minute text chats that it is human. The founder announces that it 'understands language'. What does a result of this kind actually show?
options: That the system processes language with the same internal mechanisms as a human speaker
That the system has passed a formal proof of language understanding
That its conversational behavior was hard to tell from a human's under those conditions
That the system will be as good as humans on any other language task you give it
explain: The Turing test is deliberately behavioral: it says something about indistinguishability in a conversation, and nothing about mechanism. Whether that suffices for 'understanding' is the part people have argued about since 1950.

q: Suppose a corpus follows Zipf's law exactly: the word of rank r occurs 100,000 / r times. Your method needs at least 100 occurrences of a word to learn anything about it. For how many word types does it work?
options: About 100
About 1,000
About 10,000
About 100,000
explain: 100,000 / r >= 100 means r <= 1,000. The other few hundred thousand types in the tail get nothing, which is the practical meaning of Zipf.

q: Sentence, 10 tokens: 'We took the tram to Bad Neustadt an der Saale'. Gold: the last five tokens form one LOC entity. Your tagger outputs B-LOC I-LOC for 'Bad Neustadt' and O for everything else. What are token-level accuracy and entity-level exact-match F1?
options: Token accuracy 70%, entity F1 40%
Token accuracy 40%, entity F1 0
Token accuracy 70%, entity F1 0
Token accuracy 90%, entity F1 50%
explain: Seven of ten tags are right, but the one predicted span does not match the one gold span, so precision and recall are both 0. Token accuracy flatters; the span metric is what the user experiences.

q: You expand a sentiment lexicon by adding the nearest embedding neighbors of each seed word. For the seed 'hot' the list proudly returns 'cold', for 'good' it returns 'bad'. Why?
options: The embedding dimension is too small to separate any two adjectives from each other
Antonyms occur in almost the same contexts, so distributional vectors place them close
Cosine similarity ignores vector direction and only compares vector lengths
The training corpus must have contained many mislabeled sentiment examples for those words
explain: 'The soup is hot' and 'the soup is cold' are distributionally twins. Context tells you two words are about the same thing, not that they agree about it.

q: Your MT system translates into Finnish. In one sentence every word has the correct stem but two of the words carry the wrong case ending. A word-level n-gram overlap metric gives those words no credit at all. Which metric design gives partial credit here?
options: An F-score over character n-grams instead of word n-grams
The same word-level metric with a longer maximum n-gram order
A word-level metric computed after lowercasing both sides
The same word-level metric with the brevity penalty removed
explain: Character n-grams match the shared stem and penalize only the ending. This is why chrF-style metrics behave better on morphologically rich languages than word-level BLEU.

q: Extractive question answering is cast as picking a start token and an end token in the passage, with start <= end. The passage has 10 tokens and there is no length limit on the answer. How many candidate spans are there?
explain: 10 spans of length one plus 9 of length two and so on: 10 * 11 / 2 = 55. In general about n^2 / 2, which is why real systems cap the span length.

q: A colleague at the conference bar mines a news corpus for common sense. He finds 'murdered' several hundred times more often than 'exhaled' and concludes the corpus is broken. What is the better reading?
options: Tokenization errors must have split 'exhaled' into several rarer pieces
Zipf's law predicts that verbs of breathing are rarer than verbs of violence
The corpus is too small, and with more news the two counts would converge
Reporting bias: text records what is worth telling, not how often things happen
explain: Nobody writes that the mayor exhaled. Corpus frequency measures what people choose to say, so using it as a census of the world is a measurement error, not a data bug.

q: 'The keys to the old wooden cabinet are missing.' The verb 'are' must agree with 'keys'. What is the smallest order n at which an n-gram model has 'keys' in its context when predicting 'are'?
explain: 'keys' is six words before 'are', and an n-gram model conditions on n - 1 previous words, so n = 7. Add one more adjective and you need n = 8; language does this for a living.

q: Heaps' law for your corpus: vocabulary V = 10 * sqrt(n) after n tokens. You have read n = 1,000,000 tokens. Treating V as a smooth function of n, about how often is the next token a word type you have never seen?
options: About once every 20 tokens
About once every 200 tokens
About once every 2,000 tokens
Almost never, since V has saturated
explain: dV/dn = 5 / sqrt(n) = 0.005, one new type per 200 tokens. The rate falls but never reaches zero, so a closed word vocabulary is always out of date.

q: Word frequencies follow Zipf's law, proportional to 1/rank, over a vocabulary of 1,000,000 types. Use the fact that 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/R is about ln R. Roughly what share of all running tokens is covered by the 1,000 most frequent types?
options: About 0.1%
About 10%
About half
About 99%
explain: ln(1,000) / ln(1,000,000) = 3/6. The top 0.1% of types covers half the text, and the other 99.9% share the rest, which is why both small vocabularies and rare-word problems exist.

q: A colleague summarizes: 'Searle's Chinese room shows that no program can ever pass the Turing test.' What is wrong with this summary?
options: The argument concerns only translation between languages, not conversation in general
The argument shows the opposite: passing the test is by definition understanding
The argument is about hardware speed: a person with a rulebook would answer too slowly
The argument grants flawless behavior and denies that such behavior implies understanding
explain: The room is stipulated to answer perfectly; the claim is that symbol manipulation alone still involves no understanding. It attacks the inference from behavior, not the possibility of the behavior.

q: A team trains embeddings on 1990s newswire and on 2010s social media, runs the same word association test for gender and career terms on both, and reports the difference as 'the change in society's bias over twenty years'. What is the main methodological problem?
options: Association tests on embeddings only work for nouns, and career terms are mostly verbs
The two corpora differ in genre and authorship, so the difference confounds time with source
Embeddings trained on different corpora always have the same association scores
Social media text is too informal to contain any measurable associations
explain: Editors and anonymous posters write differently in any decade. To attribute a difference to time you need comparable sources at both dates; otherwise you have measured the genre gap.

q: Tag set: O, B-PER, I-PER, B-LOC, I-LOC. Under strict BIO, an I-X tag may only follow B-X or I-X of the same type, so it cannot start a sentence. A tagger with independent per-token softmaxes can output any of the 25 tag pairs for a two-token sentence. How many of them are valid?
explain: The first tag can be O, B-PER or B-LOC. After O there are 3 valid tags, after each B- tag there are 4: 3 + 4 + 4 = 11. More than half of the output space is nonsense, which is the case for constrained decoding or a CRF layer.

q: Premise: 'Some of the students passed.' Hypothesis: 'Not all of the students passed.' Annotators of an inference dataset split between 'entailment' and 'neutral'. Which analysis explains the split?
options: The hypothesis is a presupposition of the premise, so it survives when the premise is negated
The hypothesis contradicts the premise, and annotators who chose otherwise misread it
The hypothesis is a pragmatic implicature: usually inferred, but cancellable, as in 'some, in fact all'
The hypothesis follows by logic alone, and the annotators who chose 'neutral' were careless
explain: Logically 'some' is compatible with 'all'; listeners infer 'not all' because the speaker would otherwise have said 'all'. Label disagreement here is signal about pragmatics, not annotator noise.

q: You train BPE on a corpus of three words, starting from single characters: 'tee' occurs 4 times, 'see' 3 times, 'set' 2 times. Which pair is merged first?
options: 't' + 'e', with count 4
's' + 'e', with count 5
'e' + 'e', with count 7
'e' + 't', with count 2
explain: 'ee' occurs in 'tee' and 'see': 4 + 3 = 7. 's e' reaches 5 and 't e' 4. BPE takes the most frequent adjacent pair, whatever it looks like.

q: The original BPE recipe appends an end-of-word marker such as '</w>' to every word before learning merges. What does the marker buy you?
options: It makes every word the same length, which simplifies batching during merge learning
It lets the model tell a word-final piece from the same letters inside a word
It guarantees that no word is ever split into more than two pieces
It removes the need for a base alphabet of single characters before merging starts
explain: 'est</w>' in 'newest' and 'est' in 'estimate' become different symbols, and the token sequence can be turned back into words unambiguously.

q: Vocabulary of 10,000 words, each represented as a one-hot vector. What is the cosine similarity between 'cat' and 'dog', and between 'cat' and 'carburetor'?
options: High for cat and dog, low for cat and carburetor
Exactly 1 for both pairs
About 1/10,000 for both pairs
Exactly 0 for both pairs
explain: Different one-hot vectors are orthogonal, all of them, equally. The representation knows that two words differ and nothing else.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt builds a bag-of-words classifier for incident reports. Two reports arrive: 'pump damaged valve' and 'valve damaged pump'. How do their feature vectors compare?
options: They are identical, because word order is discarded
They are orthogonal, because the subjects differ
They differ in the positions of the nonzero entries
They differ in sign, because the roles are swapped
explain: A bag of words keeps counts and throws away order, so who damaged whom is gone. Fine for topic, awkward for liability.

q: A collection has 1,000 documents and the word 'the' occurs in every one of them. With idf = log(N / df), what TF-IDF weight does 'the' get in a document where it occurs 50 times?
options: About 150
explain: log(1,000 / 1,000) = 0, and 50 times 0 is still 0. A word that appears everywhere distinguishes nothing, however often it shows up.

q: Two strings both display as 'café'. One stores 'é' as a single code point, the other as 'e' followed by a combining accent. Your deduplication script says they are different. What is the standard fix?
options: Lowercase both strings with a locale-aware function before comparing
Strip all non-ASCII characters from both strings before comparing them
Compare the strings by length instead of by content
Apply the same Unicode normalization form (such as NFC) to both
explain: Unicode allows several code point sequences for the same visible character. Normalize first, or your tokenizer will also treat the two cafés as strangers.

q: A byte-level tokenizer with no merges learned encodes text as its UTF-8 bytes. The letter 'ü', stored as one code point, takes two bytes in UTF-8; the other letters of 'Würzburg' take one each. How many tokens is 'Würzburg'?
explain: Eight characters, one of which costs two bytes: 9 tokens. Cyrillic costs two bytes per letter and Chinese three per character, so byte-level sequences are not equally long for everyone.

q: A BPE tokenizer learned exactly two merges, in this order: first 'b' + 'c' -> 'bc', then 'a' + 'b' -> 'ab'. Encoding applies merges in the order they were learned. How is the string 'abc' segmented?
options: ['abc']
explain: The earlier merge has priority: 'b c' becomes 'bc' first, after which there is no free 'b' left for 'a' to merge with. The merge list is a ranking, not a set.

q: Collection of 1,000 documents, idf = log10(N / df). In one document 'tram' occurs 3 times and 'wine' 5 times. 'tram' appears in 10 documents of the collection, 'wine' in 100. Which term has the higher TF-IDF weight in this document (tf times idf)?
options: 'wine', with 10 against 6
'wine', with 5 against 3
They tie at 6 each
'tram', with 6 against 5
explain: idf is 2 for 'tram' and 1 for 'wine', so 3 * 2 = 6 beats 5 * 1 = 5. In Würzburg wine is not a distinguishing feature.

q: WordPiece encodes a word by greedy longest-match from the left; non-initial pieces carry the prefix '##'. Vocabulary: u, un, ##n, ##a, ##aff, ##ff, ##able, ##le. How is 'unaffable' encoded?
options: ['[UNK]'], since the word is not in the vocabulary
explain: Longest prefix in the vocabulary is 'un', then '##aff', then '##able'. No merge order is consulted at encoding time, which is one of the practical differences from BPE.

q: A student at 3 a.m. loads a checkpoint together with a tokenizer from a different model that happens to have the same vocabulary size. No error is raised, and the output is confident gibberish. Why?
options: The token ids now index embedding rows that were trained for other strings
The attention masks are inverted when the two vocabulary files differ
The model silently retrains its embeddings to fit the new tokenizer
The positional encodings are stored in the tokenizer and were replaced
explain: The model only ever sees integers. Same range of ids, different meaning per id, and nothing in the shapes complains. The worst bugs are the ones that type-check.

q: BPE-dropout skips each applicable merge with some probability p during training-time tokenization. What is the effect?
options: The vocabulary shrinks, because skipped merges are permanently deleted from the merge table
Each word is always mapped to single characters, as in a character-level model
The same word gets several segmentations, which regularizes and helps with rare words
Random tokens are replaced by a mask symbol, as in masked language modeling
explain: The model sees 'unrelated' as 'un related', 'unre lated' and so on, and learns that pieces compose. At inference the standard deterministic segmentation is used.

q: A subword language model writes good essays but miscounts the letter 'r' in 'strawberry'. Which explanation fits how the model sees the word?
options: The context window is too short to hold all the letters of a ten-letter word at once
The word arrives as a few subword ids; its letters are never shown as separate symbols
The softmax temperature is too high for exact counting tasks
The embedding matrix stores each word's letters, but in reversed order, so counts come out wrong
explain: The model gets something like 'str', 'aw', 'berry' as three integers. Spelling has to be learned indirectly, token by token, from text that happens to spell things out.

q: The term-frequency part of BM25, ignoring length normalization, is tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1). Take k1 = 1. Document A contains the query term once, document B three times. How much larger is B's term-frequency score than A's?
options: 1.5 times
2 times
3 times
9 times
explain: A gets 1 * 2 / 2 = 1, B gets 3 * 2 / 4 = 1.5, and no document can ever exceed 2. Saturation: the third mention of 'tram' is weaker evidence than the first.

q: Read idf(t) = log2(N / df) as the surprisal, in bits, of a random document containing t. N = 1,024 documents; term A occurs in 16 of them, term B in 64. A two-term query sums the IDFs. If A and B occurred independently, how many documents would you expect to contain both?
options: About 1
About 4
About 10
About 40
explain: IDFs are 6 and 4 bits; 10 bits means probability 2^-10, and 1,024 * 2^-10 = 1. Summing IDFs is adding surprisals, which assumes independence of the terms.

q: BM25's term score is tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * L / avgL)), with document length L and average length avgL. Someone pastes a document twice into one file, so every tf and L double; avgL barely moves. With b = 1, what happens to each term's score?
options: It doubles, as with raw term frequency
It halves, since the length penalty dominates
It rises, but stays below double due to saturation
It stays the same, since tf / L is unchanged
explain: With b = 1, numerator and denominator both scale by 2 and the factor cancels. With b = 0 the duplicate would score higher, though less than double, which is the verbosity problem b exists to fix.

q: BPE from single characters, no end-of-word marker. Corpus: 'neu' 5 times, 'neue' 4 times, 'treu' 3 times. You learn exactly two merges and then encode the unseen word 'teuer'. How many tokens does it get?
explain: Merge 1 is 'e'+'u' (count 12), merge 2 is 'n'+'eu' (count 9). 'teuer' becomes t, eu, e, r: four tokens. 'teuer' is German for expensive, and at this rate it is.

q: You add 1,000 new tokens to a pretrained language model and set their output embeddings to zero, so each has logit 0 in every context. For a typical context, the 50,000 existing tokens have logits around -5, except one near +5. Before any fine-tuning, what happens to the next-token distribution?
options: Nothing changes, because zero vectors contribute no probability mass to the softmax at all
The new tokens get exactly 1/1,000 of the probability mass in total, split evenly among them
The new tokens together take most of the mass, since exp(0) beats exp(-5) by far
The softmax becomes undefined, because logit 0 cannot be exponentiated
explain: A thousand tokens at exp(0) = 1 give 1,000. The old vocabulary gives about 50,000 x exp(-5) = 337 plus exp(5) = 148, so the newcomers hold roughly two thirds of the mass. Initializing new rows at the mean of existing embeddings avoids this.

q: A tokenizer applies NFKC normalization before splitting, which maps compatibility characters to plain ones: superscript two becomes the digit 2, the ligature 'fi' becomes the letters f and i. You fine-tune on formulas like 'x²' and score by exact string match against the raw references. What should you expect?
options: No effect, since normalization only changes whitespace handling
Outputs can never contain '²', so every such reference fails exact match
The model learns '²' anyway, since decoding inverts normalization
Training crashes, since NFKC produces invalid UTF-8 byte sequences
explain: NFKC is lossy: 'x²' enters the model as 'x2', and no token decodes back to the superscript. Normalize the references the same way, or pick a tokenizer that round-trips.

q: Classic BM25 uses idf = log((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)). In a collection of N = 1,000 maintenance reports, the query term 'pump' occurs in df = 800. What does this formula do to a document that contains 'pump', compared with one that does not?
options: It ranks it higher, by a small positive amount
It ranks it the same, since the weight is exactly zero
It ranks it lower, since the weight is negative
It ranks it higher, by the largest weight in the query
explain: 200.5 / 800.5 is below 1, so the log is negative: once a term is in more than half the documents, matching it costs points. Common implementations add 1 inside the log or clip at zero for this reason.

q: A bigram model gives P(the | <s>) = 0.5, P(tram | the) = 0.1, P(is | tram) = 0.4 and P(late | is) = 0.5. Ignoring the end-of-sentence symbol, what probability does it assign to 'the tram is late'?
explain: Chain rule: multiply the conditionals, 0.5 x 0.1 x 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.01. Adding them gives 1.5, which is not a probability, though it does describe the tram schedule.

q: A language model's next-token distribution puts 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8 on four tokens and nothing elsewhere. What is the entropy of this distribution in bits?
explain: 0.5 x 1 + 0.25 x 2 + 2 x 0.125 x 3 = 1.75 bits. Two bits would be the uniform case over four tokens.

q: Your German flatmate samples text from a bigram model. Every pair of adjacent words looks fine, yet a sentence that starts with football ends in a recipe for dumplings. Which property of the model explains this?
options: The model was trained with too few epochs, so the counts did not converge
Each word is drawn given only the previous word, so no topic information persists
Sampling always picks the most frequent continuation, which pulls text to common topics
The vocabulary is too small, so football words are mapped to cooking words
explain: A first-order Markov chain forgets everything except the last word. Local fluency is all it can promise.

q: A trigram model over a vocabulary of 10,000 word types stores P(w3 | w1, w2) for every possible combination. Roughly how many probabilities is that?
options: About 3 x 10^4
About 10^8
About 10^7
About 10^12
explain: V^3 = (10^4)^3 = 10^12. No corpus fills that table, which is the curse of dimensionality in one line.

q: Your grandmother in Omsk plays Shannon's guessing game: she guesses the next letter of an English text and usually needs one or two tries. Such experiments put English near 1 bit per character, far below log2(27), about 4.75. What does the gap reflect?
options: Human guessers skip rare letters, so the alphabet in the game is effectively smaller
The estimate counts bits per word and was never converted back to characters
Letters are highly predictable from their context, so English is very redundant
Letters are close to uniformly distributed, which is what lowers the entropy
explain: 4.75 bits assumes independent, equiprobable letters. Context removes most of the uncertainty, and retired schoolteachers are excellent language models.

q: A test set has four tokens. The model assigns the correct tokens probabilities 1/2, 1/2, 1/8 and 1/8. What is the perplexity?
explain: Average log2 loss is (1 + 1 + 3 + 3)/4 = 2 bits, and 2^2 = 4. Perplexity is the inverse geometric mean of the probabilities, not the arithmetic one.

q: Training corpus, three sentences: '<s> I like wine </s>', '<s> I like trams </s>', '<s> you like wine </s>'. Under an unsmoothed maximum likelihood bigram model, what is the probability of the new sentence '<s> you like trams </s>'?
options: 0, because this sentence never occurred in the training corpus
1/27, because each of the three words has probability 1/3
1/3, because one of three training sentences starts with 'you'
1/9, because every bigram was seen: factors 1/3, 1, 1/3, 1
explain: P(you | <s>) = 1/3, P(like | you) = 1, P(trams | like) = 1/3, P(</s> | trams) = 1. N-gram models generalize by recombining seen pieces, and fail only when a piece is missing.

q: Your training log reports a validation loss of 2.08 nats per token (ln 2 is about 0.693). A paper you want to compare with reports bits per token and perplexity. What are your numbers?
options: About 1.44 bits per token; perplexity about 2.7
About 3 bits per token; perplexity about 8
About 3 bits per token; perplexity about 20
About 1.44 bits per token; perplexity about 8
explain: Divide nats by ln 2 to get bits: 2.08/0.693 = 3. Perplexity is e^2.08 = 2^3 = 8, the same number whichever base you use.

q: Model A scores 3.0 bits per token with a tokenizer that averages 4 characters per token. Model B scores 2.4 bits per token with a tokenizer that averages 3 characters per token. Same test text. A startup founder announces that B is better. Is it?
options: Yes: B has the lower per-token loss, and token length does not enter
No: A needs 0.75 bits per character, B needs 0.8
Yes: B needs 7.2 bits per character, A needs 12
It cannot be decided without knowing both vocabulary sizes
explain: Total bits for the text are what matter: 3.0/4 = 0.75 against 2.4/3 = 0.8 bits per character. Per-token numbers across different tokenizers compare different units.

q: A 5-gram model's test perplexity falls from 120 to 35 after the training crawl is extended by one month of web text. The test set is news from that same month. Before celebrating, what should be checked first?
options: Whether the smoothing constants were re-tuned on the extended crawl
Whether the vocabulary grew, since a larger vocabulary lowers perplexity
Whether test sentences or long test n-grams now occur verbatim in training
Whether the test set is long enough for the perplexity estimate to be stable
explain: News is syndicated and copied, so the crawl probably contains the test articles. A model that has seen the exam predicts it very well.

q: Bigram model, add-one smoothing, vocabulary of 99,000 types. The context 'drink' occurs 1,000 times with 200 distinct continuations; 'drink wine' occurs 100 times. The unsmoothed estimate of P(wine | drink) is 0.1, the smoothed one is about 0.001. What happened?
options: About 99% of the mass in this context went to continuations never seen after it
The smoothed estimates no longer sum to one over the whole vocabulary
Add-one subtracts a fixed discount of one from each of the seen counts
The count of 'drink' is too low for any estimator to give a stable answer
explain: The denominator becomes 1,000 + 99,000, so seen events share (1,000 + 200)/100,000, about 1%. With a large vocabulary add-one is a redistribution program with no sense of proportion.

q: Model A maps everything outside its 10,000-word vocabulary to <unk>; model B has a 100,000-word vocabulary. On the same test text A reports the lower perplexity, and a colleague at the conference bar declares A the better model. What is wrong with the comparison?
options: Nothing: both are per-token perplexities measured on the same text
B is penalized twice, since its larger softmax is harder to normalize
A must be overfitting, since small vocabularies memorize the training data
A gets credit for predicting <unk>, one easy class standing in for many rare words
explain: Predicting 'some rare word' is much easier than predicting which one. Perplexities are comparable only over the same event space, so fix the vocabulary or score at the character level.

q: A feed-forward neural language model: 4 context words, 50-dimensional embeddings, one hidden layer of 200 units, softmax over a vocabulary of 100,000. Where does most of the computation per training example go?
options: The hidden layer, about 200 x 200 = 40,000 multiplications
The embedding lookup, since the table has 100,000 x 50 = 5 million entries
The output layer, about 200 x 100,000 = 20 million multiplications
The backward pass through the embeddings of all 100,000 words
explain: The lookup touches only 4 rows, the hidden layer is tiny, and the softmax needs a score for every word. Hence hierarchical softmax, sampling tricks and a decade of related papers.

q: A text file has 1 million characters stored at 8 bits each. A language model reaches 2 bits per character on it, and you feed its predictions to an arithmetic coder. Ignoring the size of the model, how large is the compressed file, roughly?
options: About 500 kB
About 125 kB
About 250 kB
About 750 kB
explain: An arithmetic coder spends about -log2 p bits per symbol, so 2 million bits, which is 250 kB. Better prediction is better compression; it is the same quantity.

q: In natural text, the mutual information between symbols d positions apart falls off roughly as a power law in d. A student at 3 a.m. raises his n-gram order from 3 to 5 so that samples show the same long-range behaviour. What will the samples show?
options: Power-law decay, since 5-grams are long enough to hold a whole clause
Exponential decay at large d, as for any fixed-order Markov chain
No decay at all, since higher orders memorize the training text
Power-law decay up to distance 5 and exactly zero beyond it
explain: A finite-order ergodic Markov chain forgets its past exponentially fast, whatever the order. A larger n changes the rate, not the shape.

q: Kneser-Ney's lower-order distribution is P_cont(w) = (number of distinct words seen before w) / (number of distinct bigram types). The corpus has 1,000 bigram types. 'Kong' occurs 100 times, always after 'Hong'. 'wine' occurs 40 times, after 20 different words. What are P_cont(Kong) and P_cont(wine)?
explain: 1/1,000 and 20/1,000. 'Kong' is frequent but only in one company; continuation counts measure how willing a word is to follow strangers.

q: The true source emits three symbols with probabilities p = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4). You build an optimal code for the wrong model q = (1/4, 1/2, 1/4). How many extra bits per symbol do you pay on average, compared with a code built for p?
explain: Cross-entropy H(p, q) = 0.5 x 2 + 0.25 x 1 + 0.25 x 2 = 1.75 bits; entropy H(p) = 1.5 bits. The difference, 0.25 bits, is KL(p || q).

q: In Shannon's guessing game a subject guesses each next letter until correct, and you record how many guesses each letter took. The entropy of that guess-number distribution is an upper bound on the entropy of English. Why does the argument work?
options: Guess numbers are independent of each other, so their entropies add up exactly to that of the text
The subject knows English perfectly, so her guess order reproduces the true letter distribution
Each guess removes one letter, so n guesses cost exactly log2 n bits
An identical predictor can turn the guess numbers back into the text, so coding them codes it
explain: The mapping from text to guess numbers is invertible given the same predictor, so the text needs no more bits than the numbers. Coding the numbers without their context wastes some, hence an upper bound only.

q: Vocabulary 10,000. A feed-forward neural LM uses 30-dimensional embeddings, concatenates them and feeds a hidden layer of 100 units. You extend the context from 5 to 10 words. Compare the growth of this model with that of a full table of n-gram probabilities.
options: The network gains 15,000 weights; the table grows by a factor of 10^20
The network gains 150,000 weights; the table grows by a factor of 2
The network doubles in size; the table grows by a factor of 50,000
Both grow by the same factor, since both must cover every possible context
explain: Five more embeddings add 5 x 30 x 100 = 15,000 input weights; the table gains a factor V^5 = 10^20. Shared word vectors make the cost linear in context length.

q: A subword language model defines a probability for each token sequence, and several token sequences can spell the same string. You compute test perplexity using only the tokenizer's canonical segmentation. How does this relate to the perplexity the model truly assigns to the text?
options: It underestimates it, since the canonical segmentation is the most probable one
It is exact, since the model gives zero probability to other segmentations
It overestimates it, since the mass on other segmentations is left out
It can err in either direction, depending on the vocabulary size
explain: The string's probability is the sum over all segmentations that spell it, so one segmentation gives a lower bound on probability and an upper bound on perplexity. Usually the gap is small, but it is never in your favour.

q: Skip-gram with a fixed window of 2 words on each side reads 'the tram to Würzburg is late'. For the center word 'Würzburg', how many (center, context) training pairs are generated?
explain: Two words to the left ('tram', 'to') and two to the right ('is', 'late'). 'the' is three steps away and misses the tram.

q: fastText wraps a word in boundary markers and represents it by its character n-grams. Using only 3-grams, how many does '<tram>' contribute?
explain: '<tr', 'tra', 'ram', 'am>'. A string of 6 characters has 6 - 3 + 1 = 4 trigrams.

q: A student is alarmed that in her word2vec space the nearest neighbour of 'hot' is 'cold'. What is the explanation?
options: Antonyms appear in nearly the same contexts, and context is all the model sees
Negative sampling pushes opposites together, since they are drawn as negatives
The two vectors point in opposite directions, and cosine ignores the sign
The corpus was too small, and with more data antonyms move far apart
explain: 'The soup is ___' takes both. Distributional similarity means substitutability, not agreement; separating antonyms takes extra supervision such as lexicon constraints.

q: Query vector q = (1, 0). Document vectors A = (5, 5) and B = (1, 0). Which document is ranked first by dot product, and which by cosine similarity?
options: Dot product: B; cosine: A
Dot product: A; cosine: A
Dot product: A; cosine: B
Dot product: B; cosine: B
explain: Dot products are 5 and 1; cosines are about 0.71 and 1. The dot product rewards a long vector, cosine only the direction.

q: A baseline sentence embedding is the plain average of the word vectors. What is the cosine similarity between its embeddings of 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog'?
options: Exactly 1, since the average ignores word order
Exactly 0, since subject and object are swapped
Close to -1, since the meanings are opposite
About 0.5, since one word of three keeps its role
explain: Same bag of words, same average, identical vectors. The newspaper editor sees a difference; the mean does not.

q: You train word2vec twice on the same corpus: once with a context window of 2, once with a window of 15. How do the nearest neighbours typically differ?
options: Window 2 gives topically related words; window 15 gives words of the same type and function
Window 2 gives words of the same type and function; window 15 gives topically related words
Window 2 gives rare words; window 15 gives frequent function words
The neighbours are the same; only the training time changes
explain: Narrow windows capture what can replace a word in its slot, so 'Würzburg' sits next to other cities. Wide windows capture what it is talked about with: wine, trams, the Main.

q: Skip-gram with a full softmax must update an output vector for every word in a vocabulary of 100,000 at each training pair. With negative sampling and k = 5 negatives, how many output vectors are updated per pair?
explain: One observed context word plus five sampled negatives. A 100,000-way classification becomes six binary ones.

q: word2vec subsamples frequent words: each occurrence of a word with relative frequency f is kept with probability sqrt(t/f), capped at 1. With t = 0.0001, what fraction of the occurrences of a word with f = 0.01 survives?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 50%
About 90%
explain: sqrt(0.0001/0.01) = sqrt(0.01) = 0.1. Function words lose most of their occurrences, which speeds training and widens the effective window for the rest.

q: GloVe starts from ratios of co-occurrence probabilities. Consider P(k | beer) / P(k | wine) for a probe word k. For which probe word should this ratio be much greater than 1?
options: 'grape'
'glass'
'tensor'
'hops'
explain: 'hops' goes with beer and not wine, so the ratio is large; 'grape' gives a small ratio. 'glass' fits both and 'tensor' neither, so both give ratios near 1.

q: GloVe's weighting function gives weight zero to word pairs that never co-occur, so the loss sums over nonzero cells only. With a vocabulary of 100,000 and 1% of the co-occurrence matrix nonzero, how many terms does the loss have?
options: About 10^10
About 10^5
About 10^8
About 10^3
explain: The matrix has 10^10 cells and 1% of them is 10^8. The zero weight also spares everyone from taking log 0.

q: By default, analogy solvers return the nearest word to vec(king) - vec(man) + vec(woman) after excluding the three input words. You remove the exclusion and accuracy collapses. What does the solver now return for most analogies?
options: A random frequent word, since without the filter the query vector has a large norm
The second input, here 'man', since subtracting it leaves the largest residue
One of the inputs, usually 'king', since the offset is small next to the vectors
The same correct word as before, but with a lower cosine similarity
explain: The offset 'woman' minus 'man' is short, so the query lands close to 'king'. Much of the famous arithmetic is 'nearest neighbour of king that is not king'.

q: A startup founder takes the [CLS] vector of an off-the-shelf BERT, with no fine-tuning, as a sentence embedding. On a similarity benchmark it loses to averaged GloVe vectors. What is the most plausible reason?
options: The [CLS] vector only encodes the first word of the sentence
BERT has too many dimensions for cosine similarity between two vectors to be defined properly
The sentences were too short for the self-attention layers to produce a usable [CLS] vector
Pretraining never asked that cosine between [CLS] vectors track sentence similarity
explain: Masked language modeling shapes token predictions, not distances between sentence vectors. A contrastive objective on sentence pairs is what turns the encoder into an embedding model.

q: A contrastive loss takes a softmax over cosine similarities between a query and 1,000 in-batch candidates, with the similarities divided by a temperature of 0.05. A colleague sets the temperature to 1 'for simplicity' and training stalls. Why?
options: Cosines lie in [-1, 1], so the softmax stays nearly flat and the positive never gets much mass
A temperature of 1 makes the softmax one-hot on the hardest negative, and the gradients vanish
A temperature of 1 removes the in-batch negatives from the denominator of the loss
Cosines above 0.05 are clipped at that temperature, so most positives produce no gradient
explain: Even with a positive at cosine 1 and all negatives at -1, the positive gets e/(e + 999/e), under 1%. Dividing by 0.05 stretches the logits to a range of 40.

q: You store 10 million embeddings of 1,536 float32 dimensions, about 61 GB. You keep only the first 256 dimensions and renormalize, about 10 GB. Under what condition does retrieval quality survive this?
options: Always, since the leading dimensions of any embedding carry the most variance
If the model was trained with the loss also applied to nested prefixes of the vector
If the embeddings were trained with a dot product instead of cosine similarity
Never, since any 256 of the 1,536 dimensions hold only one sixth of the information
explain: Matryoshka-style training makes each prefix a usable embedding on its own. An ordinary model spreads information over all coordinates in no particular order.

q: At the optimum of skip-gram with negative sampling, the dot product of a word and a context vector equals PMI(w, c) - ln k, with k negatives per positive. With k = 5, what happens to a pair that co-occurs exactly as often as chance predicts?
options: Its dot product is 0, as the two words are statistically independent
Its dot product is about +1.6, as every observed pair is pulled together
Its dot product is undefined, as PMI diverges for independent words
Its dot product is about -1.6; only pairs above 5 times chance come out positive
explain: PMI is ln 1 = 0, so the dot product is -ln 5, about -1.6. The shift means mild association still counts as repulsion.

q: You map German word vectors into an English space and translate by nearest neighbour. The same few English words turn up as the translation of hundreds of unrelated German words. What is this effect, and what is a standard remedy?
options: Polysemy: those words have many senses and so attract many sources; replace the static vectors with contextual ones
Overfitting: the mapping memorized its seed dictionary and collapses elsewhere; add L2 regularization to the mapping
Hubness: some points are near neighbours of very many others; penalize candidates that are close to everything
Anisotropy: all vectors share one dominant direction; reduce the dimensionality until the effect disappears
explain: In high dimensions a few points become universal neighbours. Scores such as CSLS discount a candidate by how close it is to everything else, so popularity stops paying.

q: You train word2vec separately on texts from 1900 and from 2000 and take the cosine between the 1900 vector and the 2000 vector of 'broadcast' to measure semantic change. Reviewer #2 says the number is meaningless. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: The two vocabularies differ; restrict both models to their 1,000 most frequent words
Each run's space is arbitrary up to rotation; align the two with orthogonal Procrustes first
Cosine is not defined across corpora of different size; use Euclidean distance instead
Word frequencies changed over the century; rescale each vector by its word frequency
explain: The objective depends only on dot products within a run, so each run picks its own axes. An orthogonal map aligns the spaces without changing within-space cosines; comparing neighbour sets also works.

q: A taxonomy is a tree with branching factor 3 and depth 10, so it has 3^10, about 59,000 leaves. Embeddings in a two-dimensional Euclidean plane distort it badly; a two-dimensional hyperbolic disk does not. What is the geometric reason?
options: Hyperbolic distance is non-symmetric, which matches the parent-to-child direction
Hyperbolic space has no origin, so a root node can be placed anywhere
The Euclidean plane cannot represent more than a few thousand distinct points
Hyperbolic circumference grows exponentially with radius, as tree width does with depth
explain: A Euclidean circle offers room proportional to r, a hyperbolic one room proportional to roughly e^r. Trees need exponential room, so they fit with low distortion.

q: SIF sentence embeddings weight each word by a/(a + p(w)), where p(w) is its unigram probability, average the vectors, then remove each sentence vector's projection on the first principal component of all sentence vectors. With a = 0.001: what weight does 'the' (p = 0.009) get, and what is the removal for?
options: Weight 0.9; it removes the rare words that carry the most noise
Weight 0.1; it reduces dimensionality so that search runs faster
Weight 0.1; it removes a direction shared by all sentences that inflates every cosine
Weight 0.9; it removes a direction shared by all sentences that inflates every cosine
explain: 0.001/0.010 = 0.1, while a rare word with p = 0.000001 keeps a weight near 1. The top component mostly encodes frequency and function-word content common to every sentence.

q: An association test finds that in embeddings trained on news, male names lie closer to career words and female names closer to family words, with a large effect size. Which conclusion does this measurement support?
options: Any classifier built on these embeddings will make gender-biased decisions
The corpus statistics tie these word sets together; downstream harm needs separate tests
Projecting out one gender direction from the space will remove the bias entirely
The embedding algorithm itself adds a bias that is not present in the corpus
explain: The test measures geometry inherited from co-occurrence, and is sensitive to the chosen word lists. Intrinsic scores correlate poorly with downstream behaviour, and projection-style debiasing largely hides the association.

q: A scalar linear RNN computes h_t = 0.5 * h_(t-1) + x_t. You nudge the very first input x_0 by one unit. By roughly how much does h_10 move?
options: About 0.05, since 0.5 is divided by the 10 steps
About 0.5, since the weight is applied once
About 5, since 0.5 is applied 10 times and adds up
About 0.001, since 0.5 is multiplied 10 times
explain: The influence is 0.5^10 = 1/1024. This is the goldfish problem in one line: the memory decays geometrically, not linearly.

q: An LSTM reads 'The keys that my grandmother in Omsk left on the cabinet next to the door are gone' and must remember 'plural subject' from 'keys' until 'are'. Which gate has to stay close to 1 across the words in between?
options: The input gate, so that each new word is written into the cell
The forget gate, so that the old cell content is carried forward
The output gate, so that the cell is exposed at every single step
The candidate tanh layer, so that the cell values stay bounded
explain: c_t = f_t * c_(t-1) + i_t * candidate. With f near 1 the stored feature survives the relative clause, cabinet and door included.

q: A bidirectional LSTM gives each position a state that has read the whole sequence from both ends. For which of these jobs is that legitimate?
options: Suggesting the next word while a user is still typing a message
Sampling a poem word by word from left to right
Tagging parts of speech in a sentence that is already complete
Captioning a live talk where each word must be emitted at once
explain: Tagging a finished sentence may look at both sides. The other three need tokens that have not been written or spoken yet.

q: A plain autoencoder for sentences reconstructs its training data nicely. A student samples a random latent vector from a standard normal and decodes it, expecting a new sentence, and gets word salad. Why?
options: The decoder was trained with teacher forcing and cannot run freely
The latent vector is too small to hold a whole sentence
Nothing in the loss made the codes fill a known distribution
The encoder is deterministic, so the decoder must be as well
explain: The reconstruction loss only cares about points the encoder actually produces. Everything between and around them is unvisited territory, which is what the KL term of a VAE is for.

q: A sentence has 30 tokens. In a unidirectional RNN, how many recurrent updates lie between token 1 and the state at token 30, and how many attention steps does one self-attention layer need to connect the same two tokens?
options: 29 updates for the RNN, 1 step for self-attention
30 updates for the RNN, 30 steps for self-attention
1 update for the RNN, 29 steps for self-attention
29 updates for the RNN, about 5 (log2 of 30) for self-attention
explain: Recurrence passes the message hand to hand, attention connects any pair directly. The logarithmic path belongs to dilated convolutions.

q: A vanilla RNN layer with input size 10 and hidden size 20 has 20 * (20 + 10) + 20 = 620 parameters. How many does an LSTM layer of the same sizes have, with one bias vector per gate block?
explain: An LSTM has four such blocks (input, forget, output gates and the candidate): 4 * 620 = 2,480. The 1,860 would be a GRU.

q: Your gradient vector is (3, 4) and you clip by global norm with threshold 1. What is the gradient after clipping?
explain: The norm is 5, so the vector is rescaled by 1/5. Direction is kept, which is the whole point; (1, 1) would be clipping by value and changes the direction.

q: A character RNN must close a bracket opened 200 steps earlier and never learns to. Your German flatmate looks at the config and says: 'Gradient clipping at norm 1.0 is on, so gradients are taken care of.' What is wrong with that?
options: Clipping at 1.0 is too tight, and raising the threshold to 5.0 would restore the long-range signal
Clipping only shrinks gradients that are too large and cannot revive a signal that has vanished
Clipping removes the long-range components of the gradient first, since they have the largest norm
Clipping is applied per time step, so the 200-step gradient is cut 200 times and ends up at zero
explain: Clipping treats explosion. Vanishing needs a different architecture or path: gates, attention, or at least a better initialization.

q: An RNN computes h_t = tanh(W h_(t-1) + U x_t). The largest singular value of W is 0.9. What can you say about the gradient of h_50 with respect to h_0?
options: Its norm is at most 0.9^50, about 0.005, so it vanishes whatever the inputs are
Its norm is exactly 0.9^50, since tanh has slope 1 around zero
Nothing, since explosion and vanishing depend on eigenvalues and not on singular values
Its norm is at most 0.9 * 50 = 45, so it may still explode on some inputs
explain: The gradient is a product of 50 Jacobians diag(tanh') W, each with norm at most 1 * 0.9. An upper bound, since tanh' is usually below 1 and makes it worse.

q: A colleague swaps an LSTM layer for a GRU layer with the same input and hidden size. Roughly what share of the parameters remains, and what did the layer give up?
options: About 50%, since two gates replace four, and it gave up the forget mechanism
About 75%, and it gave up the ability to reset its memory
About 67%, since two of three gates remain, and it gave up the output gate
About 75%, and it gave up the separate cell state with its output gate
explain: A GRU has three weight blocks (update, reset, candidate) against four in the LSTM, and exposes its whole state as output. In practice the two are usually close.

q: A student trains a trigram model on folk melodies, one note per token. The output sounds fine bar by bar but never returns to its opening theme. In terms of the mutual information I(d) between symbols d steps apart, what is the mismatch?
options: A fixed-order Markov model gives I(d) that decays exponentially, while real music and text decay roughly as a power law
A fixed-order Markov model gives I(d) that decays as a power law, while real music and text decay exponentially fast
A fixed-order Markov model gives I(d) = 0 beyond three steps, while real music and text have constant I(d) at all distances
A fixed-order Markov model overestimates I(d) at long range, since it counts each returning theme several times over
explain: Finite memory means exponential forgetting. Melodies, like prose, have themes that come back after a long time, and a trigram has no way of knowing that.

q: Dot-product attention in a seq2seq model. Decoder state s = (10, 0). Encoder states: h1 = (1, 0), h2 = (0, 3), h3 = (1, 2). The scores s . h_j go through a softmax, giving one row of the alignment matrix. What is the context vector, approximately?
explain: Scores are 10, 0, 10, so the weights are about 0.5, 0, 0.5 and the context is the mean of h1 and h3. The row sums to one, so (2, 2) is out.

q: You train a sentence VAE with an LSTM decoder. After a few thousand steps the KL term is 0.01 nats, the reconstruction loss equals that of a plain LSTM language model, and decoding different z gives the same kind of sentences. What happened?
options: The encoder overfitted, so every sentence gets its own isolated code
The decoder ignores z and the posterior has collapsed onto the prior
The reparameterization noise is too large for gradients to pass
The latent dimension is too large, so the KL term underflows
explain: A decoder that predicts well from the previous words alone has no use for z, and then KL = 0 is free. Standard countermeasures: KL annealing, word dropout, a weaker decoder.

q: You train a character LSTM with truncated backpropagation through time: the hidden state is carried across the whole document, but gradients are cut after 50 steps. The task needs a quotation mark opened 300 characters earlier to be closed. What does truncation do here?
options: The forward state cannot reach back 300 characters, so the information is simply gone
The state can carry the information, but no gradient ever rewards storing it that long
Nothing is lost, since gradients cut at 50 steps are restored when the chunks are concatenated
The model overfits to the last 50 characters, since earlier ones are dropped from the loss
explain: Truncation cuts the backward pass, not the forward one. The state may happen to keep the open quote, but credit is never assigned across more than 50 steps, so the model learns it only by luck.

q: A sentence VAE reports, per sentence of 24 tokens on average: reconstruction term 90 nats and KL term 6 nats. Which per-token perplexity may you honestly report as an upper bound, to compare with a language model?
options: About 43, which is exp(90/24)
About 33, which is exp(84/24)
About 55, which is exp(96/24)
About 20, which is exp(72/24)
explain: The negative ELBO is 90 + 6 = 96 nats, an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood, so 4 nats per token and exp(4) is about 55. Quoting exp(90/24) forgets that the latent code is not free.

q: In a Gaussian VAE you write z = mu + sigma * eps with eps drawn from N(0, 1), and gradients reach the encoder. A colleague wants a categorical latent and tries to do 'the same thing' by sampling a category from the encoder's probabilities. Why does it not carry over directly?
options: A categorical KL term to a uniform prior has no closed form, so the loss cannot be differentiated for the encoder at all
A discrete sample is not differentiable in the probabilities, so a relaxation or score-function estimator is needed
A categorical distribution has no variance parameter for the noise to scale, and the trick requires one
A discrete latent removes the sampling noise entirely, so nothing is left for the trick to reparameterize
explain: The trick moves the randomness outside a smooth function of the parameters. An argmax over categories has zero gradient almost everywhere, hence Gumbel-softmax, straight-through or REINFORCE.

q: A text VAE suffers from posterior collapse. A student at 3 a.m. reasons: 'The model does not use the latent, so I will raise the weight on the KL term from 1 to 5 to push it.' What will this do?
options: It helps, since a larger KL weight rewards the encoder for informative codes
It changes nothing, since a collapsed KL term is zero and its weight is irrelevant at any stage of training
It helps the latent but hurts fluency, the usual rate-distortion trade
It makes collapse more likely, since the KL term is the price of putting information into z
explain: KL(q(z|x) || p(z)) is zero exactly when z says nothing about x. The cure goes the other way: start the weight near 0 and anneal up, or guarantee a minimum of free nats.

q: A sentiment transfer system turns negative reviews positive. Someone notices that simply appending ' and I love it' to each input already gives 85% accuracy under the style classifier and a BLEU of 90 against the input. What does this say about the usual pair of metrics?
options: Classifier accuracy and BLEU can both be high for an output that no reader would call a transfer
Classifier accuracy is reliable, but BLEU should be replaced by a different n-gram overlap such as ROUGE
BLEU is reliable, but the classifier needs a larger test set
The pair is fine, the two numbers should just be multiplied into one score
explain: One marker phrase satisfies the classifier and near-copying satisfies BLEU, while the complaint about the cold soup is still there. Neither metric checks meaning or fluency.

q: Formality transfer. Human rewrites of the test sentences score BLEU 30 against their source sentences. System A scores BLEU 70 against the source at 60% style accuracy; system B scores 32 at 85%. Reviewer #2 says A 'preserves content far better'. What is the sound reading?
options: A is better on content, since BLEU against the source is a direct and sufficient measure of preserved meaning
A edits much less than humans do, so its high BLEU mostly reflects copying, not better content preservation
B is worse on content, since any score near the human level of 30 means that most of the meaning was lost
Neither can be judged, since BLEU is undefined when source and output differ in style
explain: A proper rewrite changes words, so humans land at 30. Overlap far above the human level signals under-editing, and a good paraphrase can share few n-grams and all of the meaning.

q: To build a 'bidirectional language model', a student stacks two bidirectional LSTM layers, where layer 2 reads the concatenated forward and backward states of layer 1, and predicts token t from the layer-2 forward state at t-1 and the layer-2 backward state at t+1. Training loss falls to almost zero. Why?
options: Two layers have enough capacity to memorize the training corpus token by token
The forward and backward states at the same position are averaged, which cancels the noise
The layer-1 backward state at t-1 has already read token t, and the layer-2 forward state reads it
The softmax over the vocabulary is shared between both directions and so counts each token twice
explain: Once directions are mixed between layers, the target is visible through the back door. Hence either separate forward and backward stacks, or masking the token outright.

q: One attention head, one query q = (1, 0), two keys k1 = (3, 1) and k2 = (3, -5), with scalar values v1 = 10 and v2 = 20. Using softmax over the dot products q . k, what is the output?
explain: Both scores are 3, so the weights are 0.5 each and the output is the average. Attention outputs a weighted mean of values, never a sum.

q: A decoder-only model processes 5 tokens with a causal mask, where each token may attend to itself and to earlier tokens. How many (query, key) pairs are allowed?
explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, the lower triangle including the diagonal. Without the mask all 25 would be open and the answer could be read off the future.

q: In an encoder-decoder transformer for translation, the decoder has a cross-attention sublayer. Where do its queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries from the encoder output, keys and values from the decoder
Queries and keys from the decoder, values from the encoder output
Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output
Queries, keys and values all from the decoder, shifted by one
explain: The decoder asks, the source answers. Each target position forms a query and retrieves a mix of encoder states.

q: A model has vocabulary size 50,000 and d_model = 512. You tie the input embedding matrix to the output projection, with no output bias. How many parameters does this save?
options: 25.6 million
12.8 million
51.2 million
512 thousand
explain: One 50,000 x 512 matrix is used twice instead of two being stored: 25.6M saved. For small models that is a large share of everything.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt wants one model to label incoming tickets and asks why a BERT-style encoder is awkward for also writing the replies. What is the core reason?
options: Its vocabulary has no punctuation tokens, so generated sentences could never be properly ended
Its attention is bidirectional and it was trained to fill in masked tokens, not to predict the next one
Its layers lack residual connections, so long outputs degrade quickly after the first few generated tokens
Its positional embeddings are learned, so it cannot produce tokens at any new position in a reply
explain: An encoder sees both sides of every position and defines no left-to-right factorization of text. Fine for labelling a ticket, clumsy for answering it.

q: Self-attention with d_model = 512 and bias-free projections W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O. You go from 1 head of dimension 512 to 8 heads of dimension 64 each. What happens to the number of attention parameters?
options: It grows 8 times, since each head needs its own full set of projections
It shrinks 8 times, since each head is 8 times narrower than before
It stays the same, the projections are just split into 8 slices
It doubles, since the heads need an extra matrix to mix their outputs
explain: 8 heads x (64 x 512) is again 512 x 512 per projection. Multi-head buys several attention patterns per position at the same price.

q: A model uses learned absolute position embeddings, a table with 512 rows, one per position. A user sends 600 tokens. What is the immediate problem at position 513?
options: The attention matrix becomes too large to be normalized by a single softmax
The causal mask stops working for any position beyond the trained length
The embedding is extrapolated linearly from rows 511 and 512, which is inaccurate
There is no row in the table for it, so the position has no representation
explain: A lookup table has no opinion on rows it does not have. Sinusoidal or relative schemes at least produce something, whether or not it works.

q: Query and key vectors have d_k = 64 components, all independent with mean 0 and variance 1. What is the standard deviation of the raw dot product q . k, and what does dividing by sqrt(d_k) do to it?
options: 64 before scaling, 8 after
8 before scaling, 1 after
8 before scaling, 0.125 after
1 before scaling, 0.125 after
explain: A sum of 64 independent terms of variance 1 has variance 64, so the standard deviation is 8, and dividing by sqrt(64) brings it to 1. Logits of size 8 would already push the softmax towards one-hot.

q: Autoregressive generation with a KV cache. A startup founder says: 'With caching, every new token costs the same, however long the context is.' For the token at position t, how does the attention cost per layer actually scale?
options: O(1), since all earlier work is cached and nothing is revisited
O(t^2), since the whole attention matrix is rebuilt for every new token
O(log t), since the cached keys are searched like a sorted index
O(t), since the one new query still attends over t cached keys
explain: The cache spares you recomputing old positions, not looking at them. Per token O(t), over n tokens O(n^2) in total, against O(n^3) without the cache.

q: A tiny decoder-only model: vocabulary 10,000, d_model = 100, learned positions for 100 positions, 2 layers. Each layer has attention with four d x d matrices and an MLP with two matrices and hidden size 4d. Embeddings are tied to the output head; ignore biases and norms. How many parameters in total?
explain: Token embeddings 1,000,000, positions 10,000, and 2 layers x (40,000 + 80,000) = 240,000. The transformer part is under a fifth of the 'transformer', and two thirds of that is MLP.

q: Per layer, self-attention costs on the order of n^2 * d operations and a recurrent layer n * d^2, with sequence length n and width d. With d = 1024, for which sequence lengths is the attention layer the cheaper one?
options: For n below 1024
For n above 1024
For n below 32, the square root of d
For every n, since attention runs in parallel
explain: n^2 d < n d^2 exactly when n < d. Parallelism affects wall-clock time, not the operation count, and at long contexts the quadratic term takes over.

q: Rotary embeddings in 2 dimensions: a vector at position p is rotated by p * 30 degrees. A query at position 5 and a key at position 2 are both (1, 0) before rotation. What is their dot product after rotation, and what is it if both positions are shifted by 100?
options: 0.5 in the first case, and a different value after the shift
1 in both cases, since rotations preserve length
-1 in the first case, and 0 after the shift
0 in both cases, since only the offset of 3 matters
explain: The angle between them is (5 - 2) * 30 = 90 degrees, so the dot product is cos(90) = 0, at positions 105 and 102 as well. Absolute rotation in, relative offset out.

q: A team switches its attention kernel to a flash-attention implementation. In the stand-up, three claims are made about what changed. Which description is accurate?
options: Outputs are approximate, time is linear in sequence length, memory use is left unchanged
Outputs are the same up to rounding, time is still quadratic, the full n x n matrix is never stored
Outputs are the same up to rounding, time is linear, since pairs of distant positions are skipped
Outputs are approximate, time is still quadratic, memory drops through the use of lower precision
explain: It computes exact attention block by block, so memory for the score matrix goes away while the n^2 work remains, done more cache-efficiently. Sparse and low-rank variants are the ones that change the result.

q: A model uses sliding-window attention: each token attends to itself and the 3 tokens before it. The stack has 6 such layers. At the top layer, how many positions back can information have travelled?
options: 3 positions
24 positions
18 positions
729 positions
explain: Each layer extends the reach by 3, so 6 * 3 = 18. Depth buys range linearly here, which is why such models keep a few global layers or tokens.

q: One attention head, final layer. Token A gets attention weight 0.9, token B gets 0.1. After the value and output projections, A's vector has norm 0.1 and B's has norm 10. A colleague at the conference bar concludes 'the model is looking at A'. Which token contributes more to the head's output, and by how much?
options: A, by a factor of 9, since the weights decide
B, by a factor of about 11 in norm
Both equally, since softmax normalizes the contributions
B, by a factor of 100, since only the norms matter
explain: Contributions are weight times vector: 0.9 * 0.1 = 0.09 against 0.1 * 10 = 1. Attention weights say where the head reads, not how much what it reads matters.

q: A colleague says: 'A decoder-only transformer without any positional encoding is a bag-of-words model, it cannot know word order.' Is that right?
options: Yes, since self-attention is permutation equivariant in every configuration, masked or not
Yes, unless the input and output embeddings are tied, which breaks the symmetry
No, since the causal mask makes position t see exactly t tokens, which breaks the symmetry
No, since the MLP blocks process the positions one after another in a fixed order
explain: With a mask, earlier and later tokens are not interchangeable. For instance, uniform attention over the prefix puts weight 1/t on the first token, which gives away t. The bag-of-words claim holds for unmasked encoders.

q: A model with rotary embeddings is trained on sequences up to 2,000 tokens. The founder argues: 'Rotary is relative, so 8,000 tokens work for free.' Quality collapses. Which explanation fits the mechanism?
options: The rotation table has 2,000 learned rows and nothing is defined beyond them
Rotations by large angles shrink the vectors, so keys at distant positions get no weight
All frequencies wrap around at 2,000 tokens, so position 8,000 aliases back to position 0
Offsets beyond 2,000 give angles in the slow dimensions that were never seen in training
explain: Relative does not mean in-distribution. The low-frequency pairs never completed their turn during training, and attention at those offsets is untested. Hence position interpolation and frequency rescaling.

q: In a 12-layer pre-norm transformer you take the residual stream after layer 6, apply the final normalization and the unembedding, and get sensible next-token guesses. Which architectural property makes this trick meaningful at all?
options: Every sublayer adds its output to one shared stream, so intermediate states live in the same space as the final one
Every layer has its own copy of the unembedding matrix, trained with an auxiliary loss on next-token prediction
Attention weights are identical across layers, so layer 6 already holds the pattern used by the final layer
Layer normalization inside each sublayer erases everything the earlier layers wrote, so each layer starts fresh
explain: The final state is the embedding plus a sum of updates, and layer 6 is a partial sum of the same series. In post-norm models, where the stream itself is renormalized each layer, this works less well.

q: A model has 32 query heads. The team moves from 32 key-value heads to grouped-query attention with 4. The press release says attention is now '8 times faster'. What is the accurate statement?
options: True, since the score matrix is now computed for only 4 heads instead of the earlier 32
True for training and false for inference, where the KV cache hides the gain from the smaller projections
Mostly false: all 32 query heads still score every position, and the gain is an 8 times smaller KV cache
Mostly false: the gain is an 8 times smaller MLP block, since it now reads from fewer key-value heads
explain: Queries stay at 32 heads, so the n^2 scoring work is unchanged. What shrinks is the K and V projections and the cache, which matters because long-context decoding is memory-bound.

q: A head must retrieve one target token. Its logit is higher than that of every other token by ln(99); all other tokens have equal logits. In a context of 100 tokens the target gets weight 0.5. The same logits in a context of 10,000 tokens give the target what weight?
options: About 0.5, since softmax depends only on the logit gap
About 0.01
About 0.1
About 0.005, since the weight falls with the context length 100 times
explain: The weight is 99 / (99 + n - 1): 99/198 = 0.5 at n = 100 and 99/10,098, about 0.01, at n = 10,000. A fixed gap is diluted by the crowd, one reason attention trained on short contexts blurs on long ones.

q: A startup freezes all 110M weights of a BERT-base encoder and trains only a linear classifier with bias on the 768-dimensional [CLS] vector, for 3 classes. How many parameters receive gradient updates?
options: about 590,000
about 110 million
explain: 768 x 3 weights plus 3 biases. This is feature extraction: the encoder is a fixed function and the whole training job fits in a spreadsheet.

q: BERT-style masking on a 400-token input: 15% of positions are selected for prediction; of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token and 10% are left unchanged. How many positions show [MASK], and how many contribute to the loss?
options: 60 show [MASK]; 60 contribute to the loss
48 show [MASK]; 48 contribute to the loss
48 show [MASK]; 54 contribute to the loss
48 show [MASK]; 60 contribute to the loss
explain: 60 positions are selected and all 60 are predicted, but only 0.8 x 60 = 48 are visibly masked. The unchanged 6 still count: the model cannot know they were left alone.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt wants to tag every token in maintenance logs as 'part name' or 'other'. There are 3,000 labeled sentences and nothing needs to be generated. Which kind of pretrained model is the natural starting point, and why?
options: A causal decoder, because the tag of a token depends only on the tokens to its left
A masked-LM encoder, because each token's vector is computed from context on both sides
A causal decoder, because only next-token pretraining yields any per-token output vectors
A masked-LM encoder, because it was pretrained with tagging labels on similar log files
explain: Whether 'spindle' is a part name may depend on the word after it, and a bidirectional encoder sees that word. Causal models suit generation; tagging is reading, not writing.

q: You fine-tune a multilingual encoder on English entailment data with labels, then evaluate it directly on Swahili entailment. It has seen no labeled Swahili example. What is this setup called?
options: Multi-task learning, since two languages are trained jointly
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of a task learned in English
Few-shot in-context learning with English demonstrations
Supervised domain adaptation with labeled target data
explain: The task is learned in one language and applied in another with no target-language labels. It works because pretraining on many languages put them in one shared representation space.

q: Your German flatmate feeds BERT an entailment pair as '[CLS] premise [SEP] hypothesis [SEP]' and asks two things: which vector goes into the 3-way classifier, and how the model knows which sentence a token belongs to. The answers:
options: The final [SEP] vector feeds the classifier; position embeddings alone mark the two sentences
The mean of the input embeddings feeds the classifier; two separate encoders read the sentences
The final [CLS] vector feeds the classifier; segment embeddings mark premise and hypothesis
The final [MASK] vector feeds the classifier; attention masks hide the premise from the hypothesis
explain: Each input embedding is token plus position plus segment (A or B), and the [CLS] position is the conventional summary vector for sentence-level tasks. One encoder reads both sentences at once, which is the point.

q: In 2015 a student initializes the embedding layer of an LSTM sentiment classifier with pretrained word2vec vectors and trains on 5,000 reviews. What exactly has been transferred from the large unlabeled corpus?
options: Only the per-word vectors; the LSTM that combines words in context starts from random weights
The per-word vectors and the LSTM weights, since word2vec is itself trained as a recurrent model
Only the vocabulary list; the vector values are relearned from the 5,000 labeled reviews
The whole classifier, since word2vec already encodes the sentiment label of each sentence
explain: Word vectors transfer the first layer and nothing above it. Everything about composition, negation and word order still has to be learned from 5,000 reviews, which is why later work pretrained the whole network.

q: At 3 a.m. a student fine-tunes a pretrained encoder on 8,000 examples using the learning rate from a from-scratch recipe, 1e-3, instead of the usual 2e-5 or so. Accuracy sits at the majority-class rate from the first epoch. What most likely happened?
options: The steps were too small to move the classifier head away from its random initialization
The large steps wrecked the pretrained weights, so the useful features were gone early
The model memorized the 8,000 examples in one epoch and then stopped generalizing
The tokenizer silently switched to a new vocabulary because of the high learning rate
explain: Fine-tuning is a small correction to good weights; a from-scratch learning rate overwrites them in a few hundred steps. Catastrophic forgetting, in its fastest available form.

q: A founder wants to route 50 million support tickets a day into 12 categories and proposes prompting an 8B-parameter causal decoder for each ticket. Modernized encoders (same masked-LM idea, longer context, newer positional schemes) of about 150M parameters exist. What is the main argument for the encoder here?
options: Encoders are immune to distribution shift, so the classifier never needs to be retrained
Encoders can classify with no labeled tickets, while decoders always need fine-tuning
Encoders handle longer inputs than any decoder, since they have no causal mask to store
One cheap bidirectional pass gives a pooled vector and a label, with no generation loop
explain: For classification and retrieval you need a vector, not prose. A model 50 times smaller doing one forward pass per ticket is why encoders keep being rediscovered.

q: During BERT-style pretraining, next sentence prediction (NSP) accuracy reaches 98% very early, and removing NSP later leaves downstream results unchanged or slightly better. Negatives are sentences drawn from a different random document. Which explanation fits?
options: NSP labels are noisy, so the model memorizes them and overfits within a few steps
NSP competes with masked LM for the [CLS] vector, which cancels the gradient of both
A random-document negative differs in topic, so NSP is solved without modeling coherence
NSP needs sentence pairs, which makes the inputs too short for attention to learn anything
explain: Telling 'same document' from 'some other document' is mostly topic matching, which masked LM already teaches. An easy task adds little signal; harder variants such as sentence order prediction were tried for this reason.

q: Layer-wise learning rate decay on a 12-layer encoder: the top layer (12) uses 3.2e-5, and each layer below uses the rate of the layer above times 0.5 (aggressive, but kind to mental arithmetic). What rate does layer 9 get, and what is the rationale?
options: 8e-6; lower layers have smaller gradients, so they need less
2.56e-4; lower layers are far from the loss, so they need more
1.6e-5; all layers below the top one share a single reduced rate
4e-6; lower layers hold general features worth changing least
explain: Three layers down means 3.2e-5 x 0.5^3 = 4e-6. Lower layers carry general lexical and syntactic features, upper layers are closest to the pretraining task and need the most rewriting.

q: A law firm has 2,000 labeled contract clauses and 5 million unlabeled contracts. A general-domain encoder fine-tuned on the 2,000 clauses underperforms, and contract language is clearly unlike the web text it was pretrained on. Which next step is the standard, cheap remedy?
options: Continue masked-LM pretraining on the unlabeled contracts, then fine-tune on the clauses
Pretrain a new encoder from random weights on the 2,000 labeled clauses alone
Fine-tune on the same 2,000 clauses for ten times as many epochs at a higher rate
Freeze the whole encoder and train only a linear layer on the 2,000 clauses
explain: Continued in-domain pretraining adapts the model to the vocabulary and style using data that needs no labels. The 5 million contracts were the asset all along.
