q: Your retriever puts a passage with the answer into the top 5 for 80% of questions. When such a passage is present, the generator answers correctly 90% of the time; when it is absent, 10% of the time, from what the model happens to know. What is the end-to-end accuracy?
explain: 0.8 x 0.9 + 0.2 x 0.1 = 0.74. Note that even a perfect generator given the passage would only reach 0.82 here: the retriever sets the ceiling.

q: An inverted-file (IVF) index partitions 1,000,000 vectors into 1,000 cells of equal size around k-means centroids. A query is compared with all centroids and then with every vector in the 10 nearest cells. Roughly how many distance computations is that?
options: About 1,000
About 11,000
About 100,000
explain: 1,000 centroids plus 10 cells of 1,000 vectors each. About 1% of brute force; the price is missing neighbors that sit just across the border of an unvisited cell.

q: Your provider caches prompt prefixes: tokens of a prefix identical to an earlier request are billed at a fraction of the price. Your prompt is: current timestamp, then a 100k-token reference document, then the user question. The bill shows no cache hits at all. Why?
options: Prefix caches only apply to prompts that are shorter than a few thousand tokens
The user question differs between requests, which invalidates the whole prompt
Caching only works when the sampling temperature is set to exactly zero
The timestamp changes each request, so no prefix ever matches the cached one
explain: A prefix cache matches from the first token onward. Put the stable material first and whatever changes last; the timestamp at the top costs you the whole document, every time.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt asks the RAG bot: 'What was the average downtime per machine last year?' The answer lives in a table with 10,000 rows. The bot retrieves the 5 most similar rows and averages them, with confidence. What is the appropriate design?
options: Have the model write a query over the table, execute it, and report the result
Raise top-k from 5 to 50 so that the average is taken over more rows
Embed each cell separately so that the numbers are retrieved more precisely
Rerank the rows with a cross-encoder so the most typical ones come first
explain: Aggregation is computation over all rows, not similarity search for a few of them. Let the database do the arithmetic; it has been good at it since the 1970s.

q: You index 100 million 768-dimensional vectors with a graph-based ANN index. Each node stores 32 neighbor links as 4-byte ids. To save memory, the vectors are replaced by 64-byte product-quantization codes. Ignoring upper layers and other overhead, what does memory look like now?
options: Codes about 6.4 GB and links about 12.8 GB: the graph is now the larger part
Codes about 6.4 GB and links about 1.3 GB: the graph is still negligible
Codes about 64 GB and links about 12.8 GB: the codes clearly dominate
Codes about 6.4 GB and links about 128 GB: quantization was pointless here
explain: 10^8 x 64 bytes = 6.4 GB; 10^8 x 32 x 4 bytes = 12.8 GB. Next to 307 GB of raw float32 nobody noticed the links; after quantization they are two thirds of the index.

q: You evaluate a RAG system on questions about famous people and score only answer correctness: 91%. Reviewer #2 asks whether the retrieval contributes anything. Which observation would show that the 91% says little about the RAG pipeline?
options: The retriever's recall@5 on these questions is higher than its recall@1
Accuracy drops when the retrieved passages are replaced by random ones
The same generator with no retrieved passages scores nearly as high
The answers quote the retrieved passages almost word for word
explain: If the model knows the answers from pretraining, correctness does not measure the use of context. Evaluate on facts it cannot know, and score groundedness separately from correctness.

q: You raise the number of retrieved passages from 5 to 30. Recall of the gold passage goes up, answer accuracy goes down. Experiments that pad the context with different kinds of non-answer passages help to explain this. Which kind typically hurts the generator most?
options: Passages sampled at random from an unrelated part of the corpus
Exact duplicates of the gold passage placed at several positions
Very short passages that contain only a title and no body text
High-ranked passages on the same topic that do not contain the answer
explain: Random text is easy to ignore; a plausible near-miss about the same entity is not. A retriever supplies exactly such near-misses, which is why more context is not monotonically better.

q: Question: 'Which river flows through the city where the inventor of the X-ray tube in our museum catalog was born?' The catalog names the inventor; a separate page gives his birthplace; a third describes the city. Single-shot dense retrieval finds only the catalog page. Why, and what helps?
options: The query is too long for the encoder to embed faithfully in one vector; truncating it to the first clause fixes retrieval
The later pages share no terms or meaning with the query until the bridge entity is known; retrieve iteratively
The pages sit in different chunks of the index; increasing the chunk overlap will join them into one passage
Dense retrievers cannot represent rivers and cities as entities; switch to a purely lexical retriever alone
explain: The birthplace page is about a man and a town the query never mentions. Retrieve, read off the bridge entity, then query again: each hop builds the next query.

q: To measure how much a RAG generator relies on the context, you edit the retrieved passage so that it states a counterfactual: the passage now says the Main flows through Munich. Asked which river flows through Munich, the model answers 'the Isar'. What does this outcome tell you?
options: The retriever failed, since a correct retriever would not return an edited passage
The model resolved the conflict in favor of its parametric memory over the context
The model is faithful to the context, because the answer it gave is in fact true
The passage was placed too late in the prompt for the model to have attended to it
explain: The passage was in the context, so retrieval is not at fault; the model overrode it with what it already believed. True in the world and faithful to the context are different properties, and here they come apart.

q: A corpus holds 5,000 interview transcripts. Users ask: 'What are the main recurring complaints across all interviews?' Top-k chunk retrieval gives anecdotes from a handful of transcripts. Some systems instead extract entities and relations into a graph offline, cluster it, and summarize each cluster. Why does that suit this query?
options: Graph traversal is faster than vector search, so many more chunks fit within the same time budget
Graph nodes are embedded with higher dimension, so similarity scores are more exact
No single chunk holds a corpus-level answer; precomputed summaries aggregate across documents
The graph removes the need for an LLM at query time, so hallucinations cannot occur in the answer
explain: A global question has no nearest neighbor. Similarity search returns the k chunks most like the question, not a census of the corpus; the aggregation has to be done somewhere, here at indexing time.

q: Writing out intermediate steps gives a model extra serial computation, at the price of extra tokens. Which of these tasks is likely to gain the least from 'think step by step'?
options: Multiplying two four-digit numbers without a calculator tool
Tracking who holds which coin after six swaps among three people
Recalling the capital city of a well-known European country
Solving a word problem that takes four chained arithmetic steps
explain: A single stored fact is either retrievable in one step or not; reasoning aloud about Paris adds latency, not knowledge. The other three need intermediate results.

q: An application offers a model three functions: search_trains, book_ticket, cancel_ticket. How does the model know that these tools exist and which arguments they take?
options: Their names are added to the tokenizer vocabulary as special tokens before deployment
Their names, descriptions and argument schemas are placed as text in the model's context
The model inspects the application's source code through a side channel at run time
The model was fine-tuned on these three functions when the application was registered
explain: Tool definitions are prompt content, read like everything else. This is why a vague description produces vague tool use, and why definitions cost tokens.

q: A reasoning model answers with 200 visible tokens, after 3,800 hidden thinking tokens. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, at 10 dollars per million. What does the output of one query cost?
options: 0.002 dollars
0.038 dollars
0.04 dollars
0.40 dollars
explain: 4,000 output tokens at 10 dollars per million is 4 cents, twenty times what the visible answer alone suggests. The thinking is hidden; the invoice is not.

q: An office agent can do four things on your behalf. With a limited budget of human attention, which action most deserves a mandatory approval step before it runs?
options: Searching the shared drive for last year's budget file
Drafting a reply and saving it to the drafts folder
Summarizing the unread messages in the inbox
Sending a signed purchase order to an external supplier
explain: Put the gate where an error cannot be undone. A bad draft is deleted; a purchase order sent to a supplier is a contract with a delivery date.

q: Your German flatmate asks a language model how many times the letter 'f' occurs in 'Schifffahrt'. It says two. Capable models often fail such tasks. What is the usual explanation?
options: The model sees subword tokens, not letters, so spelling is only indirectly available
The model's context window is too short to hold a compound word of this length in full
German compound words are absent from the training data of most models
The softmax over the vocabulary cannot assign probability to digits of three or above
explain: The word arrives as a few token ids, and nothing in an id says how many f's it contains. It is three, as the spelling reform insisted.

q: A founder wants an agent to book meeting rooms. The booking system has a documented API, but a colleague suggests a computer-use agent that looks at screenshots and clicks through the web interface. Why is the API usually the better choice when it exists?
options: Computer-use agents cannot read text that appears in screenshots, such as room names or times
One structured call replaces many screenshot-and-click steps, each of which can fail
APIs let the model execute the booking inside its own forward pass, without any external call
Screenshots cannot be given as input to a model that also calls tools
explain: GUI control turns one action into a long sequence of perception and clicking steps: slower, costlier, and more places to slip. It earns its keep where no API exists.

q: A model is asked for 48,271 x 9,733 and produces a number with the right length and the wrong digits. A code execution tool is available. What is the sensible division of labor?
options: The model writes the expression as code, the interpreter computes it, the model reports the result
The model computes the product itself, and the interpreter is asked to confirm the number of digits
The interpreter generates the code, and the model executes it step by step in its reasoning
The model samples the answer five times, and the interpreter picks the most frequent one
explain: Models are decent at writing programs and unreliable at long exact arithmetic; interpreters are the reverse. The answer is 469,821,643, according to the party that should be asked.

q: An agent task has 20 sequential steps. Each attempt at a step succeeds with probability 0.8. Failures are always detected and can be retried, with up to 3 attempts per step; a step that fails 3 times ends the task. Roughly what is the probability of finishing?
options: About 0.01
About 0.50
About 0.85
About 0.99
explain: A step fails for good with probability 0.2^3 = 0.008, and 0.992^20 is about 0.85. Without retries it is 0.8^20, about 0.01: detecting errors is worth more than avoiding them.

q: An agent is connected to 120 tools, each defined in about 250 tokens, and all definitions are sent with every request. Users report that it often picks a similar but wrong tool. What does this setup cost per request, and what is a reasonable remedy?
options: About 3,000 tokens; add a line to the system prompt asking for careful tool choice
About 30,000 tokens; raise the temperature so that rarely used tools get a chance
About 3,000 tokens; sort the tools alphabetically so the model finds them faster
About 30,000 tokens; expose a small relevant subset and merge overlapping tools
explain: 120 x 250 = 30,000 tokens before the user has said anything. Many near-duplicate descriptions make selection a harder discrimination task; fewer, clearer tools help both the bill and the accuracy.

q: A model writes a function, and you ask the same model: 'Is this code correct?' It says yes. The code has an off-by-one error. Why is running a test suite a stronger check than this self-review?
options: The test suite is written in a different programming language than the function
The reviewer shares the author's blind spots; tests give independent evidence
Self-review is run at a lower temperature, which makes the model less critical
The model cannot read its own output, since generated tokens leave the context
explain: A second pass by the same model makes errors correlated with the first pass. Executing the code brings in information the model does not have: what actually happens.

q: An orchestrator agent sends 5 sub-agents to investigate 5 independent questions. Each sub-agent reads about 60,000 tokens of documents in its own context and returns a 2,000-token summary. What is the effect on the orchestrator's context and on total token use?
options: It receives about 10,000 tokens; the total is still above 300,000
It receives about 300,000 tokens; the total falls to about 10,000
It receives about 10,000 tokens; the total falls to about 10,000
It receives about 62,000 tokens; the total stays at about 62,000
explain: Sub-agents protect the orchestrator's context, not the budget: someone still reads the 300,000 tokens. Worth it for independent, read-heavy subtasks; wasteful for small or tightly coupled ones.

q: A coding agent runs model-written shell commands in a container. The container has unrestricted internet access and mounts the developer's home directory, SSH keys included. The agent also reads issue comments from strangers. What is the main risk of this configuration?
options: The container will run commands more slowly than the developer's own machine would
The model may memorize the SSH keys and reproduce them for other customers
Text in a comment could steer the agent into sending the keys to an outside server
The mounted directory makes the model's context window fill up more quickly
explain: Untrusted input, access to secrets and a way out to the internet: any two are survivable, all three are an incident. Sandbox with no credentials and restricted egress.

q: An agent benchmark grades a run by comparing the agent's sequence of tool calls with a reference sequence written by the benchmark authors. A stronger agent starts scoring lower than a weaker one. What is the likely flaw, and the better design?
options: Stronger agents use more tokens; the grader should normalize by tokens used
Valid alternative routes are marked wrong; check the final state of the environment
The reference sequence is too short; add more required tool calls to it
Tool calls are nondeterministic; the grader should check the agent's final message only
explain: There are many correct ways to finish a task, and a trajectory match punishes all but one. Grade outcomes in the environment, not the route, and not the agent's own claim of success.

q: An agent scores 60% on a benchmark of 100 tasks. After a prompt change it scores 64% on the same tasks, and a colleague at the conference bar announces a breakthrough. Treating tasks as independent, what is the standard error of the 60% figure, and what follows?
options: About 0.5 points; the gain is far outside the noise
About 2 points; the gain is twice the standard error and thus significant
About 5 points; a 4-point gain is well within the noise
About 24 points; no conclusion can be drawn from 100 tasks at all
explain: sqrt(0.6 x 0.4 / 100) is about 0.049, so the 95% interval is roughly plus or minus 10 points. Flaky environments add run-to-run variance on top of that. A paired test on the per-task flips would be the sharper tool, and the right one to ask for.

q: A model is fine-tuned on many invented facts of the form 'Daphne Barrington directed the film A Journey Through Time', always in that order. Afterwards you ask: 'Who directed A Journey Through Time?'. What is the well-documented pattern?
options: It answers both directions well, since a stored fact is a symmetric relation in the weights
It fails the reversed question, and also fails it when the sentence is given in the prompt
It often fails the reversed question, yet answers it when the sentence is in the prompt
It answers the reversed question well, but can no longer complete the original order
explain: Training on 'A is B' does not automatically give 'B is A': the weight update serves prediction in the trained direction. In context the same inference is easy, so it is a limit of storage, not of logic.

q: An agent has a '50% time horizon' of 2 hours: it completes tasks that take a human 2 hours with probability 0.5. Assume a constant failure rate per unit of task time, so success on a task of length t is 0.5^(t/2h). Roughly how long are the tasks it completes with probability 0.8? (0.5^(1/3) is about 0.8.)
options: About 40 minutes
About 96 minutes
About 2 hours
About 3 hours 12 minutes
explain: 0.5^(t/2h) = 0.8 gives t = 2h / 3, about 40 minutes. A 50% horizon is a median, not a promise; for reliable work, plan with a much shorter one.

q: A model solves 95% of a set of classic logic puzzles. You suspect recall instead of reasoning, since the puzzles are all over the web. Which experiment separates the two hypotheses most directly?
options: Rerun the same puzzles at temperature zero and check that the answers are stable
Ask the model to explain each of its solutions and rate how fluent the explanation is
Translate the puzzles to German and check whether the accuracy stays the same
Alter each puzzle so the familiar answer becomes wrong, and see if it is still given
explain: A model that reasons follows the altered conditions; a model that recalls delivers the famous answer to a question nobody asked. Translation alone preserves the memorized structure, and fluent explanations are cheap.

q: A system has a language model translate competition math problems into a formal language, generate candidate proofs, and keep only those a proof checker accepts. For a proof that passes the checker, what remains the main thing to verify by other means?
options: That each inference step in the proof follows from the previous ones
That the formal statement actually expresses the original informal problem
That the proof was found with fewer samples than a human would have needed
That the proof checker was run with the same random seed as the generator
explain: The checker guarantees the proof proves the formal statement. Whether that statement is the problem you meant is outside its jurisdiction: a wrong formalization can be proved flawlessly.

q: On a hard problem, a model's sampled answers are: the correct answer with probability 0.3, one particular wrong answer with probability 0.4, and assorted other wrong answers for the rest. You compare plurality voting over N samples with best-of-N using a reliable external verifier. What happens as N grows?
options: Both approach certainty of a correct answer, voting only somewhat more slowly
Voting approaches the correct answer, while the verifier is misled by the frequent wrong one
Voting converges on the wrong answer; the verifier's success tends to 1, about 0.97 at N = 10
Both converge on the wrong answer, since the correct one is sampled in a minority of cases
explain: Voting estimates the mode of the model's distribution, and the mode here is wrong. A verifier needs one correct sample: 1 - 0.7^10 is about 0.97. Consensus is not correctness.

q: A transformer answers 'who holds the red ball?' after 5 described swaps directly, with no visible reasoning. After 50 swaps it fails, unless allowed to write down the state after each swap. Which explanation fits best?
options: The 50-swap description exceeds the context window, and written reasoning extends the window by compressing the swaps
The model has never seen the number 50 in training and needs the written steps to tokenize it
Written reasoning lowers the sampling temperature step by step, which makes long state tracking fully deterministic
One forward pass has fixed depth, so only so many dependent updates fit; written state lets each step be shallow
explain: Each swap depends on the result of the previous one, and a fixed stack of layers can chain only a bounded number of such steps per token. Writing the state down converts depth into length.

q: A founder wants a 3B-parameter model on a phone with 8 GB of RAM, most of it already claimed by the operating system and a weather app. How much memory do the weights alone take in fp16, and in 4-bit?
options: 12 GB in fp16, 3 GB in 4-bit
6 GB in fp16, 3 GB in 4-bit
6 GB in fp16, 1.5 GB in 4-bit
3 GB in fp16, 0.75 GB in 4-bit
explain: fp16 is 2 bytes per parameter, 4-bit is half a byte: 3B x 2 = 6 GB and 3B x 0.5 = 1.5 GB. The weather app will still win some of the fights.

q: A service answers 'yes' or 'no' to questions about a 20,000-token contract. The decoder emits a healthy 80 tokens per second, and users still complain that it feels slow. Which number explains the complaint?
options: Tokens per second, because decoding speed dominates any request
Time to first token, set by the prefill pass over the long prompt
Model load time, because weights are reloaded for each request
Sampling temperature, because low temperature slows the softmax
explain: With a one-token answer, almost all the waiting is prefill: the model must process 20,000 prompt tokens before it can say anything. Decode speed matters for long outputs, not long inputs.

q: A student prunes 90% of a model's weights to zero, one weight at a time by magnitude, and keeps the matrices in the usual dense format. On the GPU the model runs exactly as fast as before. Why?
options: Zeroed weights are restored by the optimizer state during inference
Pruning by magnitude only removes biases, which cost nothing anyway
GPUs skip zeros automatically, so the dense model was already this fast
Dense matrix products multiply the zeros like any other number
explain: Unstructured sparsity leaves the tensor shapes unchanged, so a dense kernel does the same work. Speed needs sparse formats with hardware support, or structured pruning that removes whole rows, heads or layers.

q: Post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) both produce a low-precision model. What does PTQ need that makes it the cheap option?
options: The full training set and several epochs of training with simulated rounding
Only a trained model and a small calibration set to estimate value ranges
A larger teacher model whose logits guide the quantized student
Special hardware that stores the gradients themselves in 4-bit integers
explain: PTQ converts a finished model, using a few hundred calibration examples to pick scales and clipping ranges. QAT trains with quantization in the loop: better at very low bit widths, and much more expensive.

q: A GPU server draws 720 W and, with batching, generates 200 tokens per second in total. How much electrical energy does one million generated tokens cost?
options: About 0.2 kWh
About 3.6 kWh
About 1 kWh
About 5 kWh
explain: One million tokens take 5,000 s; 720 W x 5,000 s = 3.6 MJ, which is exactly 1 kWh. Cooling and idle time are extra, as the facility manager will mention.

q: A vendor releases the weights of a language model under an open licence, but no training data and no data documentation. Your compliance officer asks what you can now check for yourself. Which answer is accurate?
options: You can run and probe the model locally, but cannot verify its training data
You can list the training documents, because the weights store them in a readable form
You can check nothing, because inference still requires the vendor's servers
You can verify the training data by comparing the weights with a public checksum
explain: Open weights give you local inference, behavioural testing, quantization and inspection of internals. An audit of the training data needs the data, or at least its documentation.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt must sort tickets into 12 fixed categories. She has 50,000 labelled tickets, a latency budget of 50 ms and no permission to send data outside the plant. Which option fits best?
options: A large general model behind an API, since bigger models are always more accurate
A large general model with a 12-example prompt, since labels then add nothing
A small unadapted model with a long instruction prompt, to save on training
A small model fine-tuned on the tickets and run locally, since the task is narrow
explain: A narrow, stable task with plenty of labels is where a fine-tuned small model matches a large one at a fraction of the latency and cost, and it stays on site. Generality is what you pay for when you do not know the task in advance.

q: A decoder has 32 layers, 32 attention heads per layer and head dimension 128. The KV cache is stored in fp16. How much memory does the cache take for one sequence of 4,096 tokens?
options: About 64 MB
About 1 GB
About 4 GB
About 2 GB
explain: 32 x 32 x 128 values per token, times 2 for keys and values, times 2 bytes is 2^19 bytes, half a megabyte per token. Times 4,096 tokens gives 2 GB, per sequence.

q: A decoder uses 32 query heads per layer, and its KV cache for a long document takes 6 GB. You switch to grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads per layer, everything else unchanged. What happens to the cache?
options: It shrinks to 1.5 GB, since only 8 key and value heads per layer are stored
It stays at 6 GB, since the cache size is set by the query heads
It shrinks to 3 GB, since keys are shared and values are still per head
It shrinks to 0.75 GB, since both the heads and the layers are grouped
explain: Groups of 4 query heads share one key head and one value head, so the cache stores 8 instead of 32 per layer: a factor of 4. Queries are never cached, so keeping 32 of them costs no memory.

q: You quantize a linear layer to 4 bits with one min-max scale for the whole weight tensor. Accuracy collapses. A histogram shows that one output channel has weights 50 times larger than all the others. What went wrong, and what is the usual remedy?
options: The large channel overflowed the 4-bit range and wrapped around; store that one layer in 2 bits instead
The scale was stretched to fit the outliers, so the other weights share a few levels; use per-channel scales
The calibration set was too large and averaged out the scale; use fewer samples so the outliers dominate
Rounding made the weights sparse, which the layer cannot handle; switch to stochastic rounding for all the channels
explain: Sixteen levels spread over a range set by the outliers leave almost no resolution for everything else. Per-channel scales, or clipping the range, give the ordinary weights their levels back.

q: A startup serves 200 customers, each with its own LoRA fine-tune of the same base model. The base weights take 14 GB, each adapter 40 MB. Compare keeping one base plus all adapters in memory with keeping 200 merged models.
options: About 14 GB against 2,800 GB
About 22 GB against 220 GB
About 22 GB against 2,800 GB
About 8 GB against 2,800 GB
explain: 200 x 40 MB = 8 GB of adapters plus one 14 GB base is 22 GB; 200 merged copies are 2,800 GB. Merging removes the small adapter overhead per request and, with it, the business model.

q: A cascade sends every query to a small model first (cost 1 per query). On 70% of queries it is confident and answers itself, correctly in 90% of those cases. The other 30% are escalated to a large model (cost 10 per query, 95% correct). What are the cascade's accuracy and average cost per query?
options: 95% accuracy at an average cost of 4
91.5% accuracy at an average cost of 3.7
92.5% accuracy at an average cost of 4
91.5% accuracy at an average cost of 4
explain: Accuracy is 0.7 x 0.9 + 0.3 x 0.95 = 0.915. Every query pays the small model, so cost is 1 + 0.3 x 10 = 4, against 10 for the large model alone. The 3.5 lost points are the small model being confidently wrong.

q: A server decodes for a single user at 50 tokens per second. With 16 users batched together, each decoding step takes 1.6 times as long, because the weights are read once per step whatever the batch size. What do the users and the operator see?
options: About 3 tokens per second per user, and 50 tokens per second in total
About 31 tokens per second per user, and 500 tokens per second in total
Still 50 tokens per second per user, and 800 tokens per second in total
About 31 tokens per second per user, and 31 tokens per second in total
explain: Each user gets 50 / 1.6, about 31 tokens per second, while the server emits 16 of those streams: 500 in total. Batching trades a little latency for a lot of throughput, which is why your tokens are cheap and slightly late.

q: At batch size 1, each decoded token requires reading all the weights from memory once. A laptop has a memory bandwidth of 70 GB/s and runs a 7B model. Roughly what upper bound does this put on decoding speed in fp16, and after 4-bit quantization?
options: 5 tokens/s in fp16 and 20 tokens/s in 4-bit
10 tokens/s in fp16 and 20 tokens/s in 4-bit
5 tokens/s in fp16 and 5 tokens/s in 4-bit
20 tokens/s in fp16 and 5 tokens/s in 4-bit
explain: 14 GB of fp16 weights at 70 GB/s is 5 passes per second; 3.5 GB of 4-bit weights allows 20. Decoding is bound by memory bandwidth, which is why quantization speeds it up and not only shrinks it.

q: A student is trained with a hard-label cross-entropy term plus a soft-target term that matches the teacher's softmax, both softmaxes computed at temperature T. When T goes from 1 to 4, the soft-target gradients on the logits shrink and the student drifts towards ignoring the teacher. By what factor should the soft term be multiplied to keep its relative weight?
options: By 4, that is T
By 16, that is T^2
By 2, that is sqrt(T)
By 1/16, that is 1/T^2
explain: Dividing logits by T shrinks the soft-target gradient by roughly 1/T^2: one factor from the chain rule, one from the smaller difference between the softened distributions. Hence the T^2 in the classic recipe.

q: You only have API access to a teacher: text out, no logits. For each of a million prompts you store one greedily decoded teacher answer and train a small student on these pairs with ordinary cross-entropy. What does the student inherit?
options: The teacher's full output distribution, since cross-entropy on its outputs is an unbiased estimate of it
Abilities beyond the teacher's, since hard targets carry less noise than soft ones
Nothing of value, since distillation needs the teacher's logits or hidden states
The teacher's typical answers, mistakes included, but not the spread of its distribution
explain: Greedy outputs show the student one mode per prompt: easier to fit for a small model, and also all it will ever know. The teacher's alternatives, its uncertainty and anything it gets wrong consistently are either lost or faithfully copied.

q: A mixture-of-experts model has 2B shared parameters and 32B expert parameters, split evenly over 16 experts per layer with top-2 routing. Weights are stored in 8 bits. On a machine with 60 GB/s memory bandwidth, decoding one sequence, which estimate is right for the memory needed and the bandwidth-bound decoding speed?
options: About 6 GB of memory, and at most about 10 tokens per second
About 34 GB of memory, and at most about 2 tokens per second
About 34 GB of memory, and at most about 10 tokens per second
About 6 GB of memory, and at most about 2 tokens per second
explain: All 34B parameters must be resident, since the next token may pick any expert. Each token touches only 2 + 32 x 2/16 = 6B of them, so 6 GB per token at 60 GB/s gives about 10 tokens per second.

q: Speculative decoding: a draft model proposes 4 tokens per round, each costing 0.05 of a target forward pass. The target model checks all 4 in a single pass. On average 2 are accepted, and the same pass supplies 1 further token from the target itself. What is the speedup over plain decoding, at one token per target pass?
options: About 2.5x
About 3x
About 1.7x
About 4x
explain: A round costs 1 + 4 x 0.05 = 1.2 target passes and yields 2 + 1 = 3 tokens, so 3/1.2 = 2.5 tokens per pass. The acceptance rule keeps the output distribution that of the target, so the gain depends entirely on how often the draft agrees.

q: State-space and linear-attention models summarize the past in a state of fixed size, giving O(n) time in sequence length n and constant memory per generated token. A colleague at the conference bar says this is free lunch. Which task exposes the price most directly?
options: Predicting the next word of fluent prose from a few preceding sentences
Classifying the sentiment of a short product review in a single pass
Continuing a text in the same style and language as the prompt
Copying a long random string verbatim from far back in the context
explain: A fixed-size state cannot hold an arbitrary amount of exact information, while attention can look the string up in its cache. The cache that costs so much memory is also the reason transformers recall so well.

q: Quantization-aware training puts a rounding operation into the forward pass. Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere. How does training make progress anyway?
options: Rounding is replaced by a sigmoid in both passes, so the deployed model stays in full precision
The backward pass treats rounding as the identity and updates full-precision latent weights
The rounded weights are updated directly with integer steps of the gradient's sign
Gradients are taken only for the biases, which are never quantized and absorb the error
explain: This is the straight-through estimator: quantized weights in the forward pass, gradients passed through as if rounding were not there, accumulated in latent full-precision weights. Mathematically cheeky, empirically reliable.

q: A vision transformer uses non-overlapping 16 x 16 pixel patches. You feed it a 640 x 480 image without resizing. How many patch tokens does it produce?
explain: 640/16 = 40 patches across and 480/16 = 30 down: 40 x 30 = 1,200 tokens. Resolution is paid for in sequence length.

q: An autoregressive model writes a 200-token answer one token per forward pass. A masked diffusion language model starts from 200 mask tokens and fills them in over 20 denoising steps, one forward pass per step. How many forward passes does each need?
options: 200 for the autoregressive model, 20 for the diffusion model
200 for the autoregressive model, 4,000 for the diffusion model
1 for the autoregressive model, 20 for the diffusion model
200 for the autoregressive model, 200 for the diffusion model
explain: One pass per token against one pass per step, and each step fills in many positions at once. Fewer sequential passes is the whole sales pitch; whether each pass is as cheap is a separate question.

q: A quarterly report is a PDF with a bar chart of revenue by region; the numbers appear only in the chart. Pipeline A extracts the text layer and gives it to an LLM. Pipeline B gives the rendered page image to a vision-language model. Asked 'Which region grew fastest?', A fails and B answers. Why?
options: The text layer is tokenized with a different vocabulary than the one the LLM was trained on
Vision-language models have larger context windows than text-only models of the same size
The answer was never in the extracted text, since the chart exists only as graphics on the page
Text extraction reverses the reading order of pages, so the LLM saw the regions backwards
explain: Extraction can only pass on what is text. Bars, axes and layout are information too, and the text-only pipeline never saw them. No prompt recovers what was not in the input.

q: A pipeline runs OCR on invoices and passes the plain text to an LLM. On invoices with multi-column tables, amounts get attached to the wrong line items, although every single word was recognized correctly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The LLM cannot handle numbers that come with currency symbols
The reading order and layout were lost when the page became a text stream
The OCR engine is rounding the amounts to whole numbers
The invoices are too short for the LLM's context window to activate
explain: A table is two-dimensional, a text stream is not. An end-to-end vision-language model sees the layout directly, at the price of many image tokens and its own reading errors.

q: An image-text model trained with a contrastive objective gives almost the same score to 'a red cube on a blue ball' and 'a blue cube on a red ball' for the same picture. What does this illustrate?
options: The image encoder converts everything to grayscale before embedding it
Contrastive training makes all captions equally similar to all images
The text encoder truncates every caption after its first three words
Such embeddings capture which concepts occur better than how they are bound
explain: One vector per caption, trained to tell captions apart inside a batch, rarely needs word order or attribute binding to win. The result behaves much like a bag of words; counting and negation suffer for the same reason.

q: On a visual question answering benchmark, a model that is given a blank grey image instead of the real one still answers 55% of the questions correctly. What should you conclude?
options: The model has memorized the benchmark's images and recalls them from the question
Many questions are answerable from language priors, without any image
The vision encoder is so robust that it reconstructs the scene from noise
The benchmark is too hard, since a grey image should give exactly 0% accuracy
explain: 'What colour is the banana?' does not need a banana. A blind baseline is the cheapest sanity check in multimodal evaluation and among the most humbling.

q: A common vision-language design puts a small trained 'projector' between a pretrained vision encoder, whose patch features have 1,024 dimensions, and a language model whose token embeddings have 4,096. What is the projector's job?
options: To translate each image patch into the nearest word of the text vocabulary
To compress the whole image into a single vector that replaces the system prompt
To map patch features into the embedding space of the language model, as extra input vectors
To convert the language model's output tokens back into pixels of an image
explain: The projected patches enter the sequence like token embeddings that no tokenizer produced. They are continuous vectors, not words, which is why nobody can print the prompt the model 'read'.

q: A vision-language model handles large images by cutting them into 448 x 448 tiles and adding one downscaled 448 x 448 overview of the whole image. Patch size is 14, and the patch grid of every crop, tiles and overview alike, is then pooled 2 x 2 before the projector. How many image tokens does a 1,344 x 896 image cost?
explain: 3 x 2 = 6 tiles plus the overview is 7 crops. Each has 32 x 32 = 1,024 patches, pooled to 256, so 7 x 256 = 1,792 tokens. Without pooling it would be 7,168, and the text would have to squeeze in next to them.

q: Contrastive image-text training uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss: cross-entropy over each image's similarities to all N texts in the batch, plus the same for each text over all images, averaged over the two directions. At initialization all similarities are equal and N = 1,024. Using ln 2 = 0.693, what is the loss?
options: About 13.86
About 6.93
About 0.69
Exactly 0
explain: Uniform predictions over 1,024 candidates cost ln 1024 = 10 ln 2 = 6.93 in each direction, and the average of the two is the same number. A handy value to compare against the first log line.

q: The projector of a vision-language model is a two-layer MLP: 1,024 to 4,096, then 4,096 to 4,096, biases ignored. The language model has 7 billion parameters, and in the first training stage only the projector is trained. Roughly what share of the language model's size is being trained?
options: About 0.03%
About 0.3%
About 3%
About 30%
explain: 1,024 x 4,096 is about 4.2M and 4,096 x 4,096 about 16.8M, so 21M in total: 0.3% of 7B. Aligning two pretrained models is cheap; the expensive parts were paid for earlier.

q: A user wants the gap in the middle of a contract filled in: 'The tenant shall [...] before the end of the month.' You compare a left-to-right language model, prompted with the text before the gap, with a masked or diffusion-style model that fills masked positions. What is the structural difference for this task?
options: The left-to-right model sees both sides, but can only emit one token for the gap
The masked model conditions on text on both sides of the gap; the left-to-right one only on the left
The masked model needs the gap to be at the end of the text, where masking is applied
Both condition on the same context, and they differ only in the speed of generation
explain: A causal model continuing from the left has not read 'before the end of the month' and may write something that cannot connect to it. Bidirectional denoising sees both banks of the river before building the bridge.

q: A non-autoregressive translator predicts all target positions in parallel, each independently of the others given the source. Trained on human translations it produces blends of several valid translations. Trained instead on the outputs of an autoregressive teacher, it improves clearly. Why does the teacher's data help?
options: The teacher's outputs are longer, which gives the student more tokens to learn from
The teacher's outputs contain fewer rare words, which shrinks the softmax
The teacher's outputs are of higher quality than the human reference translations
The teacher's outputs are more consistent, leaving fewer alternative translations per source
explain: Independent positions cannot coordinate a choice among several valid outputs. A teacher that translates the same construction the same way every time removes much of that choice; the data gets no better, only less varied.

q: A masked diffusion language model generates 256 tokens. With a uniform schedule and 16 steps it reads well; a colleague cuts it to 4 steps for speed and the text becomes incoherent. What changed?
options: 4 network calls now commit 64 tokens each, sampled without seeing one another
4 network calls now commit 4 tokens each, so most positions stay masked
The model now runs strictly left to right, which it was never trained to do
The noise level per step is lower, so the model overfits to the prompt
explain: Tokens unmasked in the same step are sampled independently given the current context: 16 per step is tolerable, 64 is a committee that never met. An autoregressive model would need 256 calls, which is the speed argument and its price.

q: A masked diffusion language model generates on a fixed canvas of 128 positions, all masked at the start. The right answer to the prompt is 15 tokens long. What must such a model do that a left-to-right model handles with a single end-of-sequence token?
options: Decide the length inside the canvas, filling surplus positions with padding or end tokens
Run exactly 15 denoising steps, since the number of steps has to equal the output length
Shrink the canvas during sampling by deleting every position that is still masked at step 15
Nothing, since unused positions stay masked and masks are invisible in the decoded text
explain: An autoregressive model decides when to stop as it goes. A fixed-canvas model must commit to a length inside the canvas, so length becomes something it predicts, pads, or gets wrong.

q: BERT is trained to fill in masked tokens at a fixed masking rate of about 15%. A masked diffusion language model is trained with what amounts to the same cross-entropy on masked positions. What is the essential difference that makes the second one a usable generator?
options: It replaces the bidirectional attention with a causal mask during training and at generation time
It adds Gaussian noise to the token ids instead of using a mask token, as image diffusion does
It trains over all masking rates from near 0 to 1, with a weight depending on the rate
It predicts only one masked token per forward pass during training, like a left-to-right model
explain: With absorbing-state (masking) noise the diffusion objective reduces to a weighted masked-LM loss averaged over all noise levels. Generation starts from a fully masked sequence, a situation a 15% model has never seen.

q: A masked diffusion language model answers a question over 32 steps. You record its most likely prediction for every position at every step. At most positions the prediction settles early; at the position of a date it flips between two years until the last steps. What is a reasonable use of this observation?
options: As proof that the final year is wrong, since correct tokens never change during generation
As a signal of uncertainty at that position, to be validated against correctness
As evidence that the sampler has a bug, since predictions must be fixed after step one
As a reason to drop the date position, since unstable positions are always padding
explain: The trajectory is extra information that a single left-to-right pass does not offer: instability across steps tends to mark positions where the model is torn, for instance between retrieved context and its own memory. It is a signal to calibrate, not a verdict.

q: Two masked positions remain. Given the context, the true distribution puts probability 0.5 on 'thank you' and 0.5 on 'many thanks'. A sampler unmasks both positions in one step, drawing each from its own marginal. With what probability is the result neither of the two valid phrases, and what if it unmasks one position per step instead?
options: 0.25 in one step, and 0.5 with one position per step
0.5 in one step, and 0.25 with one position per step
0.25 in one step, and 0 with one position per step
0.5 in one step, and 0 with one position per step
explain: Each marginal is 50/50, so independent draws give 'thank thanks' or 'many you' half the time. Unmasking one position first lets the second condition on it, and the error vanishes. This is the multimodality problem on a beer mat.

q: An early-fusion model turns images into discrete tokens with a learned codebook and puts them into the same sequence and vocabulary as text, trained with one next-token loss. Compared with a design that feeds continuous vision-encoder features through a projector into a language model, what is the characteristic trade?
options: It can generate images as well as read them, but quantization loses fine detail such as small print
It needs no image tokenizer at all, but it can only handle images of one fixed size
It uses fewer tokens per image, but it cannot attend from text positions to image positions
It reads small print better, but it must keep the language model frozen during training
explain: Discrete image tokens make images an output modality with no extra machinery. The codebook is a lossy bottleneck, though, and fine detail is the first casualty, which continuous features feeding a projector avoid.

q: A colleague at the conference bar claims a masked diffusion LM with 32 steps is 'about 30 times cheaper' than an autoregressive transformer for 1,024 tokens, since 32 is far less than 1,024. The diffusion model is bidirectional, so each step recomputes all 1,024 positions; the autoregressive model uses a KV cache. Same architecture size. How does total computation compare?
options: Diffusion is about 32 times cheaper, since computation is proportional to the number of passes
They are about equal, since both end up computing every position exactly once
Autoregression costs about 1,024 full passes, so diffusion is cheaper by a wide margin
Diffusion costs about 32 full-sequence passes; cached autoregression totals roughly one
explain: With a cache, token t only computes its own position against t cached ones, so 1,024 steps add up to about one full forward pass. Bidirectional denoising cannot cache across steps and pays the full pass 32 times. Its advantage is latency through parallelism, not total compute.

q: A vision-language model resizes every image to 336 x 336 pixels and uses 14 x 14 patches. Reviewer #2 feeds it a scanned page with 60 lines of text and asks for a transcription; the result is fluent and almost entirely invented. The team proposes a larger language model. What does the arithmetic say?
options: Each line gets 14 pixels, exactly one patch, so a larger language model will read it
Each line gets about 24 pixels, so the vision encoder is fine and the projector is at fault
Each line gets about 14 pixels after patching, so more fine-tuning data will fix it
Each line gets about 5.6 pixels, so the text is gone before the language model
explain: 336/60 = 5.6 pixels per line, and 14/5.6 = 2.5 lines per patch: no letter survives the resize. A language model with nothing to read falls back on its priors, so the fix is resolution or tiling, not parameters.

q: Shannon built 'approximations to English': letters drawn at random, then by their frequencies, then by digram statistics, then words chosen given the previous word. Each step looked more like English, yet his word-bigram sample ('the head and in frontal attack on an English writer that...') stops making sense after a few words. A modern LLM sampled token by token is the far end of this series and stays coherent for pages. Which change in the series is mainly responsible?
options: Each token is conditioned on thousands of previous tokens instead of on one previous word
Tokens are chosen by taking the single most probable continuation instead of by sampling
The vocabulary is much larger, so each token carries more meaning than a word did
The statistics are estimated from far more text, which sharpens the same bigram probabilities
explain: Shannon's samples are locally fluent because each word fits its one predecessor and nothing else. Lengthening the conditioning context is what buys global coherence; more data for the same bigram table would only produce better bigrams.

q: Turing replaced the vague question 'can machines think' with a concrete game that an observer can score. A startup founder replaces 'does our model understand tax law' with 'accuracy on 1,000 tax exam questions'. Which description of this move is accurate?
options: It proves that the property is present whenever the score is high, since the test was designed to detect exactly that property
It removes the need for any held-out data, since exam questions are by construction unseen by the model
It is only valid when the model is also asked to explain its answers, since Turing required a conversation
It makes the property measurable, at the price that the test can be passed by means other than the property, such as memorized items
explain: Operationalizing a vague property as an observable score is the whole point of the imitation game, and so is the catch: the score measures behavior, and behavior can have other causes. Leaked exam questions are the modern version of a prepared witness.

q: An older design trained one network for POS tagging, chunking, NER and semantic role labeling at once: a shared lookup table and shared layers, then one small output layer per task that emits that task's label set. An instruction-tuned LLM does POS tagging, NER and summarization with one set of weights and no per-task layer. What replaced the task-specific output layers?
options: A router network that picks one of several hidden task-specific models based on the prompt
A fixed block of label ids appended to the vocabulary for each supported task
The task description and the answer are both ordinary text, so the same next-token output serves every task
A separate softmax layer per task, selected at inference time by a task id that is passed to the model alongside the input tokens
explain: Once the task is stated in the input and the labels are spelled out as words, every task is text generation and one output layer suffices. The shared representation idea survived; the per-task head did not.

q: A smoothed n-gram model saw 'the Silvaner from Randersacker is dry' many times but never 'the Riesling from Randersacker is dry'. For the second sentence it backs off to short contexts and assigns a low probability. A neural LM, including a transformer, assigns a reasonable probability. Which property makes the difference?
options: The neural model stores every training sentence in its weights and retrieves the closest one at test time by nearest neighbour
Words are represented as learned dense vectors, so a sentence with a similar word gets a similar probability
The neural model is trained on more text, so it has seen the second sentence somewhere
The neural model treats all grape varieties as one symbol, which the n-gram counts keep separate
explain: 'Riesling' and 'Silvaner' land near each other in embedding space, and probability is a smooth function of the vectors, so one sentence's evidence transfers to the other. To the n-gram table the two words are unrelated integers.

q: The night before its roadshow a project team reports that its TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline sorts forum posts into sub-forums with 99% accuracy, while the fine-tuned encoder reaches 91%. The top-weighted features are strings like 'Posted in: Hardware' and user signatures. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Sparse models are inherently better at topic classification than neural encoders
The fine-tuned encoder was undertrained on the team's 300 labelled posts and would overtake the baseline with more epochs
The test set is too small, and the two numbers are within noise of each other
The inputs contain metadata that encodes the label, so the baseline reads the answer instead of the text
explain: Label leakage: headers, footers and signatures carry the sub-forum name, and a bag of words finds them instantly. Strip the metadata and both numbers will drop, the honest one less.

q: A sentence-level sentiment model reads the review 'The battery is great, the screen is a disaster' and returns 'neutral'. The product team wants to know what is wrong with the screen. Which task formulation do they actually need?
options: Binary sentiment with a higher decision threshold, so that mixed reviews are not called neutral
Document-level sentiment averaged over all reviews of the same product
Aspect-based sentiment: identify each aspect mentioned and assign a polarity to each one
Emotion classification with more labels than positive, negative and neutral
explain: Mixed reviews are not neutral; they are positive about one thing and negative about another. One label per sentence throws away exactly the structure the product team wants.

q: A German flatmate texts: 'Hab das Meeting gecancelt, war total awkward.' A language identification model returns 'German, 0.92'. Which phenomenon makes a single language label a lossy description of this text?
options: Dialect: the text is Franconian, which the model has mapped to standard German
Code-switching: English material is mixed in, some of it even inflected with German morphology, within one utterance
Transliteration: the English words are written in a non-Latin script that the model normalizes away
Spelling noise: the dropped pronoun and the informal words lower the confidence but do not change the language
explain: 'gecancelt' is an English verb wearing a German participle. Mixed-language text is normal in chat data, and a one-label-per-document task definition cannot say so.

q: Shannon defined the redundancy of a language as one minus the ratio of its actual entropy rate to the maximum possible rate for the same alphabet. A character-level model achieves 1.2 bits per character on English text written with an alphabet of 32 symbols. Treating the model's rate as the entropy estimate, what redundancy does this imply?
options: About 24%
About 76%
About 60%
About 96%
explain: The maximum is log2(32) = 5 bits per character, so 1 - 1.2 / 5 = 0.76. Three quarters of the characters are predictable from the rest, which is why fill-in-the-blank games and masked language modeling both work.

q: In the imitation game a human interrogator decides which of two conversation partners is the machine. A team automates this: a judge LLM reads pairs of transcripts and picks the one it believes is human, and the team reports the fooling rate as its system's score. What is the main thing lost in the automation?
options: The criterion becomes indistinguishability to a model, which may share the candidate's blind spots and reward its own stylistic habits
Nothing is lost, since a judge model with far more parameters than a human interrogator is strictly harder to fool and removes rater noise
The test becomes undefined, since the imitation game requires that all three participants sit in separate rooms
The judge cannot process two transcripts of different lengths, so the longer one must be truncated first
explain: Turing's criterion is behavior that a human cannot tell apart from human behavior; a model judge measures something else, and it is often fooled by the same surface cues the candidate system produces. Measure the judge's agreement with humans before the automated score means anything.

q: A team fine-tunes one encoder with a shared body and two heads, NER and sentiment, on the same batches. Compared with two single-task runs, NER gains one point and sentiment loses six. What is the standard diagnosis?
options: Catastrophic forgetting of the pretraining objective, since two heads double the fine-tuning signal and overwrite it twice as fast
The sentiment head is too small to express its label set and needs more layers before it can match the single-task run
Sentiment requires a decoder, so it cannot be learned by an encoder with a classification head
Negative transfer: the tasks compete for the shared representation, and the sentiment gradient is being overridden
explain: Sharing a body helps when tasks want similar features and hurts when they do not; loss weighting, task-balanced sampling or per-task adapters are the usual remedies. The old one-network-for-all-tasks results already showed that the gains are uneven.

q: A team asks an LLM to extract organization names from news paragraphs. Prompt A says 'List all organizations.' Prompt B adds three worked examples showing a JSON list. On inspection both prompts find the same entities, but A's outputs cannot be parsed by the team's code in 30% of cases and B's in 1%. What did the demonstrations mainly provide?
options: Knowledge of what counts as an organization, which the model lacked without examples
A specification of the output format and conventions, rather than the ability to do the task
Additional training signal that updated the model's weights for this task
A longer context, which by itself improves extraction recall
explain: The entities were already found with prompt A; what the examples pinned down was the shape of the answer. Much of what looks like few-shot learning in practice is format and convention following.

q: A PII guardrail is tested on 200 adversarial inputs, 40 of which contain personal data. It flags 60 inputs, 36 of which really contain personal data. What are its precision, recall and false-positive rate on this set?
options: Precision 0.90, recall 0.60, false-positive rate 0.12
Precision 0.60, recall 0.90, false-positive rate 0.40
Precision 0.60, recall 0.90, false-positive rate 0.15
Precision 0.60, recall 0.60, false-positive rate 0.15
explain: 36 of 60 flags are right (0.60), 36 of 40 positives are caught (0.90), and the 24 false flags fall among 160 clean inputs (0.15). The false-positive rate is what the users of a redaction tool complain about first.

q: Two teammates label 150 paragraphs as 'supportive' or 'critical' and agree on 85% of them. Each of them labels 80% of the paragraphs 'supportive'. What is Cohen's kappa?
options: About 0.85
About 0.53
About 0.68
About 0.17
explain: Expected chance agreement is 0.8 * 0.8 + 0.2 * 0.2 = 0.68, so kappa = (0.85 - 0.68) / (1 - 0.68) = 0.53. Skewed labels make raw agreement flattering; kappa is the number to report.

q: A translation system processes a manual sentence by sentence into German: 'The engineer checked the pump. Then she restarted it.' In the second sentence 'it' must become 'sie', because 'die Pumpe' is feminine. The system outputs 'es'. What kind of problem is this?
options: A morphological problem: the system has not learned the grammatical gender of German nouns and defaults to the neuter pronoun
A tokenization problem: 'it' and 'she' were merged into one token by the subword model
A discourse problem: resolving the pronoun needs the antecedent from the previous sentence, which the system never sees
A word order problem: German places the pronoun before the verb in subordinate clauses
explain: The information is in the document, not in the sentence. Sentence-level systems guess; document-level translation, or simply giving the model the surrounding context, is the fix.

q: A language model reaches 0.7 bits per byte on English text, measured as its average cross-entropy per UTF-8 byte. Shannon's source coding result says an arithmetic coder driven by this model spends about -log2 p(byte) bits per byte. To roughly what fraction of its original size does such a coder shrink the text?
options: About 9%
About 30%
About 70%
About 0.7%
explain: A byte holds 8 bits; 0.7 / 8 = 0.0875. Lower cross-entropy and better compression are the same statement, which is why bits per byte is the tokenizer-independent way to compare language models.

q: A model scores 95% on a reasoning benchmark and a report concludes that it 'understands' the domain. A follow-up swaps the entity names in every item for unfamiliar ones, keeps the logic identical, and accuracy drops to 40%. Read in terms of the classic debates about behavioral tests, what does the follow-up show?
options: That no behavioral test can ever bear on understanding, so the original claim and the rebuttal are both meaningless
That the benchmark was mislabeled, since a correct item cannot change its answer when names change
That swapping names changes the logical content of the items, so a drop is expected and tells us nothing about the model's reasoning
That a behavioral criterion is only as informative as its probes: a high score on familiar items is compatible with a lookup-like strategy
explain: The behaviorist wager is that a sufficiently varied interrogation rules out tricks; a fixed benchmark is not sufficiently varied. Robustness under meaning-preserving perturbations is the minimum before a score counts as evidence.

q: Entity mentions in a corpus are Zipfian: the 1,000 most frequent names account for half of all mentions, the remaining 99,000 distinct names for the other half. A NER system recognizes head names with 100% accuracy and tail names with 70%. The test set is sampled by mention. The product's users look up distinct names, each about equally often. What are the test score and the user-experienced score?
options: 85% and about 70%
About 70% and 100%
explain: By mention: 0.5 * 100 + 0.5 * 70 = 85. By type: 0.01 * 100 + 0.99 * 70 = 70.3. Micro-averaging over running text weights the head; the users live in the tail.

q: Two versions of a terms-of-service document differ only in that the final section was moved to the front. A line-based diff built on the longest common subsequence reports the section as deleted at the end and inserted at the start. An alignment that scores every paragraph of version A against every paragraph of version B and matches the best pairs reports a move. Why can the first method not report the move?
options: Line-based diffs compare hashes of lines, and the moved lines were rehashed after moving
The moved section was reformatted during the move, so no line matched exactly any more
Longest common subsequence alignment is order-preserving, so a block that changed position can be matched at only one of its two locations
The longest common subsequence has exponential cost in the number of lines, and the implementation fell back to a heuristic that gave up on the long block
explain: A common subsequence must appear in the same order in both documents; a move breaks monotonicity, so the algorithm sees a deletion plus an insertion. Any-to-any similarity matching has no order constraint, which is why it catches moves and also why it needs a tie-breaking rule for repeated boilerplate.

q: To check claims against a source, a team replaces its NLI model with cosine similarity between sentence embeddings and a threshold of 0.8. The claim 'The pump was replaced in 2019' and the source sentence 'The pump was not replaced in 2019' score 0.93 and are marked 'supported'. Which property of the task does the similarity approach lack?
options: Multilinguality: the claims and the sources were written in different languages by different authors
Context length: the source sentence is too long for the embedding model's input window
Calibration: the threshold of 0.8 is too permissive for sentence pairs, and at 0.95 this pair would have been rejected as unsupported
Directionality and polarity: entailment is asymmetric and negation-sensitive, while cosine is symmetric and measures topical closeness
explain: Two sentences about the same pump, year and action are neighbors in embedding space whatever their truth values. Entailment asks whether A supports B, not whether A and B are about the same thing; a cross-encoder reads both together and can see the 'not'.

q: A document parser extracts 8 fields from each receipt. A team wants at least 90% of receipts to come out with every field correct. Assuming field errors are independent and equally likely, what per-field accuracy do they need?
options: About 98.7%
About 90%
About 95%
About 99.9%
explain: 0.9^(1/8) is about 0.987; a respectable 95% per field gives only 0.95^8, about 66%, fully correct receipts. Field-level and document-level accuracy are different metrics, and the user sees the second.

q: A translation model uses separate BPE vocabularies for English and German. On the source side 'Schweinfurt' comes out as 'Schwein furt', on the target side as 'Sch wein furt'. Training BPE jointly on both languages is the classic fix. What does it buy for names like this?
options: The name becomes a single token in both languages, since joint training doubles the merge budget available for rare strings
The same string is segmented identically on both sides, so copying it is a one-to-one mapping of shared symbols
The model is forced to translate the name instead of copying it, which is more accurate for places
Rare names are removed from both vocabularies and replaced by a shared placeholder token that the decoder copies through
explain: With shared merges, the pieces seen on the source side are exactly the pieces to emit on the target side, and the alignment is trivial. A decoder-only LLM takes this to the limit: one vocabulary for prompt and answer.

q: A word-level model maps the rare compound 'Hundeschlittenrennen' to UNK. A BPE tokenizer splits it into 'Hunde', 'schlitten', 'rennen'. Beyond avoiding the unknown token, what does the split give the model?
options: A guarantee that the word is translated literally, one piece at a time
A record of the word's morpheme boundaries, which BPE is designed to find and which the model needs for German compounding rules
Pieces whose embeddings are trained on many other words, so the rare word inherits representation from frequent material
Three positions in the sequence, which triples the attention the word receives
explain: 'Hunde' and 'rennen' occur all over the corpus, so their vectors are well trained before this compound ever appears. BPE finds frequent strings, not morphemes; here the two happen to coincide.

q: A textbook describes an LLM's input layer as 'the one-hot vector of the token multiplied by a 32,000 by 512 matrix'. What is the result, and why is it implemented as a table lookup?
options: A 32,000-dimensional sparse vector; the lookup avoids storing the one-hot vector in memory
A 512-dimensional vector that already depends on the whole sentence; the lookup caches it once per sentence so that attention can reuse it
A scalar similarity between the token and the matrix; the lookup stores the 32,000 scalars
The 512-dimensional row of the matrix for that token; a one-hot vector selects exactly one row, so indexing is equivalent and cheaper
explain: A one-hot vector picks a row, and the multiplication is just notation for that. The old idea that each discrete symbol owns a learned dense feature vector is unchanged; only the table got bigger.

q: In a corpus, 'Bad' appears in 1 of every 1,024 token positions and 'Neustadt' in 1 of every 1,024 as well. The bigram 'Bad Neustadt' appears once every 4,096 positions. What is the pointwise mutual information of the pair in bits, log2 of P(w1, w2) / (P(w1) P(w2))?
options: 2 bits
8 bits
12 bits
20 bits
explain: P(w1) P(w2) = 2^-20 and P(w1, w2) = 2^-12, so the ratio is 2^8. PMI measures how much more often two words co-occur than independence predicts, and it is the quantity hiding under both co-occurrence embeddings and term weighting.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt searches a ticket archive for 'error E-4711'. The dense retriever returns tickets about errors in general; the BM25 index returns the three tickets that mention E-4711. Why does the sparse method win here?
options: The code is a rare string that the embedding model splits into meaningless pieces, while BM25 matches it exactly with a high idf weight
BM25 recognizes that E-4711 is an error code and boosts it, while dense models are trained only on natural language words and skip such codes
Dense retrievers are case-insensitive and lose the capital E that identifies the code
BM25 indexes the tickets at the character level, so any substring of any ticket can be found
explain: An exact rare token is where lexical matching shines: it is close to unique and idf says so. Hybrid search exists because paraphrases and identifiers are both common in real queries.

q: A tokenizer attaches the preceding space to a word, so ' Würzburg' with a leading space and 'Würzburg' at the start of a text are different tokens. A prompt ends with 'The capital of Lower Franconia is ' including a trailing space. Why can the model's answer get worse than without the trailing space?
options: The trailing space becomes a token of its own, a boundary that rarely occurs in training, where the space belongs to the following word
The trailing space is treated as the end-of-sequence symbol, so the model stops generating
Trailing whitespace is stripped by the tokenizer, so the two prompts are identical and nothing changes
The space increases the token count by one, which pushes the first token of the prompt out of the context window and loses the instruction
explain: In training the model almost always sees ' Würzburg' as one piece; given a lone space token it must produce 'Würzburg' without its usual space, a sequence it barely knows. Prompt formatting bugs of this kind survive every type check.

q: A unigram bag-of-words sentiment classifier is given two reviews: 'not good, quite bad' and 'not bad, quite good'. What does it see, and which cheap feature change fixes it?
options: Two different vectors, since word order changes the counts; no change is needed
Two identical vectors, since both reviews contain the same words once each; adding bigram features separates 'not good' from 'not bad'
Two identical vectors; raising the regularization strength lets the classifier weight 'good' and 'bad' differently and so learn the difference
Two vectors that differ only in sign; using TF-IDF weights instead of raw counts fixes it
explain: Same four words, same counts, same vector. Bigrams put negation back into the representation; it is the smallest step away from a pure bag.

q: A BPE vocabulary of 32,000 covers the frequent words as single tokens. On news text, 90% of running words are such whole-token words and the remaining 10% split into 3 pieces on average. On chemistry text only 70% of words are whole tokens, the rest also 3 pieces each. How much more does a word of chemistry text cost in tokens, on average?
options: About 20% more
About 33% more
About 60% more
About 3 times as much
explain: News: 0.9 * 1 + 0.1 * 3 = 1.2 tokens per word. Chemistry: 0.7 + 0.9 = 1.6, and 1.6 / 1.2 is 1.33. Merges follow corpus frequency, so a domain full of rare words pays per token for the Zipfian tail.

q: Character-level BPE trained on English and German text has no symbol for a Georgian letter, so such text became UNK. A byte-level tokenizer, or one with byte fallback, encodes any Georgian text without an unknown token. For a model pretrained mostly on Latin-script text, what does this change and what does it not?
options: Every string becomes encodable and, since all 256 byte values were seen in pretraining, the model handles Georgian about as well as it handles German or English
Nothing changes in practice, since the model still emits an unknown token for byte sequences it has not seen in training
Georgian is encoded in one token per character by looking up the Unicode code point directly in the vocabulary
Every string becomes encodable, but a Georgian character costs about three byte tokens and the model has little training signal for them, so encodable is not understood
explain: Byte fallback removed the UNK failure mode and replaced it with a slow, expensive, under-trained one. The rare-word problem that subwords were invented for has become a rare-script problem.

q: A user's query contains the misspelling 'Wurzbrg', which occurs in exactly one document of a 100,000-document collection, also as a typo. With TF-IDF or BM25 scoring the query, what happens, and which classic pathology of co-occurrence statistics is this?
options: The term is ignored because its df is below the default minimum of two; the same way PMI is undefined for words seen once
The term gets idf zero because it never co-occurs with the other query terms in any document of the collection; the same way PMI is zero for independent words
The term gets the highest idf in the query and that one document is pushed to the top; the same way raw PMI is largest for pairs of words seen once
The term is corrected by the index because idf is computed on stemmed forms; the same way PMI is computed on lemmas
explain: Low counts produce extreme statistics, whether the statistic is idf or PMI, and both treat a one-off as maximally informative. Spelling correction, minimum frequency cutoffs and PMI shifts or smoothing are the same fix wearing different clothes.

q: A team fine-tunes a chat model with a template that marks turns with '<|user|>' and '<|assistant|>'. They forgot to register these as special tokens, so the tokenizer splits them into ordinary pieces like '<', '|', 'user', '|', '>'. Training runs without error. What is the practical consequence?
options: None in practice; the model learns the character sequence as a delimiter, and after convergence the result is equivalent to having registered a special token
The model fails to converge because the pieces of a delimiter cannot be embedded consistently
The delimiter is just text the model learned to imitate: a user can type the same characters to forge an assistant turn, and the special token embeddings go unused
The pieces are automatically merged into one token after the first epoch, once the model has seen them often enough
explain: A special token is atomic and cannot be produced by typing; a string of ordinary pieces can. Chat template mismatches between training and inference are among the most common and least visible fine-tuning bugs.

q: Two language models are compared on the same English text. Model A reports perplexity 12 per token with a tokenizer that produces 1.2 tokens per word. Model B reports perplexity 8 per token with 2.0 tokens per word. Which model predicts the text better, measured per word?
options: B, with 3 bits per token against about 3.6
They are equal, since perplexity already normalizes for tokenization
B, with per-word perplexity 16 against 24
A, with about 4.3 bits per word against 6
explain: log2(12) is about 3.58 bits per token, times 1.2 is 4.3 bits per word; log2(8) = 3 times 2.0 is 6 bits per word. Per-token perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers; bits per word or per byte is.

q: A project team measures tokenizer fertility as tokens per whitespace-separated word and reports English 1.3, German 1.9, Chinese 9.5. Why is the Chinese figure not comparable, and what is a fair way to compare?
options: Chinese has no whitespace between words, so the denominator counts clauses or whole sentences; tokenize the same content in each language, for example a parallel corpus, and compare total tokens

Chinese characters are not supported by most tokenizers, so most of them became unknown or byte-fallback tokens; switch to a tokenizer trained on Chinese only and repeat the measurement on the same text
The Chinese figure is correct and shows that Chinese is about seven times more expensive than English for this tokenizer
Fertility should be measured as tokens per UTF-8 byte, which makes all scripts equal and removes the need for a word count or a parallel corpus
explain: The denominator is the problem, not the numerator. On translated content, Chinese usually does cost more tokens than English with English-heavy tokenizers, but far less than sevenfold; and bytes do not equalize scripts either, since a Chinese character is three of them.

q: A byte-level model's output is streamed to a browser one token at a time, each token decoded to text as it arrives. The word 'Würzburg' briefly shows a garbage character where the 'ü' should be, then corrects itself. What is going on?
options: The 'ü' is encoded as two bytes that landed in two different tokens, so the first token alone is an invalid UTF-8 fragment until the second arrives
The model first predicted the wrong letter and then revised it with a backspace-like correction token, which streaming interfaces apply as soon as it arrives
The browser's font lacks the character and falls back to a placeholder until the font has loaded
The tokenizer normalizes 'ü' to 'u' plus a combining accent, and the browser renders the base letter first and the accent one step late
explain: Byte-level tokens do not respect character boundaries. Decode with a buffer that waits for a complete UTF-8 sequence, or you will ship a model that visibly stutters on every umlaut.
