q: Skip-gram with negative sampling, at its optimum, makes the dot product of a word and a context equal PMI(w, c) minus log k. A dense retriever is trained with a contrastive loss in which the other documents in the batch act as negatives. By the same style of argument, what does its query-document score estimate at the optimum, up to a constant?
options: The probability that the document is relevant to the query, directly usable as a confidence because the softmax over the batch is normalized
The cosine similarity between the human-written query and a summary of the document
The log ratio of how likely the document is given the query to how likely it is in general, a PMI-like quantity
The number of query terms that appear in the document, as in a lexical model, since in-batch negatives reward term overlap
explain: Contrastive objectives against sampled negatives recover a density ratio, log P(d | q) / P(d), not a calibrated relevance probability. Retrieval scores therefore rank well and read badly as confidences, and documents that are popular everywhere get discounted.

q: The classic objection to neural language models was the cost of the softmax over the whole vocabulary at every step. Take a small modern model: 500 million parameters in the transformer blocks, vocabulary 128,000, hidden size 4,096, input and output embeddings tied. The input lookup is free; the blocks and the output projection each cost about 2 floating point operations per parameter per token, and attention scores are ignored. Roughly what share of the per-token compute goes to the output projection?
options: About 5%
About 25%
About 50%
About 90%
explain: 128,000 * 4,096 is about 524 million parameters, roughly equal to the blocks, so the output layer is about half of the work. The objection never went away; it is just invisible for large models, where the blocks dwarf the vocabulary.

q: A single BPE tokenizer is trained on a mix of 90% English and 10% German text with a fixed merge budget. German ends up with far higher fertility than English. What determines the split of the merge budget between the languages, and what happens if the team upsamples German to 50% for tokenizer training only?
options: Merges are split evenly between the languages by the algorithm itself, so the fertility gap comes from German compounding and inflection alone and upsampling changes nothing
Merges go to whichever language has more characters per word, so German already gets most of them and upsampling to 50% would make English fertility collapse
The budget is not shared at all, since each language gets its own merge list inside one vocabulary file, so upsampling only changes the file order
Merges go to the most frequent pairs in the mix, so the minority language gets few; upsampling gives German more merges and lower fertility, English slightly higher fertility
explain: BPE is frequency-greedy and does not know what a language is; the effect that gives English rare words long segmentations gives minority languages long segmentations everywhere. Rebalancing the tokenizer's training data is cheap; retraining the model for a new tokenizer is not.

q: A hybrid search fuses BM25 and dense rankings with reciprocal rank fusion: each list contributes 1 / (60 + rank). Document X is ranked 1 by BM25 and 10 by the dense retriever. Document Y is ranked 3 by both. Which document is ranked higher after fusion?
options: X, with about 1.10 against about 0.67
Y, with about 0.0317 against about 0.0307
They tie, since 1/61 + 1/70 equals 2/63 within rounding
X, with about 0.0307 against about 0.0159
explain: X: 1/61 + 1/70 = 0.0307. Y: 2/63 = 0.0317. The constant 60 flattens the difference between rank 1 and rank 10, so consistent agreement between retrievers beats one spectacular hit; that is the design intent, and the constant is tunable.

q: A code completion model is prompted with a file ending in 'def calc_' and performs clearly worse than when the prompt ends in 'def calc'. In the training data, the underscore was almost always merged by BPE with what followed it, as in 'calc_total'. What explains the drop, and what is the standard fix?
options: The underscore is treated as a stopword that the tokenizer drops at the end of a prompt, so the model never sees it; escape it with a backslash so that it is kept
The model treats a trailing underscore as the end of the function name; add a space after it so the name is complete
The model has learned that identifiers ending in an underscore are private helpers; rename the function before prompting
The prompt ends on a boundary that BPE never produces for the full text, so the model is in a state it rarely saw; back up one token and constrain generation to continue it
explain: BPE segments a text greedily from its merge list; cutting the text mid-merge creates a boundary that training never produced. Token healing restores the natural segmentation by letting the model regenerate the last piece under a prefix constraint.

q: A bag-of-words model uses the hashing trick with 2^16 = 65,536 buckets instead of a vocabulary dictionary. A long document contains 1,000 distinct words. Treating the hash as uniform, about how many pairs of these words collide into the same bucket within this document?
options: About 8
About 0.1
About 64
About 500
explain: There are 1,000 * 999 / 2 = 499,500 pairs and each collides with probability 1 / 65,536: about 7.6 pairs. Hashing saves the vocabulary file and handles unseen words, and this is the price: usually acceptable, never zero.

q: Shannon built n-gram approximations to English: an order-n source in which each letter depends on the previous n - 1 letters. A decoder-only LLM predicts each token from at most the 4,095 tokens before it. In Shannon's terms, what kind of source is it?
options: A Markov source of order 4,095 over tokens, with transition probabilities computed by a network rather than stored in a table
A zero-order source over tokens, since each token is drawn independently from the softmax distribution at its position
A source of unbounded order, since the model also conditions on everything it generated in earlier conversations
A first-order Markov source, since each token depends only on the hidden state at the previous position
explain: Beyond the window the model is blind, so it is a finite-order Markov source; the order is simply enormous and the table is replaced by a function. Shannon's order-3 samples read 'IN NO IST LAT WHEY'; order 4,095 reads like your inbox.

q: Shannon's n-gram approximations: as the order grows, the samples move from 'XFOML RXKHRJFFJUJ' through 'ON IE ANTSOUTINYS' to 'IN NO IST LAT WHEY'. Alongside he defined F_n, the conditional entropy of a letter given the previous n - 1 letters. How does F_n behave as n grows, and what is its limit?
options: It increases, since longer contexts make more letter combinations possible, and it tends to log2(27)
It decreases, since extra context can only remove uncertainty, and it tends to the entropy rate of the source
It stays constant, since letter frequencies do not change with context, and it equals the unigram entropy
It decreases to exactly zero, since with enough context the next letter is fully determined
explain: Conditioning never increases entropy, so F_n is non-increasing and converges to the per-letter entropy rate. A language model's loss plotted against context length is the same picture drawn with a GPU.

q: An unsmoothed 5-gram model assigns probability zero to 'the dog was running in the kitchen' because that sequence of 5-grams never occurred, although 'the cat was walking in the bedroom' did. A neural language model gives the new sentence a reasonable probability. Which mechanism makes the difference?
options: The neural model backs off to shorter n-grams whenever the full five-word context was never seen in the training data
The neural model stores every training sentence and returns the probability of the stored sentence that is closest in edit distance
Similar words get similar feature vectors, and the probability is a smooth function of those vectors, so nearby inputs give nearby outputs
The neural model splits unseen words into bytes, so no sequence can ever receive probability zero
explain: 'dog' sits near 'cat' and 'kitchen' near 'bedroom' in feature space, so the learned function carries the probability across. The same shared embedding table is still the first layer of every transformer.

q: A character-level model reaches 1.9 bits per character on a text written in a 32-symbol alphabet (log2(32) = 5). Shannon's redundancy is 1 minus the ratio of the achieved entropy to the maximum possible entropy. What is the redundancy of this text under the model?
explain: 1 - 1.9/5 = 0.62. Three fifths of the symbols are, from a coding point of view, filler; from a reader's point of view they are what makes typos survivable.

q: The same LLM scores perplexity 6 on a corpus of Python code and perplexity 30 on a corpus of modern poetry. A startup founder concludes that the model 'understands code five times better than poetry'. What is the correct reading?
options: The founder is right: perplexity is a pure measure of model quality, and lower always means better understanding of the domain
The comparison is invalid, since perplexity can only be compared between two models on one text, never for one model on two texts
Poetry contains more rare tokens, and perplexity mainly counts how many tokens fall outside the vocabulary
Perplexity measures the text as much as the model; poetry is intrinsically less predictable, so even an ideal model scores higher on it
explain: Cross-entropy is the entropy of the source plus the model's gap to it. Boilerplate is cheap to predict; a poet who was predictable would be out of a job.

q: A model's next-token distribution gives exactly 0.5 to each of two tokens and zero to all others, an entropy of 1 bit. You apply temperature 0.5 to the logits before the softmax. What is the entropy of the sampling distribution now?
options: 1 bit
0.5 bit
2 bits
0 bits
explain: Dividing the logits by a constant keeps equal logits equal, so the two tokens still share the mass evenly. Temperature sharpens differences between logits; where there is no difference there is nothing to sharpen.

q: A lexical index covers 1,024 documents. 'tram' occurs in 16 of them, 'the' in all 1,024. With inverse document frequency defined as log2(N / df), what are the two idf values, and what does the quantity measure?
options: 64 and 1; the number of documents a query for the term returns on average
16 and 1,024; the count of documents that contain the term at least once
6 and 0; the surprise, in bits, of finding the term in a randomly drawn document
4 and 10; the expected number of occurrences of the term per document
explain: log2(1,024/16) = log2(64) = 6, and log2(1) = 0. A term found everywhere tells you nothing about which document you are in, which is why BM25 pays 'the' nothing and 'tram' six bits.

q: A character model has an entropy rate of 1 bit per character over a 27-letter alphabet. Consider all 27^100 strings of length 100. Roughly how many of them are 'typical' under the model, and what probability does each carry?
options: About 27^100 / 2 strings, each with probability close to 2 x 27^-100, since half the alphabet is redundant
About 100 x 27 strings, each with probability close to 1/2,700, one per letter position and symbol
About 2^475 strings, each with probability close to 2^-475, since log2(27) is about 4.75
About 2^100 strings, each with probability close to 2^-100, and together they carry almost all the mass
explain: Asymptotic equipartition: a long sequence from a source of rate H almost surely has probability about 2^(-nH), and about 2^(nH) such sequences exist. 2^475 counts all strings; the model considers nearly all of them absurd.

q: A multilingual LLM is scored in bits per byte on UTF-8 text: 1.0 on English and 0.6 on Russian. English letters take one byte each; Cyrillic letters take two. A colleague at the conference bar concludes the model predicts Russian better. Per character, what are the numbers?
options: English 1.0 bits per character, Russian 0.3, so Russian is indeed predicted better
English 1.0 bits per character, Russian 1.2, so Russian costs more per letter
Both 1.0 bits per character, since bits per byte already normalizes for the script
English 2.0 bits per character, Russian 0.6, since English needs more bytes per word
explain: Bits per character equals bits per byte times bytes per character: 0.6 x 2 = 1.2. Bits per byte flatters two-byte scripts, bits per token flatters whoever has the fattest tokenizer; pick a unit and say which.

q: In the first neural language models the softmax over the vocabulary dominated the compute. Take a decoder with 7 billion non-embedding parameters, d_model = 4,096 and a vocabulary of 128,000, with a forward pass costing about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token. Roughly what share of the forward FLOPs per token goes to the unembedding (logit) layer?
options: About 7%
About 25%
About 50%
Over 90%
explain: The logit layer has 4,096 x 128,000, about 5.2 x 10^8 weights, against 7 x 10^9 in the body, so roughly 1 in 14. Bengio's bottleneck is still there; it just stopped being the largest item on the bill, except in small models, where it still is.

q: You flag every test item of a benchmark that shares a 13-token span with your pretraining data: 40% of the items are flagged. Your model scores 80% on the flagged items and 78% on the clean ones. What does this analysis support?
options: The model memorized the 40% flagged items, so the true score is the clean 78% and the benchmark must be dropped
The two-point gap proves memorization of exactly 2% of the items, which should be subtracted from the result
Contamination moved the headline score by at most about a point here, so the result stands, with a note
The analysis is uninformative, since any overlap at all means the whole benchmark is compromised
explain: If memorization drove the score, the flagged subset would stand out; a two-point gap on a 40% slice shifts the overall mean by under a point. Overlap detection finds the exposure, the subset comparison measures the harm.

q: You evaluate the perplexity of a model with a 1,024-token window on a 100,000-token document. Method A cuts the document into non-overlapping 1,024-token chunks and scores each independently. Method B slides the window with a stride of 512 and scores only the last 512 tokens at each position. Which reports the lower perplexity, and why?
options: Method A, since fewer forward passes mean less accumulated numerical error in the summed log-probabilities of the document
Both give the same number, since the model assigns a token the same probability wherever the chunk boundary falls, as long as the window is full
Method A, since Method B scores some tokens twice and inflates the token count in the denominator
Method B, since every scored token has at least 512 tokens of context, while Method A scores the first tokens of each chunk nearly blind
explain: A token right after a hard cut is predicted from nothing, and a few of those per chunk add up. Method B costs twice the compute and is the honest number; a stride of 1 would be the honest and unaffordable one.

q: A hallucination detector scores answers by the probability the model assigned to them. Answer A has 10 tokens, each with probability 0.9; answer B has 2 tokens, each with probability 0.7. Which answer gets the higher sequence probability, and which the higher per-token confidence?
options: Sequence probability: A; per-token confidence: A
Sequence probability: B; per-token confidence: A
Sequence probability: A; per-token confidence: B
Sequence probability: B; per-token confidence: B
explain: 0.9^10 is about 0.35, below 0.7^2 = 0.49, yet A is the more confident answer token by token. Raw sequence probability is a length penalty in disguise; normalize per token, or use perplexity, before comparing answers of different lengths.

q: A naive Bayes spam filter with equal class priors has word likelihoods P(free | spam) = 0.2, P(free | ham) = 0.01, P(meeting | spam) = 0.01 and P(meeting | ham) = 0.1. The message is 'free meeting'. What posterior probability of spam does the filter give?
options: About 0.5
About 0.95
About 0.67
About 0.33
explain: Spam: 0.2 x 0.01 = 0.002; ham: 0.01 x 0.1 = 0.001; normalized, 2/3. Twenty lines of code, and surprisingly often the baseline the roadshow demo fails to beat on F1 per euro.

q: A source emits two symbols. From either symbol, the next one is the same symbol with probability 0.9 and the other with probability 0.1, so each symbol appears half the time overall. One compressor codes symbols by their overall frequencies, another by the conditional probabilities. In bits per symbol, what are the unigram entropy and the entropy rate? (log2(0.9) is about -0.152, log2(0.1) about -3.32.)
options: Unigram entropy 1.0; entropy rate about 0.47
Unigram entropy 1.0; entropy rate 1.0, since the stationary distribution is uniform
Unigram entropy about 0.47; entropy rate about 0.47, since both describe the same source
Unigram entropy 1.0; entropy rate about 0.1, the probability of a switch
explain: 0.9 x 0.152 + 0.1 x 3.32 = 0.137 + 0.332, about 0.47 bits. The marginal is uniform and hides all the structure; the entropy rate is what a Markov-aware coder, or a language model, actually pays.

q: A paper reports that an LLM with arithmetic coding compresses a 10 MB English text to 0.8 bits per character, beating a general-purpose compressor at 2.2 bits per character, and concludes that the LLM is the better compressor. Reviewer #2 objects. What is the legitimate objection?
options: Arithmetic coding is lossy while the general-purpose compressor is lossless, so the two figures measure different things and cannot be placed side by side
Perplexity and compression are unrelated quantities, so bits per character from a language model is not a compression figure
A general-purpose compressor adapts to the file while the LLM does not, so the LLM figure must be reported on its training data instead
The decoder needs the model's parameters, far larger than 10 MB; the comparison holds only if the model is amortized over far more data or counted in the total
explain: Compression is prediction, but the description length includes whatever the receiver must hold to decode. A model of several gigabytes that saves a few megabytes has not compressed anything; across a corpus of terabytes it has.

q: Every LLM computes its logits as h W^T + b, with h the final hidden state of dimension d and W the V x d unembedding matrix, exactly as the first neural LM did. Write the true next-token log-probabilities for every possible context as a matrix with one row per context and V columns. What limitation does this output layer impose?
options: The model can only represent distributions with at most d nonzero entries, so in each context most of the vocabulary receives exactly zero probability and must be smoothed
The model cannot represent any distribution whose entropy exceeds log2(d), since the hidden state carries only d numbers
The model's version of that matrix has rank at most about d + 1, so with d far below V some sets of context-dependent distributions cannot be represented exactly
There is no limitation: the softmax can produce any distribution over V tokens as long as the training data contains it
explain: Log-probabilities are a d-dimensional linear map plus a per-row normalizer, so the matrix has rank at most d + 1, while language plausibly needs more. This is the softmax bottleneck; mixtures of softmaxes and simply larger d are the known ways around it.

q: On a benchmark, the test items that overlap with your pretraining data score 15 points higher than the items with no overlap. Reviewer #2 says this proves that memorization inflated the result. Why is the inference not conclusive on its own?
options: A 13-token overlap filter detects only exact duplicates, so the flagged items are surely memorized and the real question is how many unflagged items were paraphrased
Items found on the web are not a random sample of the test set: famous, canonical or easy questions are copied more often, so difficulty is confounded with exposure
Benchmark scores are only valid on the full set, so any subset comparison is statistically meaningless whatever the gap, unless the subsets are of equal size
Memorization would show up as lower, not higher, scores on overlapping items, since the model reproduces the web text instead of answering
explain: The dirty subset is selected by a property correlated with difficulty, so the gap mixes two effects. Cleaner tests compare against a model that never saw the overlapping data, or check whether the model can complete the test items verbatim.

q: On a held-out text an instruction-tuned model's average cross-entropy is 2.1 bits per token, while the average entropy of its own next-token distributions at the same positions is 1.5 bits. What does the gap indicate?
options: The model is underconfident: its distributions are flatter than the text requires, since entropy below cross-entropy means hedging
Nothing: a model's predictive entropy is a property of the model alone and is unrelated to how it is scored on text
The tokenizer is mismatched to the text, since entropy and cross-entropy can only differ when tokens are split differently
The model is overconfident: it spreads less mass than its accuracy justifies; for a calibrated model the two averages would agree in expectation
explain: If the model's probabilities were calibrated, the expected surprise at the true token would equal the model's own entropy; paying 2.1 while betting as if 1.5 is overconfidence. Post-training tends to sharpen distributions, so this gap is common after RLHF.

q: You flag hallucinations by the entropy of an LLM's sampled answers. On the question 'Which city hosts the Oktoberfest?' the samples are 'Munich', 'München', 'the Bavarian capital, Munich' and 'Munich, Germany', so the string-level entropy is high and a correct answer is flagged. What is the principled fix?
options: Cluster the samples by mutual entailment and compute the entropy over meaning clusters rather than over strings
Lower the sampling temperature until the samples agree, then recompute the entropy over the strings
Score only the first token of each sample, since the entropy of the opening word carries the uncertainty
Replace entropy with the sequence probability of the single greedy answer, which is immune to paraphrase
explain: Several surface forms, one meaning: the uncertainty you care about is over what is claimed, not how it is spelled. Lowering the temperature hides real disagreement too, and the greedy sequence probability drops with every token of a long correct answer.

q: A team trains word vectors on a corpus of repair manuals full of rare part names. They can use CBOW (predict the center word from the averaged context) or skip-gram (predict each context word from the center word). Which choice usually gives better vectors for the rare terms, and why?
options: Skip-gram: each occurrence of a rare word is the input for several predictions, so its vector gets several dedicated updates
CBOW: averaging the context vectors smooths the noise around a rare word, so its vector converges in fewer passes over the data
CBOW: the rare word is predicted from frequent context words, so its vector directly inherits their well-estimated statistics
Neither: both objectives update the same vectors with the same gradients and differ only in training speed
explain: In CBOW a rare word mostly appears as one summand in an averaged context, diluted among frequent neighbours. Skip-gram puts it in the driver's seat for every window it occurs in, at the price of more training steps.

q: word2vec first merges frequent collocations such as 'New York' and 'Air Canada' into single tokens before training. Why not simply add vec(New) and vec(York) afterwards?
options: Addition would produce a vector whose norm is roughly twice that of a single word, which breaks cosine similarity against ordinary words
The phrase's contexts (airports, Broadway) are not the sum of the contexts of 'new' and 'York', so only a token of its own learns them
Vector addition is only meaningful for words of the same part of speech, and 'New' is an adjective while 'York' is a proper noun
The merge is only a speed trick: fewer tokens means fewer training pairs, and the vectors come out identical either way
explain: Non-compositional phrases are the point. Subword tokenizers in LLMs make the opposite bet, splitting 'Würzburg' into pieces and trusting the network to reassemble it; both are choices about where composition should live.

q: GloVe fits w_i . w_j + b_i + b_j to log X_ij, the natural log of the co-occurrence count. Pair A co-occurs 1,000 times, pair B 10 times. At a perfect fit, by how much does the fitted score of pair A exceed that of pair B?
options: About 4.6
explain: ln(1,000) - ln(10) = ln(100), about 4.6. Fitting log counts turns a hundredfold difference in counts into a modest additive difference in geometry, which is what lets a dot product carry it.

q: You freeze a deep bidirectional language model and train two small probes on its layers: one for part-of-speech tags, one for word sense disambiguation. Which layers tend to serve which task best?
options: Upper layers for part of speech, lower layers for word sense; the model resolves meaning first and grammar last
The top layer for both, since each layer strictly refines the one below it and nothing is lost
The embedding layer for both, since the deeper layers of a frozen model are specific to the pretraining objective
Lower layers for part of speech, upper layers for word sense; representations move from form toward meaning with depth
explain: This is the pattern that motivated learning a per-task mixture of layers instead of taking the top one. Probing transformers finds the same drift, with the last layer or two often bending back toward predicting the next token.

q: A startup founder needs a retrieval embedding and reasons that bigger is better: she mean-pools the last hidden layer of a 7-billion-parameter chat model, with no further training, instead of using a 100-million-parameter model trained on sentence pairs. On a retrieval benchmark, what should she expect?
options: The large model wins by a wide margin, since its hidden states encode more knowledge per dimension
The small trained model wins, since nothing in next-token pretraining asks cosine between pooled states to track relevance
A tie, since both produce dense vectors of comparable dimension and cosine does not care which network produced them
The large model wins on long documents only, since its context window is longer and the small model truncates them
explain: Size cannot substitute for the objective. Large decoders do become excellent embedders, after a contrastive stage with pairs and negatives, which is exactly the part she skipped.

q: A hybrid search adds the raw BM25 score (typically between 0 and 30 on this index) to the raw cosine similarity from a dense model (between -1 and 1) and ranks by the sum. What is the predictable outcome?
options: The dense component dominates, since cosine is a normalized quantity and BM25 is an unbounded raw score
The two components contribute equally, since both are monotone in relevance and the sum preserves monotonicity
The lexical component dominates and the dense score is a tie-breaker, so the system behaves like BM25
The sum is undefined because cosine can be negative while BM25 cannot
explain: A unit of cosine is worth a unit of BM25 only by accident of scale. Normalize each score list, by min-max or z-scores, or fuse by rank, as reciprocal rank fusion does.

q: A search system holds 1 million documents and receives 1,000 queries. A bi-encoder embeds queries and documents separately and compares vectors; a cross-encoder reads each (query, document) pair through the network. How many encoder forward passes does each need to score every query against every document?
options: Bi-encoder about 1,001,000; cross-encoder 10^9
Bi-encoder 10^9; cross-encoder about 1,001,000
Both 10^9, since every pair must be scored either way
Both about 1,001,000, since the cross-encoder caches document encodings
explain: One million documents once plus one pass per query, against a thousand times a million pairs. Hence the standard design: retrieve a few hundred candidates with the bi-encoder, rerank them with the cross-encoder, and watch the latency budget vanish into the second step.

q: Skip-gram with negative sampling scores a (word, context) pair with log sigmoid(w . c) and each of k negatives with log sigmoid(-w . c_neg). At initialization all dot products are zero and k = 5. What is the loss per training pair, in bits, and what does the number mean?
options: 1 bit: one binary decision between the positive and the negatives
log2(V) bits: the cost of a uniform guess over the vocabulary
5 bits: one per negative, since the positive term is zero
6 bits: six binary decisions, each at chance
explain: sigmoid(0) = 0.5, so each of the six terms costs -log2(0.5) = 1 bit. The objective replaces one V-way softmax by k + 1 coin flips, which is why the output layer stopped being the bottleneck.

q: In a skip-gram space, vec(Russia) + vec(river) lands near vec(Volga), and vec(Germany) + vec(capital) near vec(Berlin). Which property of the training objective makes plain addition work as a rough 'and'?
options: The objective is linear in its input, so the embedding of a two-word phrase equals the embedding the model would assign to the words written together
Word vectors are roughly linear in the log-probabilities of their contexts, so adding two vectors multiplies the context distributions and favours contexts likely under both
Negative sampling draws pairs of words together as negatives, so the sum of any two word vectors is explicitly trained to predict their shared neighbours and avoid the sampled ones
The vectors are unit length, so addition is equivalent to taking the midpoint, which is the word most similar to both
explain: A product of distributions is an intersection of contexts: things that go with Russia and with rivers. The trick is fragile and works best for frequent, unambiguous words, which is also why the famous examples are chosen with care.

q: GloVe weights each co-occurrence cell by f(x) = (x / x_max)^alpha for x below x_max and 1 above, with alpha = 3/4 and x_max = 100. A cell with count 1 and a cell with count 10,000 both appear in the loss. What are their weights, and why this shape?
options: About 0.03 and 1; rare co-occurrences are noisy and should count little, and very frequent ones should not dominate
0.01 and 100; the weight should be proportional to the count so that frequent pairs are fitted exactly
About 0.03 and about 31.6; the power law continues above x_max and rewards frequent pairs
1 and 1; every observed co-occurrence is one piece of evidence and should weigh the same, otherwise the factorization is biased toward frequent words
explain: (1/100)^0.75 = 10^-1.5, about 0.032, and anything above x_max is capped at 1. The same instinct appears as subsampling in word2vec: frequent evidence is cheap, and too much of it is a bias.

q: Instead of training skip-gram, you build the word-context PMI matrix explicitly and factorize it with SVD. Most cells are zero co-occurrences, where PMI = log(0) = -infinity. What is the standard fix, and what does it cost?
options: Replace the zeros by a small constant such as 10^-9, which keeps every cell finite and the matrix dense enough for a stable SVD
Clip at zero (positive PMI), keeping the matrix sparse; the information in 'these words avoid each other' is discarded
Drop every word that has any zero cell, which keeps the matrix exact and shrinks the vocabulary
Add the shift log k to every cell, which pushes all values above zero and makes the matrix dense
explain: PPMI is the usual explicit counterpart of what negative sampling learns implicitly, and sparsity is what makes the SVD affordable. Negative associations are mostly unreliable at low counts anyway, so the loss is smaller than it sounds.

q: An early neural tagger pretrained its lookup-table embeddings with a ranking objective: score the true text window higher than a corrupted window whose middle word is replaced by a random word, with hinge loss max(0, 1 - s(true) + s(corrupt)). With s(true) = 3, what losses do corrupted windows scoring 2.5 and 1.0 produce, and what does the objective share with negative sampling?
options: 0.5 and 0; both compute a softmax over the whole vocabulary but update only the parameters of the true word
1.5 and 3.0; both need every word in the vocabulary scored for each window before any update can be made
0.5 and 0; both avoid normalizing over the vocabulary by contrasting the observed word with sampled impostors
0 and 0; both update only when the corrupted window scores strictly higher than the true one, so a correct ranking costs nothing
explain: max(0, 1 - 3 + 2.5) = 0.5 and max(0, 1 - 3 + 1) = 0. A margin instead of a sigmoid, but the same economics: cheap contrast with impostors, and no probability over V ever computed.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt builds search over a knowledge base with a sentence-embedding model trained on paraphrase pairs. Users type short questions; the system keeps returning other users' questions and FAQ titles instead of the passages that answer them. What is the mismatch?
options: The model is symmetric: trained to match texts that say the same thing, it puts a question closest to another question; relevance is asymmetric and needs query-passage training
The passages are too long, so their vectors are dominated by their most frequent words and lose under cosine against short texts; truncating passages to question length fixes it
The questions are too short to embed reliably, so the model falls back on lexical overlap with titles; padding the queries with stop words fixes it
The index mixes titles and passages, and shorter texts always score higher under cosine; removing the titles fixes it
explain: Paraphrase similarity and relevance are different relations. Retrieval-trained models, often with a query-side instruction prefix, learn that 'how do I reset the router' should live next to the paragraph that explains it, not next to its twin.

q: You have an English-only embedding model that works well and a few hundred thousand English-German sentence pairs, but no German retrieval labels. You train a multilingual student so that student(English) and student(German translation) both match the frozen teacher's vector for the English sentence. What does this produce, and what does it not guarantee?
options: A German model whose space is independent of the English one, so monolingual German search works but cross-lingual search does not; no guarantee that German similarity scores are on the same scale
A translation model, since the student learns to map German sentences onto English ones token by token; no guarantee that the outputs are fluent English
A better English model, since the German pairs act as data augmentation for the teacher; no guarantee that any German capability appears at all
A German model aligned with the English space, so a German query finds English documents and vice versa; no guarantee on German text whose style the parallel data never covered
explain: Translations are forced onto the same point, so the languages share one geometry without a single relevance label in German. The student inherits the teacher's strengths and the parallel corpus's blind spots, which for most pairs means parliament and subtitles.

q: At the optimum of skip-gram with negative sampling, w . c equals PMI(w, c) minus ln k. A modern bi-encoder is trained with the InfoNCE loss on cosine similarities divided by a temperature of 0.05, and at its optimum the scaled similarity equals ln of p(d | q) / p(d) up to a per-query constant. By how much must the cosine between a query and a document rise for the implied PMI to increase by one nat?
explain: cos / 0.05 tracks PMI, so one nat of association is worth 0.05 of cosine. The temperature decides how much of the [-1, 1] range an e-fold association occupies; the shift ln k and the per-query constant are the two objectives' versions of the same normalizer.

q: A paper tunes GloVe (window, x_max, alpha, learning rate) on a development set and compares it with word2vec at default settings; GloVe wins by 3 points on word similarity. Given that negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix built from the same co-occurrence counts, what does Reviewer #2 ask for?
options: Equal tuning of both, including window, subsampling, negatives and context distribution smoothing, since these transfer across methods and explain gaps of this size
A larger corpus, since count-based methods need more data than predictive ones to converge to the same solution, which hides the difference at small scale
A comparison on analogies only, since word similarity is itself a count-based task and therefore favours GloVe by construction
A proof that SVD of the PMI matrix beats both, since an exact factorization dominates an approximate one and makes the comparison moot
explain: Once both methods are seen as factorizing nearly the same statistics, the paradigm label stops explaining much and the preprocessing choices do. 'Count versus predict' was largely a hyperparameter debate wearing a theory costume.

q: In the top layer of a contextual encoder, vectors of the word 'bank' taken from 1,000 different sentences have an average pairwise cosine of 0.85. A student at 3 a.m. concludes that the layer barely adapts the word to its context. What measurement is missing, and how could it reverse the conclusion?
options: The cosine between 'bank' in the top layer and 'bank' in the embedding layer; if it is low, the top layer has moved far from the static vector and is contextual
The norm of the 'bank' vectors across sentences; if the norms vary widely, cosine understates the real variation and the top layer is far more contextual than the 0.85 figure alone suggests
The cosine between 'bank' and 'river' in the top layer; if it exceeds 0.85, the model has fused the two senses and the layer is contextual in the wrong way
The average cosine between unrelated words in the same layer; if it is around 0.8, 'bank' varies with context nearly as much as unrelated words differ, so the layer is strongly contextual
explain: Upper layers are anisotropic: everything is close to everything, so a raw 0.85 says little. Self-similarity minus the random-pair baseline is the honest statistic, and in upper layers it tends to be small.

q: A dedup step marks two product descriptions as near-duplicates when their embedding cosine exceeds 0.9, then merges duplicate pairs into groups with union-find and keeps one text per group. After the run, one group holds 400 descriptions covering unrelated products. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: The threshold was too high, so too few pairs were merged and the remaining groups became unbalanced; lowering it to 0.8 spreads the merges more evenly across groups
Near-duplication is not transitive: chains A~B, B~C, C~D with every link above 0.9 join texts whose direct similarity is far lower; compare against a group representative, not any one member
Cosine is not a proper metric, so union-find over cosine pairs is ill-defined; replace it by Euclidean distance on the same normalized vectors and rerun the merge with the same threshold
The embedding model is anisotropic, so all 400 texts had cosine above 0.9 with each other; switch to lexical MinHash dedup, whose Jaccard estimates cannot chain in this way
explain: Single-linkage clustering with a threshold is a chain reaction waiting for a template. Comparing against a centroid or demanding complete linkage stops the creep; MinHash chains in exactly the same way if you union its pairs.

q: You fine-tune a bi-encoder on question-passage pairs from a forum where each question has one marked 'accepted answer'. For hard negatives you take the top-10 passages the current model retrieves for each question, excluding the accepted one. Retrieval quality on a held-out set gets worse with each round of mining. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hard negatives are too easy, since the current model already ranks them below the accepted answer and gets no gradient from them
The accepted answers are systematically longer than other posts, so the model learns to prefer long passages regardless of content
Many mined 'negatives' are unlabelled correct answers, so the model learns to push relevant passages away from their questions
Top-10 mining produces too few negatives per question for the contrastive loss to work, so the in-batch negatives dominate and the signal is noise
explain: One accepted answer does not mean one correct answer; a forum thread has several. False negatives are the standard trap of self-mined hard negatives; the usual fixes are to skip the very top ranks, filter candidates with a cross-encoder or a judge, or soften the labels.

q: A museum archive search embeds images and their captions with a two-tower contrastive image-text model. Text-to-image retrieval works, so the team builds one ranked list mixing images and caption texts for each text query. The images always sink below every caption, even the captions of irrelevant exhibits. What is the explanation?
options: Captions are shorter than images in token count, so their vectors have higher norms and win under cosine against the image vectors of the same exhibit, whatever the query says
The model was trained with image-to-text and text-to-image losses at different temperatures, a training bug that makes text scores systematically higher
The images were not normalized to unit length before indexing while the text vectors were, so the image dot products come out systematically smaller
Image and text embeddings occupy separate regions of the shared space, so any text is closer to any text than to any image; rankings hold within a modality, not across one
explain: The modality gap: contrastive training only needs matching pairs to be relatively closest, and the two cones never meet. Rank each modality separately and fuse, or calibrate the two score distributions before mixing.

q: Decoder-only LLMs descend from the LSTM encoder-decoder recipe for translation. Which component of that recipe did they drop?
options: A fixed-size vector that summarizes the whole input before any output token is produced
Training by teacher forcing with a cross-entropy loss on the next token of the target
A dedicated end-of-sequence token that tells the decoder when to stop producing output
Left-to-right factorization of the output probability into one token at a time, conditioned on the output so far
explain: Teacher forcing, the stop token and the autoregressive factorization all survived. What went was the bottleneck: the prompt stays accessible token by token through attention instead of being squeezed into one vector.

q: In the attention-based seq2seq translator, the decoder attends over the encoder's per-word annotations h_1..h_n at every step. When a decoder-only LLM generates a reply, what plays the role of those annotations?
options: The final hidden state of the last prompt token, copied into the first generation step as a summary of the prompt
The keys and values computed for each prompt token in every layer, kept in the KV cache
The input embeddings of the prompt tokens, averaged into a single context vector
The logits over the vocabulary that the model produced while reading the prompt
explain: Every layer of a decoder-only model keeps one key and one value per prompt token, and each new token's queries read them. The soft alignment is still there; it simply runs in every layer rather than in one place between encoder and decoder.

q: An LSTM encoder-decoder with 4 layers of 1,000 units hands the decoder the final hidden and cell state of each layer, whatever the sentence length. An attention model hands over one 2,000-dimensional annotation per source word (forward and backward state concatenated). For a 50-word sentence, by what factor is the attention model's channel to the decoder larger? Reviewer #2 wants the number, not the adjective.
explain: The fixed design passes 4 x 1,000 x 2 = 8,000 numbers; the attention model passes 50 x 2,000 = 100,000, and the ratio grows with every extra word. That linear growth is the whole cure for the bottleneck.

q: An attention-based translator renders an English sentence into German, where the main verb moves to the end of the clause. You plot the alignment matrix, target words as rows and source words as columns. What does the row for the German final verb look like?
options: Its mass sits on the last English word, since attention follows the diagonal position by position
Its mass spreads evenly over all source words, because verbs carry no content that can be aligned
Its mass sits on the English verb near the start of the sentence, far off the diagonal
Its mass is zero, since a word moved by the grammar cannot be aligned to any source word
explain: Soft alignment is learned from data, not fixed to the diagonal: the row jumps back to the English verb wherever it stands. These off-diagonal hops were the first interpretable pictures of attention, long before anyone drew heads.

q: A sentence VAE has a 2-dimensional Gaussian latent with a standard normal prior. For one sentence the encoder outputs mu = (2, 0) and sigma = (1, 1). Using KL(N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, 1)) = 0.5 * (mu^2 + sigma^2 - 1 - ln(sigma^2)) per dimension, what is the KL term for this sentence?
options: 2 nats
4 nats
1 nat
0.5 nats
explain: Only the first dimension pays: 0.5 * (4 + 1 - 1 - 0) = 2 nats; the second matches the prior exactly and costs nothing. The KL term is the rent for moving the code away from the prior.

q: A startup founder pitches a recurrent model with 32 layers that keeps a 4,096-dimensional state per layer and nothing else between tokens. The transformer it competes with has 32 layers and d_model = 4,096 and keeps one key and one value vector of size 4,096 per token per layer. After reading 10,000 tokens, by what factor does the transformer's per-sequence memory exceed the recurrent model's?
explain: The recurrent state is 32 x 4,096 numbers no matter what; the cache is 2 x 32 x 4,096 x 10,000, which is 20,000 times more. Constant memory is the recurrent model's selling point, and a lossy summary is the price.

q: A project team, the night before its roadshow, summarizes a 6,000-token forum thread with a pretrained seq2seq summarizer whose encoder takes at most 1,024 tokens. They cut the thread into 1,000-token chunks, summarize each into about 150 tokens, concatenate the chunk summaries and summarize the result once more. How many summarizer calls does this take?
explain: Six chunks give six calls, and the six summaries together are about 900 tokens, which fits in one more pass. Had they fed the raw thread in directly, the encoder would have silently kept the first 1,024 tokens and the summary would have covered the opening post and nothing else.

q: Reversing the source sentence before encoding it with an LSTM improved translation substantially. Yet the average distance between a source word and its target counterpart is unchanged by the reversal: the first words get closer, the last words get farther. What is the accepted explanation for why it still helps?
options: The LSTM reads the reversed sentence with less forgetting, since its forget gate saturates later when the sentence is presented backwards
Target sentences are usually shorter than source sentences, so the reversal aligns the two ends of the sequences
Reversal reduces the number of time steps the encoder needs, because the end-of-sentence marker is now read first
A few short source-target dependencies let the optimizer establish communication early, after which the long ones become learnable
explain: The minimal time lag matters more than the average: once the first target words can be predicted from nearby source words, gradients start flowing usefully and the rest follows. With attention the argument is moot, since every source word is one hop away.

q: An LSTM language model carries a hidden state across the entire document. A decoder-only LLM has a hard context window of 8,192 tokens. In Shannon's sense of a Markov source, where the next symbol depends only on a bounded number of preceding symbols, how do the two compare?
options: The LSTM is a finite-order Markov source because its state has finitely many dimensions; the LLM is not, since attention is nonlocal
The LLM is a finite-order Markov source; the LSTM in principle is not, since its state is a function of the entire history
Both are finite-order Markov sources, since both run in finite-precision arithmetic and so have finitely many states
Neither is a Markov source, since Shannon's definition applies only to models estimated from n-gram counts
explain: Cut the window and nothing before it can matter, so the LLM is literally an order-8,191 Markov source, if a very large one. Finite dimensions and finite precision make the LSTM a finite-state machine, which is not the same thing: one bit of state can remember an open bracket from arbitrarily far back.

q: ELMo trains a forward LSTM language model and a backward one, each with its own loss, and concatenates their states. BERT instead trains one network to predict masked tokens. Both see both sides of a word. What does the masked model get that the concatenation of two independently trained directions does not?
options: A single nonlinear function of left and right context jointly, so the two sides interact before the representation is formed
A representation that includes the word itself, which the concatenation discards because each direction stops short of the token
Twice as many training signals per sequence, since every token is predicted from both sides instead of from one
Positional information for each token, which recurrent networks cannot provide and the transformer adds explicitly
explain: In the biLM the left and right views meet only at the concatenation; nothing combines them nonlinearly. One encoder that reads both sides at once can condition 'bank' on the river and the loan together, at the price of only training on the masked positions.

q: Beam search in a seq2seq translator finishes with two hypotheses: A has 5 tokens and total log probability -10, B has 10 tokens and total log probability -15. Which one wins under the raw sum, which under per-token averaging, and what does the disagreement reveal?
options: A under both criteria; averaging cannot change the order, because dividing two negative totals by their lengths keeps their order
B under both criteria; longer hypotheses accumulate more evidence and so are preferred by any sound criterion
A under the raw sum, B under averaging; the raw sum favors short outputs, since every extra token lowers the score
B under the raw sum, A under averaging; averaging penalizes the longer hypothesis for having more tokens
explain: -10 beats -15, but -10/5 = -2 per token loses to -15/10 = -1.5. Log probabilities are never positive, so the raw sum is a length tax; length normalization and the brevity penalties of later systems exist to pay it back.

q: To fight posterior collapse, a student trains a sentence VAE with a 16-dimensional latent and 'free bits': per dimension, the first 0.5 nats of KL are not penalized. At most how much information can the code carry about the sentence before the KL term starts to cost anything?
options: About 8 bits
About 5.5 bits
About 16 bits
About 11.5 bits
explain: 16 x 0.5 = 8 nats, and a nat is 1/ln 2, about 1.44 bits, so roughly 11.5 bits for free. Enough to pick one sentence template out of a few thousand, which is usually what the latent was wanted for.

q: Two translation systems reach the same quality on short sentences. One is an encoder-decoder with 300 million parameters in the encoder and 300 million in the decoder. The other is a decoder-only model with 600 million parameters that reads the source as a prompt. Count 2 FLOPs per parameter per token processed and ignore attention over cached keys. For a 50-token source and a 50-token output, roughly how many FLOPs does each system spend?
options: About 120 GFLOP for each, since both have 600 million parameters and process 100 tokens
About 60 GFLOP for the encoder-decoder and 120 GFLOP for the decoder-only model
About 30 GFLOP for the encoder-decoder and 60 GFLOP for the decoder-only model
About 60 GFLOP for each, since the decoder-only model skips the separate encoder pass
explain: Each source token passes only the 300M encoder and each output token only the 300M decoder, 30 + 30 GFLOP; the decoder-only model pushes all 100 tokens through all 600M, twice the work. Splitting the parameters by role is the encoder-decoder's remaining economic argument.

q: A project team fine-tunes a token classifier for names and addresses and sees outputs such as B-PER O I-PER, an 'inside' tag with no entity open. Their BiLSTM-CRF baseline never produces this. Which mechanism explains the difference?
options: The CRF scores whole tag sequences with learned transition weights and decodes jointly, so a step from O into I-PER gets a hopeless score
The BiLSTM reads the sentence in both directions, so at each token it already knows whether an entity has been opened earlier and which type it has
The CRF uses a larger tag set with a dedicated tag for the second token of a name, which makes I-PER after O unnecessary
The token classifier is trained on subword tokens, and the invalid sequence disappears once predictions are merged back to whole words
explain: A per-token softmax decides each tag alone; nothing in it knows that I- must follow B- or I- of the same type. The CRF's transition matrix plus Viterbi makes the sequence a joint decision, which is why people still bolt a CRF or a repair rule onto transformer taggers.

q: Five LSTM translators with one shared vocabulary, trained on the same data from different random seeds, were ensembled by averaging their next-token distributions at every decoding step, with a clear gain. A student at 3 a.m. proposes averaging the five weight matrices instead, to pay for a single model at inference. Why does that fail here, while averaging fine-tuned checkpoints of one pretrained model often works?
options: Weight averaging cancels the LSTM gates, since the sigmoid outputs of five independently trained models average to about 0.5 and the cells stop remembering anything
Averaging weights divides every parameter by five, which shrinks the logits and makes the output softmax nearly uniform
Independently initialized networks learn similar functions in differently permuted coordinates, so their weights do not share one low-loss region
The five models segment words differently after byte-pair encoding, so their output layers cannot be aligned at all
explain: Hidden unit 17 in one net is hidden unit 802 in another; the average of two unrelated coordinate systems is noise. Checkpoints fine-tuned from a shared starting point stay in the same basin, which is what model soups and merged adapters rely on.

q: In the attention-based translator, each source annotation h_j is bidirectional and already knows the words on both sides of j. In a decoder-only LLM the representation of the third prompt token never sees the twentieth. Why does this cost less at generation time than the comparison suggests?
options: The model re-encodes the prompt from scratch after every generated token, so by the second output token all prompt positions have seen each other in both directions
Rotary positions make the attention scores depend only on relative offsets, which is equivalent to making the prompt bidirectional
The feed-forward sublayers mix information across positions, so after a few layers each prompt token has read the whole prompt
The twentieth token's state has attended to the third, and the generating query reads all prompt positions at once, so the two sides meet at the read
explain: Information flows forward inside the prompt and is combined where it is used: a later key can carry what an earlier one lacks, and the query sees both. Where this is not enough, people add a bidirectional prefix or simply repeat the prompt.

q: The lesson of the fixed-vector bottleneck was that squeezing a whole input into one vector loses the detail a reader later needs. A startup founder claims attention 'solved that for good'. Where does the same bottleneck sit in a typical retrieval-augmented pipeline today?
options: In the bi-encoder index, where each document becomes one vector that must serve every future query, while reranker and generator read the text
In the tokenizer, where every document is compressed into a fixed number of subword tokens before anything is embedded
In the generator's KV cache, where the retrieved passages are stored as one summary vector per layer rather than as one key and value per token
In the lexical index, where each document is reduced to its single most frequent term before scoring
explain: A document embedding is a thought vector with a different name, and it fails the same way: long or multi-topic documents lose the detail a specific question needs. Chunking, multi-vector retrieval and reranking over the full text are attention's answer, reinvented.

q: ELMo let each task learn its own softmax weights over the biLM's layers, and tasks that needed word senses leaned on upper layers while tagging tasks leaned on lower ones. A team now extracts features from a decoder-only LLM and finds that the final layer gives worse embeddings than a layer two thirds of the way up. Which reading of ELMo's lesson fits this observation?
options: The final layer has been normalized for the output softmax and therefore carries no semantic information that could be reused
The top layers specialize toward the pretraining objective, next-token prediction, so a general feature is often best read from an intermediate layer
Deeper layers receive fewer gradient updates than shallower ones during training, since the loss reaches them last, so their representations are less trained
The final layer encodes only position, since all lexical content has been consumed by the earlier attention layers
explain: The last layer's job is to be a good input to the unembedding, which is a narrow job. ELMo's per-task layer weights were an early admission that 'the representation' lives at different depths for different uses.

q: Two sentence VAEs reach the same negative ELBO of 100 nats per sentence. Model A has a KL term of 0 nats, model B of 20 nats. Which model reconstructs its inputs better, and what does the shared ELBO tell you about which latent space is usable?
options: A reconstructs better, since it pays nothing for the code and spends all 100 nats on fitting the sentences
Both reconstruct equally well, since the ELBO is the reconstruction term and the KL is a regularizer added afterwards
B reconstructs better, and the ELBO shows this, since a higher KL term always indicates a tighter bound on the likelihood
B reconstructs better, 80 nats against 100, and the ELBO alone cannot tell you that A's latent is useless
explain: Negative ELBO is reconstruction plus KL, so A spends 100 nats on reconstruction and B only 80, having bought 20 nats of information through z. Rate and distortion trade one for one at equal ELBO, which is why a model that ignores its latent can still look fine on the training curve.

q: Self-consistency samples several reasoning chains from an LLM for the same question and takes a majority vote over the final answers. Viewed as a latent-variable model with the chain as the latent z and the answer as the output, what is the procedure doing?
options: Maximizing the ELBO of the answer, with the sampled chains serving as a variational posterior over the latent z and the vote as its mode
Fitting a Gaussian over the chains so that answers can be interpolated between two different reasoning paths
Approximating the marginal probability of each answer, summed over chains, by Monte Carlo, instead of trusting one most probable chain
Selecting the chain with the lowest perplexity, since the most fluent explanation is the most likely to be correct
explain: Greedy decoding picks one chain, roughly a mode of p(z | x); the vote estimates the sum over z of p(a | z, x) p(z | x) by sampling. Many different roads to the same answer are evidence for the answer, not for any one road.

q: The representation of position 1 in a sequence must come to depend on the token at position 100. A stack of convolutional layers with kernel width 3, each position seeing itself and one neighbor on each side, needs how many layers for that, and how many does a stack of self-attention layers need?
options: 50 convolutional layers, 1 attention layer
7 convolutional layers, 1 attention layer
99 convolutional layers, 1 attention layer
99 convolutional layers, 2 attention layers
explain: Each convolutional layer moves information by at most one position, so covering 99 steps takes 99 layers; one attention layer connects any two positions directly. The 7 would be dilated convolutions doubling the reach per layer, and 50 is merely the depth at which the two tokens first meet at some position in the middle.

q: The transformer's case against recurrence was that all positions of a sequence can be processed at the same time instead of one after another. For a decoder-only LLM serving chat, in which phase does that advantage disappear?
options: Generating the reply, where each new token depends on the previous one and must be produced in sequence
Reading the prompt, where the causal mask forces the prompt tokens to be processed one at a time
Training, where teacher forcing requires the model to see its own previous prediction before the next step
Computing the attention scores, where each row of the score matrix must wait for the row above it
explain: Prefill and training process whole sequences in parallel, since the targets are known. Decoding is sequential for any autoregressive model, transformer or not, which is why so much engineering goes into the KV cache and speculative decoding.

q: Current decoder-only LLMs look rather different from the original transformer. Which element of the original block is still there essentially unchanged?
options: Layer normalization applied after the residual addition of each sublayer, before the next one
The residual connection that adds each sublayer's output back to its input
Sinusoidal position vectors added to the token embeddings at the input
A two-matrix feed-forward block with a ReLU between the two matrices
explain: Norms moved in front of the sublayers, positions became rotations of queries and keys, and the MLP grew a gate with a smooth activation. The skip connection stayed exactly where it was, and the residual stream it creates is the backbone of everything, interpretability included.

q: A BERT-style encoder and a GPT-style decoder are configured with the same depth, width, heads and vocabulary. A colleague at the conference bar insists the decoder needs extra parameters to enforce the causal constraint. How many extra parameters does the causal mask add per layer?
options: One per attention head
d_model, one per dimension
n^2 for a context of n tokens
explain: The mask is a fixed pattern of minus infinities added to the scores before the softmax; nothing is learned. The same block, the same parameter count, a different triangle.

q: A student implements causal attention by computing the full softmax over all positions and then setting the weights on future positions to zero. Compared with masking the scores with minus infinity before the softmax, what is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since softmax is applied entry by entry and the zeroed positions would have received zero weight in any case once the model has trained
No gradient can flow through the zeroed weights, so the model gradually stops learning to attend to past positions
The surviving weights sum to less than one by a factor set by the future scores, so outputs shrink and the future leaks in through the denominator
The output becomes a sum instead of an average, so its magnitude grows with the number of past positions
explain: Softmax normalizes over whatever it is given; zero the future afterwards and the remaining weights add up to less than one, by an amount set by tokens the position was not supposed to see. Mask before the softmax and both the normalization and the secrecy are intact.

q: A decoder layer has d_model = 4,096, 32 query heads of dimension 128, and standard multi-head attention. You switch to multi-query attention: all 32 query heads share a single key head and a single value head of dimension 128. By what factor do the parameters of the key and value projections shrink?
explain: Each of K and V goes from 4,096 x 4,096 to 4,096 x 128, a factor of 32, and the KV cache shrinks by the same factor. The query and output projections are untouched, as is the n^2 scoring work.

q: A hybrid search service retrieves 100 candidate passages for a query and reranks them with a cross-encoder. The query has 20 tokens and each passage 200 tokens. How many tokens does the cross-encoder process for this one query, and how many did the bi-encoder process at query time?
explain: The cross-encoder reads every query-passage pair as one sequence: 100 x 220 = 22,000 tokens of transformer compute. The bi-encoder embedded the passages offline and reads only the 20-token query, which is why reranking is where the latency budget goes.

q: The original transformer was trained with label smoothing of 0.1, which made its perplexity worse and its BLEU better. A team pretraining an LLM whose token probabilities will later feed uncertainty estimates and distillation decides against label smoothing. Which consequence of label smoothing justifies the decision?
options: It doubles the training cost, since the loss must be computed against a dense target distribution over the entire vocabulary at every position
It is incompatible with softmax cross-entropy and requires a separate margin loss on the correct token
It removes the model's ability to generate rare tokens, since their target probability is set to zero
It trains the model never to put more than about 0.9 on any token, so the probabilities stop reflecting the model's actual confidence
explain: Smoothed targets cap the gold token near 0.9 and spread the rest evenly, so held-out log-likelihood suffers while argmax decisions and beam search may gain. For calibration, log-prob based scoring and teacher logits, the undistorted distribution is the product.

q: A student at 3 a.m. copies the original transformer schedule into a config: the learning rate rises linearly for 4,000 warmup steps and then decays it in proportion to 1/sqrt(step). The peak is reached at step 4,000. What fraction of the peak learning rate is in use at step 16,000?
options: One half
One quarter
One sixteenth
One eighth
explain: The decay goes as 1/sqrt(step), so from step 4,000 to 16,000 the rate falls by sqrt(16,000 / 4,000) = 2. Modern recipes keep the warmup and replace the tail by a cosine or linear decay to a small floor, but the first few thousand steps look the same.

q: Sinusoidal position vectors are added to the token embeddings once, at the input. Rotary embeddings rotate the queries and keys inside every attention layer. Which statement correctly contrasts the two?
options: With sinusoidal encoding the attention score depends on the offset exactly, while rotary encoding makes the value vectors depend on the absolute position of each token
Both schemes are mathematically identical, since the dot product of two rotated vectors equals the dot product of two shifted vectors
With rotary encoding the attention score of two tokens depends on their offset exactly, while the additive scheme only makes offsets learnable through the projections
Rotary encoding requires a lookup table of trained rotations, while sinusoidal encoding is parameter-free and extrapolates to any length
explain: Rotating q by angle m and k by angle n leaves a score that depends on m - n alone, by construction and in every layer. Added sinusoids make PE(pos + k) a linear function of PE(pos), which lets the projections learn relative behavior but does not force it, and after the first layer the position has already blended into the content.

q: A team wants sentence embeddings from a decoder-only LLM and mean-pools the final-layer token states, as they would with a BERT encoder. Which problem is specific to the decoder-only case?
options: The final layer of a decoder has no states for the input tokens at all, only logits over the vocabulary, so there is nothing that could be pooled
Each token's state encodes only the tokens before it, so early states know nothing of the rest of the sentence and the mean leans toward an incomplete reading
Mean pooling discards word order, which an encoder preserves through its bidirectional attention but a decoder does not
The decoder's states live in logit space rather than embedding space, so they cannot be compared by cosine similarity
explain: The causal mask makes the first token's state the same whatever follows. Last-token pooling, an appended summary token, or briefly fine-tuning with the mask removed are the usual repairs, each of which restores some bidirectionality.

q: A decoder-only model caches the keys and values of all earlier tokens and computes only the new token at each step. Someone proposes the same cache for a BERT-style encoder that is fed a document one appended sentence at a time. Why does the cache not carry over?
options: An encoder has no key and value projections of its own; only decoders compute them, for the cross-attention sublayer that reads the encoder
Encoders process tokens as an unordered set, so there is no notion of earlier tokens whose states could be cached
The cache requires rotary positions, and BERT-style encoders use learned absolute position embeddings instead
In a bidirectional encoder every earlier state depends on later tokens, so appending a sentence changes all the cached keys and values
explain: Caching is legal exactly because the causal mask makes a past state independent of the future; a new token cannot change what is already computed. Remove the mask and every state is a function of the whole input, so there is nothing stable to store.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt batches prompts of different lengths for a decoder-only model, pads the shorter ones on the right as the training code did, and gets nonsense completions for exactly those prompts. What went wrong?
options: Generation continues from the last position of each row, which for the padded prompts is a pad token rather than the prompt's end
The attention mask on the padding tokens leaks the longer prompts into the shorter ones within the same batch, since rows share one mask
Right padding shifts the rotary positions of the prompt tokens, so the relative offsets inside the prompt are wrong
The pad token has no embedding in a decoder-only model, so the forward pass produces undefined hidden states
explain: Padding on the right is fine when every position has a target, as in training; for generation the next token is appended after the pad run, and the model continues a sequence that ends in filler. Left padding with masked and re-indexed positions puts every prompt's last real token at the end of its row.

q: A cross-encoder reranker accepts at most 512 tokens per query-document pair. The project's documents average 1,500 tokens and, for many queries, the decisive sentence is near the end. The reranker keeps demoting those documents. Which fix addresses the mechanism?
options: Retrieve more candidates in the first stage so that the demoted documents at least remain in the candidate pool
Switch to a larger cross-encoder with more layers, which can compress longer documents into its 512 tokens before scoring them
Split each document into passages, score every query-passage pair separately and rank documents by their best passage score
Give the lexical component more weight in the score fusion, since BM25 scores the whole document
explain: Tokens beyond the limit are dropped before the model sees them, so the decisive sentence never enters the attention at all. Scoring passages and aggregating by maximum gives every part of the document a hearing; more candidates or a bigger model just truncate more thoroughly.

q: Decoder states s_1..s_m and encoder states h_1..h_n, with m = n = 1,000 and d = 1,000. Additive attention scores v^T tanh(W s_i + U h_j); dot-product attention scores s_i^T W h_j. For both, W s_i and U h_j can be precomputed per side, so the multiply-add counts for the pairwise part are of the same order, about m * n * d = 10^9. Why is the dot-product form still the one that scaled?
options: The additive form cannot be differentiated through tanh at this scale, since the gradient of tanh vanishes for large d
The dot-product scores are one matrix product with an m x n result of a million numbers, while the additive form materializes an m x n x d tensor of a billion numbers
The dot-product scores are bounded between -1 and 1, so the softmax is far better conditioned than with the unbounded additive scores, which saturate it
The additive form requires m * n * d^2 operations once the two sides are combined, two orders of magnitude more than stated
explain: FLOP counts hide the shape of the work: a matrix product with a small output runs near peak on any accelerator, while an elementwise tanh over 4 GB of intermediate activations is memory traffic. Transformers took the bilinear score, then added scaling and heads to buy back expressivity.

q: A pattern like 'if token X was followed by Y earlier in the context, predict Y after the current X' is a basic in-context copying mechanism. Attention-only transformers with one layer cannot implement it, while two layers can. Why does it take two?
options: The softmax of a single layer can attend sharply to only one position, and the pattern requires attending to two positions at once, the earlier X and the Y after it
Position information is only available after the first layer, since rotary encoding is applied to the residual stream between layers
A single layer lacks the nonlinearity required for an 'if-then' rule, which the feed-forward block of the second layer supplies
One attention step must first write into each token the identity of its predecessor; only then can a second step match the current token to those predecessors and copy
explain: The key for 'the earlier X' must carry what came before it, and that information is only placed there by a previous-token head in a lower layer. Depth is the number of sequential lookups a transformer can chain, whatever the context length; a path length of one per layer does not mean one hop per model.

q: A project team prunes attention heads whose attention patterns correlate above 0.99 with another head in the same layer, reasoning that they are redundant. Quality drops noticeably. What did the pruning rule miss about what a head is?
options: The pattern only decides where a head reads; its value and output projections decide which subspace it copies, so equal patterns can move different information
Heads in the same layer share one output projection, so removing any head changes the contribution of all the others to the residual stream and must be compensated by retraining
Attention patterns are recomputed for every input, so a correlation measured on a sample of batches says nothing about other inputs
Pruning a head removes its share of the sqrt(d_k) scaling, so the logits of the remaining heads become too large
explain: Multi-head attention is several subspaces, not several patterns: the QK circuit sets the weights and the OV circuit sets what gets written to the residual stream. Identical 'where' with different 'what' is not redundancy; it is division of labor.

q: The 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling assumes query and key components of roughly unit variance. Late in a long pretraining run, loss spikes appear and the attention distributions in some layers have become almost one-hot. Normalizing queries and keys to unit norm before the dot product, with a learned scale, cures it. What was the mechanism?
options: The fixed scaling had become too strong as the effective d_k shrank during training, flattening the attention into uniform averages that carry no signal
Trained query and key norms had grown, so logits far exceeded what the fixed scaling anticipated and the softmax saturated, with near-zero gradients
Rotary rotations had accumulated numerical error at large positions, corrupting the dot products in the slow dimensions
The residual stream had shrunk toward zero, so the attention scores lost their signal and the softmax became effectively random
explain: sqrt(d_k) is a constant; the norms of q and k are not, and nothing in the loss stops them from growing. QK normalization pins the logit scale to a learned parameter, which is why it shows up in recipes for very deep or very long training runs.

q: A project team, the night before its roadshow, argues about whether attention is really the quadratic bill. Per layer and per token, a transformer spends about 24 d^2 FLOPs on its weight matrices (8 d^2 for the four attention projections, 16 d^2 for a feed-forward block of width 4d) and about 4 n d FLOPs on the attention scores and weighted values over a context of n tokens. With d = 4,096, at what context length does the attention-over-context cost catch up with the weight cost?
options: About 4,100 tokens
About 1,000 tokens
About 24,600 tokens
About 98,000 tokens
explain: 4 n d = 24 d^2 gives n = 6 d = 24,576. Below that, 'attention is quadratic' is true but not the bill; above it, the context term dominates and the KV cache, not the weights, is what the hardware spends its time reading.

q: For pretraining, three unrelated documents of 1,000 tokens each are packed into one 3,000-token sequence of a model with rotary positions. Which setup makes each document's forward pass identical to processing it alone?
options: Resetting the position counter at each document boundary; the mask is then unnecessary, since a token at position 0 cannot attend to anything that lies before it
Both a block-diagonal mask and a per-document position reset, since rotary rotations depend on absolute position and the scores would differ otherwise
Neither, since the model learns during pretraining to ignore tokens that belong to another document, which makes the extra machinery redundant
A block-diagonal causal mask that confines attention to the document; resetting positions per document is then unnecessary, since rotary scores depend only on offsets
explain: Rotary scores are functions of m - n, so a document starting at position 2,000 computes exactly the attention it would compute starting at 0, provided the mask stops it from seeing its neighbors. Without the mask, two thirds of all allowed query-key pairs in this sequence cross a document boundary.

q: A causal decoder is fine-tuned for 3-way entailment GPT-1 style: premise, a delimiter token, hypothesis, then an end token, all in one sequence, with a linear head on one hidden state.
