Your German flatmate wants to put the head on the first token's state 'like [CLS]'. Why is that the wrong position?
options: The first position is reserved for the positional encoding and carries no token information about either of the two sentences
The first state is identical for every input because the embedding table is frozen during fine-tuning
The first state would work, but only if the delimiter token is placed before the premise instead
The first position attends only to itself under the causal mask, so its state has seen neither sentence
explain: Under a causal mask the only position whose state depends on the whole input is the last one, which is why decoders pool there and encoders can afford [CLS] at the front. Same idea, opposite end.

q: Both models see the same 1,000-token sequence once. A masked-LM encoder selects 15% of positions for prediction. A causal decoder, with a beginning-of-text token in front, predicts the token at every one of the 1,000 positions. How many positions contribute to each loss, and what does the ratio suggest about sample efficiency?
options: 120 vs 1,000; only the visibly masked positions count toward the encoder's loss
150 vs 1,000; the causal model extracts more training signal from the same sequence
150 vs 150; the causal model also masks 15% of positions to stay comparable
850 vs 1,000; the encoder is trained on every unmasked position, so it actually sees slightly less signal
explain: 15% of 1,000 is 150 targets, against 1,000 for next-token prediction; the encoder pays a full forward pass for a sixth of the gradient signal. Replaced-token detection and higher masking rates were both responses to this.

q: A team builds a German and English PII tagger on a pretrained cased encoder and wants to add hand-crafted features: a capitalization flag per token and a gazetteer of first names. What is the most reasonable expectation?
options: Large gains, since subword tokens erase capitalization and the encoder cannot see it
The gazetteer is essential because an encoder cannot tag a name absent from its pretraining data
Small gains at best: cased subwords and pretrained context already carry what those features encode
The features will hurt, because concatenating them changes the input distribution the tokenizer expects
explain: Replacing hand-made features with representations learned from raw text was the whole point of pretraining embeddings, and contextual encoders finished the job. A name list helps only where the context is genuinely uninformative.

q: A team serves 10 small classification tasks on the same incoming text with one 110M-parameter encoder. Plan A: fine-tune a separate copy per task. Plan B: keep the encoder frozen and train one head per task on its features. Which comparison is right?
options: Plan A stores about 1.1B parameters and runs 10 encoder passes per text; Plan B stores one encoder, runs one pass, and usually gives up some accuracy
Plan A stores one encoder because fine-tuning changes only the head; Plan B stores 10 copies since each head needs its own frozen features
Plan B matches Plan A on accuracy in every case, since a linear head can recover any function of the frozen features it is given
Plan A runs one encoder pass shared by all 10 tasks, since fine-tuned copies produce the same hidden states on the same text
explain: Fine-tuning rewrites the whole encoder, so every task gets its own 110M-parameter copy and its own pass. Frozen features trade a few points of accuracy for sharing one pass across tasks, the classic feature-based deal.

q: At 3 a.m. a student downloads a 'base' checkpoint, types 'What is the capital of Bavaria?' and gets back five more geography questions and no answer. The 'instruct' checkpoint of the same model answers 'Munich'. What explains the difference?
options: The base model has a smaller context window, so the question was truncated before the answer
The base model was only pretrained to continue text, and a list of questions is a likely continuation
The base model lacks the geography data; the instruct version was pretrained on more factual text about cities
The base checkpoint uses a different tokenizer that splits question marks into unknown tokens
explain: Pretraining teaches 'what comes next', and after one quiz question on the internet comes another. Post-training turns the same knowledge into the habit of answering.

q: A project team fine-tunes a small encoder on 304 labelled messages (300, plus four more to make the arithmetic honest) with batch size 16 for 3 epochs. How many optimizer steps is that, and what does the number say about the usual '3 epochs' default?
options: 912 steps; one step per example per epoch, so three epochs on so few examples already risks overfitting the labels
19 steps; the three epochs run in parallel across the three classes and share one pass over the data
57 steps; the default comes from datasets a hundred times larger, so a tiny set often needs more epochs or a higher rate
304 steps; each example is one step, and the batch size only affects memory and not the step count
explain: 304 / 16 = 19 steps per epoch, 57 in total, which is barely out of warmup for most recipes. Watch the validation curve instead of trusting a default that was tuned on 100,000 examples.

q: With no fine-tuning at all, you append 'Overall, the film was' to each review and compare the model's next-token probabilities for 'great' and 'terrible'. Accuracy is well above chance. What is this, and what does it rely on?
options: Feature extraction; it relies on the final hidden state being a linear function of sentiment
Few-shot learning; it relies on the appended phrase acting as one labelled demonstration of the task format
Fine-tuning by inference; it relies on the comparison updating the output embeddings
Zero-shot prompting through label words; it relies on the task being latent in the pretraining text
explain: A pretrained LM has read enough reviews to know which word follows 'the film was'. Comparing label-word probabilities was the earliest preview of prompting, and the choice of label words still matters.

q: Forty classification tasks must run on every incoming document. Fine-tuning a copy per task averages 91.0 F1; a frozen encoder with a small head per task on the concatenated last four layers averages 90.5. One encoder pass costs 1 unit and one head costs 0.01 unit. What is the compute per document for each setup?
options: 40.4 units vs 1.4 units
40.0 units vs 1.0 unit
41.0 units vs 1.01 units
40.4 units vs 40.4 units
explain: Forty fine-tuned copies means forty passes plus forty heads, 40.4; one frozen pass plus forty heads is 1.4. Half a point of F1 for 29 times the compute is a trade the feature-based side has often won in production.

q: You fine-tune a causal decoder for 5-way classification on 50,000 labelled documents with a classification head only. Accuracy is fine, but the model's text continuation afterwards is garbage, and a second task fine-tuned from this checkpoint underperforms one started from the original weights. A colleague suggests adding the next-token loss on the input text, weighted 0.5, during fine-tuning. What is the rationale?
options: The auxiliary LM loss doubles the effective batch size, which lets the classification head converge in half the number of epochs on the same 50,000 documents
The auxiliary LM loss lets the classifier read the label from the next token, so the separate classification head becomes unnecessary
The auxiliary LM loss forces the model to memorize the training documents, which raises classification accuracy on the same documents
The auxiliary LM loss anchors the shared weights to the pretraining objective, which limits forgetting and tends to help more with larger fine-tuning sets
explain: A pure classification loss can rewrite representations into whatever separates five labels, and the general skill goes with it. Keeping the pretraining objective in the mix is the oldest regularizer against this, and the same idea returns as data replay in post-training.

q: You freeze a 12-layer encoder and, instead of using only the top layer, learn a softmax-normalized weighted average of all 13 layer outputs (input embeddings plus 12 layers) as the input to a POS-tagging head. The learned weights concentrate on layers 2 to 4. What should you expect for a sentence-level paraphrase task trained the same way?
options: The same weights, since the mixture is a property of the encoder and not of the task
Weights concentrated on the input embeddings, since paraphrase is a lexical matching task
Weights shifted toward the upper layers, since more abstract features are read out later
Uniform weights, since the softmax normalization pushes every mixture toward the average
explain: Lower layers hold surface and syntactic information, upper layers hold what the pretraining task needed, which is closer to meaning. Learned layer mixing made that visible before probing did, and 'just take the last layer' is a default, not a law.

q: A team turns a causal decoder into a sentence-embedding model by mean-pooling its hidden states and training with a contrastive loss. Retrieval quality lags behind a far smaller encoder. Which fix targets the structural cause?
options: Decoders have no [CLS] token; prepend one and the mean pooling becomes bidirectional automatically, since every later token attends to it
Under the causal mask early tokens' states know nothing about the rest of the text; pool from the last token, or lift the mask and adapt
The embedding dimension is too large for cosine similarity to be discriminative; project to 256 dimensions before pooling
Causal models cannot be used for embeddings at all, since their outputs are probability distributions
explain: Mean pooling averages states that each saw only a prefix, so the vector is dominated by context-free early tokens. Last-token pooling, or enabling bidirectional attention and continuing training, are the standard repairs for decoder-based embedders.

q: A team verifies claims with an NLI cross-encoder fine-tuned on sentence pairs. They feed each claim together with the whole 3-page source as the premise. On their 100 hand-labelled sentences the model says 'neutral' for almost everything, including claims copied verbatim from page 3. The LLM they compare against does fine. Most likely cause?
options: NLI models can only output 'neutral' when the premise is much longer than the hypothesis
The encoder's input limit truncated the source, so the evidence on page 3 never reached the model
Cross-encoders cannot process two texts of different length at once and need a bi-encoder to pre-align them
The claims are too short for the model's tokenizer, which pads them into uninformative noise
explain: A pair encoder with a 512-token window sees the first page and nothing else, and no evidence is correctly 'neutral'. Retrieve candidate sentences first and score claim-sentence pairs, which is also how the training data looked.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt continues pretraining a general 1B model on 20B tokens of maintenance logs, reusing the original peak learning rate and only log data. Loss on the logs drops nicely; loss on general text jumps at the start and never recovers. Which adjustment addresses both symptoms?
options: Rewarm to a lower peak rate and mix a small share of general-distribution data into the run
Freeze the embedding table; the jump comes from new vocabulary items receiving large updates
Train for more epochs on the logs, since general loss recovers once the new domain is fully fit
Switch to a larger batch size, which averages out the domain shift inside each update
explain: Jumping back to the original peak on a new distribution is a large perturbation of converged weights, and without any general data there is no gradient pulling the old skills back. A gentler peak plus replay is the standard recipe for continual pretraining.

q: A student builds semantic search by taking the pretrained [CLS] vector of a masked-LM encoder, no fine-tuning, and ranking by cosine similarity. Results are barely better than random, worse than averaged static word vectors. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The [CLS] vector is only meaningful after fine-tuning or contrastive training; pretraining never shaped it into a similarity space
Cosine similarity is undefined for vectors from a model with layer normalization; use Euclidean distance instead
The [CLS] vector encodes position 0 only; use the vector of the final [SEP] token, which has seen the whole sentence by the time it is computed
Masked-LM encoders are not trained on whole sentences, so no pooled vector can represent one
explain: Pretraining shapes [CLS] through a coarse pair task at best and leaves its geometry anisotropic; nothing asked nearby vectors to mean similar things. Sentence-embedding models add exactly that training, which is why they exist.

q: A decoder scores a 4-way multiple-choice item GPT-1 style: for each choice it runs 'context, delimiter, choice' as its own sequence and takes a scalar from the final state; the four scalars go through a softmax. The context is 400 tokens, each choice 20. Compared with one sequence holding the context and all four choices, how many tokens are processed, and what changes if the shared prefix is cached?
options: 1,680 vs 480 tokens; caching cannot help because the delimiter token changes the prefix of every one of the four sequences, so each needs its own forward pass
480 vs 480 tokens; the separate format already shares the context internally through the attention mechanism
1,680 vs 1,680 tokens; concatenation still re-reads the context once per choice during the causal pass
1,680 vs 480 tokens; with prefix caching the separate format needs about 480 tokens of forward work and each choice still cannot see the others
explain: Four runs of 420 tokens is 1,680; caching the 400-token prefix leaves 4 x 20 new tokens, 480 in all, the same as concatenation. The separate format keeps each score independent of the order and content of the other choices, which concatenation cannot promise.

q: A shared encoder is trained on two tagging tasks with separate heads, alternating batches across tasks. Task A has 900,000 sentences, task B has 100,000. Sampling proportional to size starves B, so you sample proportional to size^(1/T) with T = 2. What share of batches does each task get, and what is the general effect?
options: 75% A and 25% B; the temperature flattens the mixture toward the smaller task
90% A and 10% B; a temperature of 2 only changes the learning rate per task
50% A and 50% B; any temperature above 1 equalizes the two tasks
81% A and 19% B; the shares scale with the square of the size ratio rather than with its root
explain: Taking square roots turns a 9:1 ratio into 3:1. The same trick governs language mixing in multilingual pretraining: T = 1 reproduces the data, T towards infinity gives uniform sampling, and the shared weights follow whatever you sample.

q: In 'I moved to [MASK] [MASK] last year' a masked-LM encoder gives the first slot 'New' 0.4 and 'Los' 0.3, and the second slot 'York' 0.4 and 'Angeles' 0.3; the remaining mass of each slot sits on tokens that form no city name with either word. A student samples both positions at once from these marginals. Roughly how often does the output name a city that does not exist, and what property of the objective is responsible?
options: About 0%; attention between the two masked positions makes the two predictions consistent with each other, as in a causal model
At least 12%; only the lower-probability pair of words can produce an inconsistent output
At least 24%; masked positions are predicted independently given the visible context, so the joint is never modeled
At least 49%; the two marginals are multiplied, so any pair of these words is equally likely
explain: 0.4 x 0.3 + 0.3 x 0.4 = 0.24 of samples are 'New Angeles' or 'Los York', before counting the leftover mass. The masked positions attend to each other's [MASK] token, not to each other's prediction, which is why one-shot parallel generation from an encoder is incoherent and masked diffusion models unmask a few tokens per step instead.

q: A modernized encoder is pretrained with 30% masking instead of the classic 15%. On a 500-token sequence, how many positions contribute to the loss in each case, and what is the trade-off that makes a higher rate viable for large models but not automatically for small ones?
options: 150 vs 75; the higher rate only matters for speed, since loss per position is unchanged by context corruption and the model sees the same number of tokens either way
350 vs 425; the loss is taken on the unmasked positions, so a higher rate reduces the training signal
150 vs 75; larger models need more masking because their attention would otherwise copy the input exactly
150 vs 75; more positions give more loss signal per pass, but each prediction sees a more corrupted context, which hurts smaller models first
explain: 0.3 x 500 = 150 against 75: twice the gradient signal for the same forward pass, bought with harder, less informed predictions. Bigger models can afford the corrupted context; a tiny one may just see noise.

q: You extend an English sentence encoder to German by distillation on parallel pairs: the student is trained so that its vector for the German sentence matches the teacher's vector for the English one. Afterwards German-to-German retrieval works, cross-lingual retrieval works, but the student's English-to-English retrieval is worse than the teacher's. Which loss term was left out?
options: A contrastive term between German sentences, so the student learns German structure on its own
A term making the student match the teacher on the English sentences too, which keeps the source language from drifting
A translation loss, since the student has to generate the English sentence to align with it
A term pushing German and English vectors of unrelated sentences apart, so the two languages do not collapse into a single region
explain: The student is a new network; if only translations are tied to the teacher, nothing holds its English side in place. Matching the teacher on both sides of every pair is what makes the result one shared space rather than a German model pointing at an English one.

q: A causal decoder fine-tuned for classification reads the label from the hidden state at the last position. Accuracy is 90% when examples are processed one at a time and 60% when they are batched with padding. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Batching changes the attention pattern because padded tokens are attended to by real ones even with an attention mask, so the model must be retrained with batching enabled
The classifier head was trained on fp32 states and batching silently switches to fp16, which rounds the logits toward the majority class
With right padding the 'last position' of a short example is a pad token's state; gather at each example's true last index, or left-pad with correct position ids
The gradient of padded positions is nonzero during batched inference, which shifts the pooled state away from its single-example value
explain: Right padding puts the real last token somewhere in the middle of the row and the readout picks up a pad state. Single-example runs never pad, which is why the bug hides until the first batch, usually the night before the roadshow.

q: A prompt shows three English sentences each followed by its French translation, then a fourth English sentence. The model produces a correct French translation. No weights were updated. In the in-context-learning view, what has the context done?
options: It fine-tuned the attention weights for the duration of the request, which is undone when the request ends
It identified which of the many tasks seen during pretraining to perform, and set the output format
It taught the model French from three examples, which is why the fourth translation is correct
It retrieved the three translations from the training data, where the fourth sentence must also appear
explain: Three pairs do not teach a language; they tell a model that already learned translation from pretraining text what is wanted and how to lay it out. The demonstrations select and format the task, which is also why their labels matter less than you would expect.

q: A language model's average loss on a document is 2 bits per token and the document has 1,000 tokens. Using arithmetic coding driven by the model's probabilities, roughly how many bytes would the document compress to, and what is the general relation?
options: About 250 bytes; the cross-entropy in bits is the code length, so a better model is a better compressor
About 2,000 bytes; one byte per bit, since arithmetic coding rounds each coded symbol up to a whole byte boundary
About 1,000 bytes; compression cannot go below one byte per token
About 125 bytes; half the bits are redundant and the coder drops them
explain: 1,000 tokens x 2 bits = 2,000 bits = 250 bytes, plus a few bytes of overhead. Shannon's bound ties loss to code length directly, and 'lower loss' and 'better compression of the text' are the same sentence.

q: An LLM assigns a sensible probability to 'The otter is reading in the sauna', a sentence that almost certainly never appeared in its training data. A count-based n-gram model with the same data would back off to near-zero. What makes the neural model's estimate possible?
options: The model memorized every sentence of its training set and interpolates between the two nearest ones at inference time
Attention lets the model look up similar sentences in the training corpus at inference time
The tokenizer splits rare words into subwords that were all seen in training, which makes the sentence itself a seen one from the model's point of view
Words with similar usage have nearby embeddings, so probability learned for 'cat', 'sleeping' and 'kitchen' transfers to their neighbors
explain: The probability function is smooth in the word vectors, so each training sentence informs a combinatorial neighborhood of unseen ones. That argument against the curse of dimensionality is also the first reason more diverse data beats bigger count tables.

q: A synthetic-data pipeline generates 1,000,000 candidate examples. A verifier rejects 40% of them. A near-duplicate filter then removes 25% of what is left. How many examples survive, and what does the pipeline's quality mostly depend on?
options: 350,000; both filters apply to the original million independently, so 65% of the candidates is removed in total
600,000; dedup only reorders examples and does not change the count
450,000; the quality depends on the verifier and the dedup more than on the generator's fluency
450,000; the quality depends on the generator alone, since filters cannot add information
explain: 0.6 x 0.75 = 0.45 of the million. Filters cannot add information, but they decide which information is kept, and a fluent generator with no verifier produces fluent, confident mistakes at scale.

q: A classification service makes 500,000 calls per day. The prompt carries 8 demonstrations of 120 tokens each; the rest of the prompt is unchanged. How many extra input tokens per day do the demonstrations cost, and how does that compare with fine-tuning?
options: 60 million; demonstrations are only sent on the first call of each session, which is roughly one call in eight
4.8 million; the model caches demonstrations across calls, so only 1% is billed
960 thousand; eight demonstrations cost 960 tokens per day regardless of volume
480 million; the demonstrations are paid on every call, while a fine-tuned model pays for its labels once
explain: 960 tokens per call times 500,000 calls is 480 million tokens a day, every day. Few-shot is cheap to start and expensive to run; fine-tuning is the reverse, which is the whole trade-off table.

q: A causal LLM is asked to fill the gap in 'The ___ barked at the tram all night'. Why is this structurally awkward for a left-to-right model, and what pretraining trick addresses it?
options: The model cannot see 'barked' when predicting the gap; fill-in-the-middle training moves the suffix in front of the gap
The model has no token for a gap; adding a [MASK] token to the vocabulary at inference time fixes it
The gap is at an early position where attention is weak; longer context windows fix it
Causal models cannot condition on anything after the gap under any training recipe; only bidirectional encoders can fill gaps
explain: At the gap a causal model has read 'The' and nothing else, so it cannot know a dog is coming. Reordering training sequences as prefix, suffix, middle lets the same causal model learn to use the right context, which was the kind of task where unidirectional models fell short.

q: On one benchmark, a small model scores 40% zero-shot and 42% with 16 demonstrations; a much larger model of the same family scores 55% zero-shot and 70% with the same 16 demonstrations. Which conclusion follows?
options: Demonstrations hurt small models, which should always be prompted zero-shot
The ability to use demonstrations grows with scale; the large model gains far more from the same context
The large model memorized the 16 demonstrations during pretraining, which explains the 15-point gain on its own
Both models gain the same amount in relative terms, so the demonstrations work equally well
explain: Two points versus fifteen from identical context: the gap between zero-shot and few-shot widening with size was one of the clearest scaling findings. Small models mostly see the demonstrations as more text.

q: A test set has 1,000 items. 200 share a long n-gram with the pretraining corpus and are flagged; the remaining 800 form the 'clean' subset. Accuracy is 80% on the full set and 78% on the clean subset. What is the accuracy on the flagged items, and what does the gap suggest?
options: 80%; accuracy is the same on both subsets since the flagged items are a random sample, so contamination had no effect on the result
98%; the flagged items were nearly all memorized, so the benchmark is unusable
88%; the flagged items were easier for the model, consistent with some memorization, but the overall effect is 2 points
68%; flagged items are harder because long n-gram overlap marks boilerplate, so contamination cannot have helped the model
explain: 800 correct overall minus 0.78 x 800 = 624 clean leaves 176 of 200, or 88%. A ten-point gap on the flagged slice but two points on the headline number: contamination visible, score mostly survivable, which is what the clean-subset method is for.

q: Two models are compared on the same text. Model A averages 2.0 bits per token with a tokenizer producing 4 bytes per token on average; Model B averages 1.5 bits per token with a tokenizer at 2.5 bytes per token. Which model compresses the text better?
options: Model A at 0.5 bits per byte, against 0.6 for Model B; per-token loss is not comparable across tokenizers
Model B, since 1.5 bits per token is lower than 2.0 and loss is what scaling laws measure
Model B at 0.375 bits per byte, computed as its bits per token divided by Model A's bytes per token, the common reference
They tie, since compression depends on the text and not on the model that codes it
explain: Divide bits per token by bytes per token: 2.0 / 4 = 0.5 and 1.5 / 2.5 = 0.6. A coarser tokenizer takes more bits per step but fewer steps, and only the per-byte number is tokenizer-free.

q: You have 200B unique tokens of good text and compute for 800B tokens of training. Plan A: four epochs over the 200B. Plan B: one epoch over 800B tokens, where the extra 600B come from a lower-quality crawl. Which expectation matches data-constrained scaling studies?
options: Plan B; any repeated token is wasted compute, so one epoch of anything beats a second pass over anything
Plan A; repetition is strictly better than fresh data because the model converges faster on text it has already seen and never forgets it
Both plans are equivalent, since the loss depends only on the total number of tokens processed
Plan A; repeating good data for a handful of epochs loses little against fresh data, and the returns fall off only after that
explain: Up to about four passes, repeated tokens are worth almost as much as new ones; past that the value decays quickly. Four epochs of good text beats one epoch of good text plus three of noise, and 'one epoch only' was a habit of data abundance.

q: A project team draws five random sets of four demonstrations for the same prompt and measures 62%, 71%, 58%, 80% and 66% on their test set. The slide the night before the roadshow says 'few-shot accuracy: 80%'. What should it say, and why?
options: 80%; the best demonstration set is the one you would deploy, so its score is the honest one to report to the audience
58%; the worst case is the only safe number to promise a user, whatever the other draws showed
About 67% with a wide spread; the choice of demonstrations is a hyperparameter, and picking the best set on the test set is test-set tuning
80%; variance across demonstrations is sampling noise of the model and averages out in production once thousands of queries have been answered with the same prompt
explain: The mean is 67.4 with a 22-point range. Selecting the best of five on the test set and reporting it is the classic way to look 13 points better than you are; choose the set on a held-out split or report the distribution.

q: You double the training data for a count-based 5-gram model and for a neural LM of fixed size. Both improve on held-out text. On the subset of held-out 5-grams that still never occur in the doubled training set, only the neural model improves. Why?
options: The n-gram model's smoothing is disabled on larger corpora because the discounts shrink to zero, so unseen n-grams get exactly zero probability
The neural model's distributed representations let estimates learned for nearby contexts transfer to unseen ones; a count table has nothing to transfer
The neural model memorizes the doubled corpus, and the unseen 5-grams are near-duplicates of memorized ones
The n-gram model only improves on seen 5-grams because its vocabulary is frozen after the first run and every new context is mapped to the unknown token
explain: More data moves the shared embeddings and weights, which improves every context in their neighborhood, seen or not. A count table improves only the cells it fills, which is why scaling data pays off for one model family and saturates for the other.

q: A quality classifier flags 'high-quality' pages in a web crawl where 5% of pages truly are high quality. It catches 80% of the true high-quality pages and wrongly flags 2% of the rest. What fraction of the pages it keeps are actually high quality?
options: About 68%
About 80%
About 98%
About 40%
explain: Kept pages are 0.05 x 0.8 = 0.04 true positives plus 0.95 x 0.02 = 0.019 false positives, so 0.04 / 0.059 is about 68%. A 2% false-positive rate on a 95% base of noise is a third of your curated corpus.

q: Instead of a fixed set of 8 demonstrations, a system retrieves, for each query, the 8 most similar labelled examples from a pool of 2,000 and puts them in the prompt. Accuracy rises from 71% to 82%. Which interpretation is best supported, and what must the pool exclude?
options: The retriever fine-tunes the model on the retrieved examples at request time through a few gradient steps; the pool must exclude any mislabeled items so that no wrong update is ever made
The gain comes from longer prompts alone, since 8 retrieved items are longer than 8 fixed ones; nothing in the pool needs to be excluded
Retrieved demonstrations work because the model memorized the pool during pretraining and the prompt only reminds it; the pool must exclude any data newer than the model
Nearby demonstrations sharpen task recognition and supply near-matching evidence, blurring in-context learning with nearest-neighbor classification; the pool must exclude the test items
explain: A model shown eight labelled messages almost identical to the query is partly doing kNN with a very good similarity function. If the pool overlaps the test set, the nearest neighbor is the answer key.

q: A contamination study flags test items that share a 13-gram with the pretraining corpus and compares model accuracy on the flagged and clean subsets. On one benchmark the flagged subset scores lower than the clean one, and the authors conclude that contamination did not help. Where is the trap?
options: The 13-gram filter can only produce false negatives, so the clean subset is itself contaminated by every item that overlaps in fewer than 13 tokens, and the comparison is meaningless
Flagging correlates with item properties such as length and genericness, so the two subsets differ in difficulty; the gap measures difficulty and memorization together
A lower score on flagged items proves the model was trained to avoid them, which is a different kind of contamination
Accuracy on subsets of different sizes cannot be compared without first equalizing the number of items in each, since the smaller subset has a larger variance that biases its mean downward
explain: Short, formulaic items are both more likely to overlap with a web crawl and systematically different in difficulty, in either direction. Clean-versus-dirty is evidence, not a controlled experiment; the control would be a model trained without the overlap.

q: A scaling fit gives loss = 1.7 + 0.3 x (N0/N)^0.3 + 0.2, where 1.7 is the fitted floor, the middle term depends on parameter count N and the last term on the fixed dataset. At N = N0 the loss is 2.2. A founder expects 'ten times the parameters, ten times lower loss'. What does the fit predict at N = 10 N0, and what does the floor mean?
options: About 0.22; the loss scales inversely with parameters, so the floor is an artifact of small models
About 1.85; the data term also shrinks by the same factor when the model grows
About 2.05; the floor is the entropy of the text itself, which no model can predict away
About 2.05; the floor is the tokenizer's vocabulary size in bits and disappears with a larger vocabulary
explain: 10^-0.3 is about 0.5, so the parameter term halves to 0.15 and the loss goes from 2.2 to 2.05. The 1.7 is Shannon's irreducible part: text is genuinely unpredictable, and the reducible 0.5 is all there is to fight over.

q: A model was trained with a cosine schedule decaying to 10% of the peak over exactly 1T tokens. The team then decides to train to 2T tokens and resumes from the final checkpoint at the final learning rate. Loss barely moves over the next 200B tokens. What happened, and which schedule design avoids the problem?
options: The data loader restarted from the beginning, so the model is re-reading tokens it has seen; shuffling with a new seed and restarting the loader from a fresh offset restores progress at the same rate as before
The schedule had already annealed, so the tiny rate cannot make progress and rewarming costs a loss spike; a constant phase with a short final decay keeps the token budget open
Cosine schedules leave the Adam moment estimates unusable after the last step, so every update direction is corrupted; switching to plain SGD for the extension recovers the lost progress
The model has converged at 1T tokens, so no schedule would help; only more parameters can lower the loss from here
explain: A cosine schedule commits you to the total token count on day one: at the end the rate is too small to learn and too high to resume without a jump. Warmup-stable-decay style schedules let you branch a decayed checkpoint off a long constant-rate run at any point.

q: You fit loss as a power law in parameter count on models from 10M to 1B, each trained on 20 tokens per parameter, and extrapolate to a 100B model that you plan to train on 500 tokens per parameter. The prediction is badly off. Which methodological problem is responsible?
options: Power laws cannot be extrapolated by more than one order of magnitude under any conditions, because the loss surface stops being smooth once the parameter count exceeds the largest fitted model
The fit used too few points; five model sizes cannot determine the two parameters of a power law
The fit confounds parameters and data, since both grew together; a joint fit in N and D is needed before changing the ratio
Loss at 500 tokens per parameter is dominated by overfitting, since the model has by then seen each token many times over, which no scaling law can describe
explain: At a fixed ratio, L(N) is really L(N, 20N), a single curve through a two-dimensional surface. Change the ratio and you are off the curve; the joint form L(N, D) is what you needed to fit, with runs that vary data independently of size.

q: On 300 self-labelled test messages, a fine-tuned small encoder scores 88% accuracy and a prompted LLM scores 86%. Roughly what is the standard error of each accuracy estimate, and what follows for the project team's conclusion that 'the encoder wins'?
options: About 0.2 points; the 2-point gap is ten standard errors and the encoder clearly wins
About 5 points each; the gap is noise and neither model is better than the TF-IDF baseline
About 2 points each; since the encoder is ahead by about one standard error, it wins with 95% confidence on this test set
About 2 points each; the gap is within noise, so the decision should rest on cost, latency and a larger test set
explain: sqrt(0.87 x 0.13 / 300) is about 0.019, so each number carries roughly 2 points of standard error and the difference even more. With 300 items you can tell 88 from 78, not 88 from 86; the trade-off table should say so.

q: A small model is trained on 100,000 answers written by a large teacher model. On a hand-labelled test set it trails the teacher by 10 points, and on items the teacher gets wrong, the student is wrong 90% of the time. Adding 400,000 more teacher answers gains half a point. Which intervention addresses the actual cause?
options: Filter the synthetic answers with an independent check such as execution, ground truth or a verifier, since the student inherits the teacher's mistakes
Raise the sampling temperature of the teacher, so the additional examples cover a more diverse range of phrasings and the student stops overfitting to the teacher's surface style
Train for more epochs on the 500,000 examples; the student is undertrained rather than misinformed
Replace the teacher with a model of the same size as the student, so the distribution becomes learnable; the capacity gap is what prevents the student from reproducing the teacher's answers
explain: Five times more of the same distribution carries the same error pattern; the student is learning the teacher, errors included. Rejection against something that is not the teacher is how synthetic data gets to beat its source.

q: A student reproduces a classic experiment: she builds a table of which word followed each pair of words in a corpus and generates text by repeatedly drawing a next word from that table. The output is grammatical for three or four words at a time and nonsense over a sentence. She then samples from an LLM at temperature 1 with no truncation and gets paragraphs that hold together. What changed?
options: The LLM takes the most probable word at every step, while the table draw was random, so the randomness is what produced nonsense
Each draw now conditions on the whole preceding text instead of on two words; the random sampling step itself is unchanged
The LLM assigns exactly zero probability to ungrammatical continuations, so sampling can never leave the grammar
Subword tokens carry more grammatical structure than whole words, so each individual draw is much safer
explain: Both procedures sample from a conditional distribution; the n-gram table conditions on two words and forgets everything else, the LLM conditions on thousands of tokens. Temperature 1 without truncation is the old procedure with a very long memory.

q: A decoder-only model has d_model = 4,096 and a vocabulary of 128,000 tokens. At every decoding step the final hidden vector is multiplied by the output matrix to produce the logits. About how many multiply-adds does this output layer cost per generated token, and how does that compare with one 4,096 x 4,096 attention projection in the same step?
options: About 524 million, roughly 31 times one such projection
About 16.8 million, the same as one such projection
About 128,000, one multiply-add per vocabulary entry
About 4,096, one multiply-add per hidden dimension
explain: 4,096 x 128,000 = 524 million against 4,096 x 4,096 = 16.8 million. The softmax over the vocabulary was the cost center of the first neural LMs and a large vocabulary keeps it expensive today, which is one reason small models tie input and output embeddings to save parameters.

q: An API returns the log-probability of each generated token. An answer of 12 tokens has token log-probabilities (natural log) that sum to -3.0. What is the probability of this exact answer under the model, and what is the geometric-mean per-token probability?
options: Sequence probability about 0.25; per-token about 0.78
Sequence probability about 0.05; per-token about 0.05
Sequence probability about 0.05; per-token about 0.78
Sequence probability about 0.95; per-token about 0.99
explain: exp(-3) is about 0.05 for the whole string and exp(-3/12) = exp(-0.25) is about 0.78 per token. The same text can look confident per token and improbable as a whole, which is why sequence probabilities are rarely compared across lengths without normalization.

q: A team switches a hosted model to 'JSON mode' and is surprised when a response parses fine but lacks the required field 'total' and has 'date' as a number. What does JSON mode guarantee, and what does it not?
options: It guarantees that the output matches the schema described in the prompt, so the missing field must be a bug in how the tokenizer handles special characters
It guarantees nothing about the output text and only changes how the response is wrapped by the API
It guarantees valid JSON and correct types but not required fields, which must be enforced with a stop sequence
It guarantees syntactically valid JSON, not conformance to a particular schema; that needs schema-constrained decoding or a validator
explain: A JSON grammar knows about braces, quotes and commas, not about your field names and types. Schema-constrained decoding or a validator with a retry closes the gap.

q: A translation model is decoded with increasing beam widths. Greedy (beam 1) gives BLEU 33.0, beam 2 gives 34.5, beam 12 gives 34.8. What does this pattern show?
options: Most of the benefit of search comes from avoiding the first few greedy mistakes; wider beams give quickly diminishing returns
Beam search is a randomized procedure, so differences of this size are sampling noise and all three runs are equivalent
The gain grows with the width, so a beam of 48 should reach a BLEU of about 40 on the same test set
Greedy decoding and a beam of width 1 are different algorithms, so the first number must come from a bug
explain: Even a beam of two already repairs the cases where the best first token leads nowhere. Beyond a handful of hypotheses the extra candidates rarely change the winner, and very wide beams can even hurt by finding short, degenerate modes.

q: An encoder-decoder without attention compresses the source into one fixed vector, and its translations degrade steadily as sentences get longer. A modern decoder-only LLM writes a 3,000-token answer without such gradual decline, then fails abruptly beyond its context window. What explains the different failure shapes?
options: The LLM compresses the context into a much larger fixed vector, so the vector fills up later, but once it does the decline is just as gradual as before
With attention every earlier token stays directly addressable, so nothing fills up gradually; the hard limit is the context length the model was trained for
The LLM is trained on longer texts, so its fixed vector simply holds more information per dimension before it saturates
Decoder-only models do not condition on earlier tokens at all, so length cannot affect them until the window ends
explain: Attention replaced a bottleneck that had to hold everything with a lookup that reaches back to any position. What remains is the trained range of positions and the memory for the KV cache, both of which end at a wall rather than a slope.

q: A receipt-parsing pipeline uses grammar-constrained decoding, so every output already matches the JSON schema. The team nevertheless keeps a validation step that re-prompts the model when it fails. What does the validator still catch?
options: Syntax errors that slip through because the grammar mask is applied only after the generation has finished, when tokens that broke the schema can no longer be retracted
Outputs produced at a temperature above zero, since constrained decoding only works with greedy decoding
Values that are well-formed but wrong, such as a total that does not equal the sum of the line items, which no grammar can express
Field names in the wrong order, since the grammar enforces the types of values but not the key sequence, and most downstream JSON parsers reject keys that arrive out of schema order
explain: The grammar guarantees shape, not sense. Arithmetic consistency, dates in the future, a VAT rate that does not exist: those are semantic checks, and the validator with a retry is where they live.

q: Three tokens have probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 at temperature 1 (ignore the rest of the vocabulary). You set temperature T = 0.5, which squares the probabilities and renormalizes, and then apply nucleus sampling with p = 0.85. How many tokens survive, and how many would have survived with p = 0.85 at temperature 1?
options: 3 tokens in both cases, since the nucleus is chosen before the temperature is applied
3 tokens at T = 0.5, against 2 at temperature 1
1 token at T = 0.5, against 3 at temperature 1
2 tokens at T = 0.5, against 3 at temperature 1
explain: At T = 0.5 the distribution becomes about 0.66, 0.24, 0.11, and two tokens already cover 0.89 of the mass; at temperature 1 the first two cover only 0.80. Temperature reshapes the distribution that top-p then truncates, so the two knobs are not independent.

q: You fine-tune a model with label smoothing eps = 0.1: the training target puts 0.9 on the correct token and spreads 0.1 uniformly over the vocabulary of 50,000. Its per-token probabilities are later used as confidence scores. Even on text the model predicts perfectly, what is the lowest cross-entropy on the correct token, in nats, that the optimum of this objective allows, and the matching perplexity?
options: About 0.105 nats, perplexity about 1.11
0 nats, perplexity 1, since a perfectly predicted token stays perfectly predicted
About 0.69 nats, perplexity 2
About 10.8 nats, perplexity 50,000
explain: The smoothed objective is minimized when the model reproduces the smoothed target, so it is trained never to put more than about 0.9 on any token, and -ln 0.9 is about 0.105 nats. Smoothing can help beam-search rankings while worsening perplexity and every downstream use of the raw probabilities.

q: At some step a model's next-token distribution is 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125. Over many such steps, compare the average surprisal (-log2 p of the chosen token) of greedy decoding with that of sampling at temperature 1, and relate both to the entropy of the distribution.
options: Greedy averages 1 bit, sampling 2 bits, and the entropy is 1.5 bits
Greedy averages 1 bit per token, sampling 1.75 bits, which equals the entropy
Both average 1.75 bits, since the entropy is a property of the distribution, not of the decoder
Greedy averages 0.5 bits, sampling 1.75 bits, and the entropy is 2 bits
explain: Entropy is 0.5 x 1 + 0.25 x 2 + 0.25 x 3 = 1.75 bits, and sampling at temperature 1 hits it on average: that is what makes sampled text typical. Greedy text sits well below the entropy, which is why it reads as too predictable, while human text sits near it.

q: Beam search finishes with hypothesis X (4 tokens, total log-probability -5) and Y (16 tokens, total log-probability -12). The final score is the log-probability divided by L^alpha, where L is the length. Which hypothesis wins at alpha = 0.5, and which at alpha = 1?
options: Y at both values of alpha
X at both values of alpha
X at alpha = 0.5 and Y at alpha = 1
Y at alpha = 0.5 and X at alpha = 1
explain: At alpha = 0.5: -2.5 against -3.0, X wins; at alpha = 1: -1.25 against -0.75, Y wins. The exponent interpolates between the raw sum, which favors brevity, and the per-token mean, which forgives length; it is tuned on a dev set because no value is right for every model.

q: After supervised fine-tuning, a chat model answers correctly and then keeps going until max_tokens, inventing the user's next message and answering that too. In the training script, the end-of-turn token had been put in the same group as padding and excluded from the loss. What went wrong?
options: The repetition penalty suppresses the end-of-turn token because that token already appears in the prompt template and is counted as a prior occurrence
The temperature is too high, so the end-of-turn token loses the sampling lottery at every step
max_tokens is set too high; a lower value during training would have taught the model to stop earlier
The model was never trained to emit the end-of-turn token, so the serving stop criterion, which waits for that token, never fires
explain: Stopping is a learned behavior: the model has to put probability on the end-of-turn token at the right moment. Masking it out of the loss removes the only lesson about when a turn ends; the serving code then waits for a token the model has no reason to produce.

q: A project team benchmarks speculative decoding with one fixed draft model. On code completion it speeds generation up 2.3 times; on open-ended story writing at temperature 1.0 the gain is 1.1 times. What explains the gap?
options: Acceptance depends on how predictable the next token is: code is low-entropy, so the draft usually agrees with the target; hot sampled prose has many acceptable tokens, so the draft often misses
The draft model was trained on code, so its tokenizer differs from the target's on prose and the drafted tokens cannot be verified at all
Speculative decoding is only exact at temperature 0, so at temperature 1.0 most draft tokens must be rejected to preserve the output distribution, which removes almost all of the gain
Story outputs are longer, and the cost of verifying a draft grows quadratically with the length of the text generated so far
explain: A draft token is accepted with probability min(1, p/q), and where the target spreads its mass over many tokens the draft's guess rarely matches. The speedup measures the text's redundancy as much as the hardware.

q: A token currently has probability 0.1 at temperature 1. A support engineer in Schweinfurt wants it to come out roughly half the time and plans to add a constant to its logit. Approximately what bias is needed (logits in natural-log units), assuming the other logits stay fixed?
options: About +0.4
About +2.2
About +5.0
About +9.0
explain: Odds go from 1:9 to 1:1, and a logit shift of b multiplies the odds by exp(b), so b = ln 9, about 2.2. Adding 0.4 (the difference in probability) would barely move it; logit bias lives on the log-odds scale.

q: A well-trained model sampled at temperature 1 writes 800 tokens of fluent text, then falls into a loop repeating the same sentence. The log-probabilities show that each repetition of the sentence was more probable than the previous one. Which mechanism is at work, and why does a repetition penalty treat only the symptom?
options: The end-of-sequence probability decays with length, so the model cannot stop and fills the remaining budget with its most recent sentence, the cheapest thing it can emit; a penalty only delays this by a few tokens

Exposure bias forces the model into contexts never seen in training, where the softmax collapses to a single token because the attention keys of the drifted context match nothing learned; a penalty only re-randomizes that token
In-context copying raises the probability of a phrase each time it has appeared, a feedback loop that a penalty on recently used tokens dampens without removing the underlying preference
Temperature 1 is too low for long texts because entropy per token drops with position; a penalty only raises the temperature indirectly
explain: Models learn to copy from context, which is useful for names and harmful when it latches onto their own output: one chance repeat makes the next more likely. Penalties, top-p and lower temperature all intervene at the symptom level, which is why long samples remain the hardest regime.

q: An extraction service uses grammar-constrained decoding and reports the probability of each field value as a confidence. At one step the grammar allows only two tokens; the model's raw distribution gives them 0.04 and 0.01 and puts the remaining 0.95 on tokens the grammar forbids. What confidence does the service report for the first allowed token, and what does that number mean?
options: 0.04, the model's raw probability, since masking removes tokens but does not rescale the rest
0.95, since the forbidden mass is transferred to the top allowed token to keep the distribution normalized
0.80, a well-calibrated probability that the extracted value is correct, since the grammar only removes impossible tokens
0.80, a probability conditional on the grammar's allowed set that hides the model's 0.95 wish to write something else
explain: Masking and renormalizing gives 0.04 / 0.05 = 0.8. The confidence is relative to what the grammar allowed; the model's actual opinion, that the schema does not fit this document, was discarded. The raw mass on allowed tokens is the better warning light.

q: A team writes a constrained decoder for a grammar whose terminals are character strings, for example the literal 'true'. The tokenizer has tokens 't', 'tr', 'true', ' true' and 'trueish'. The decoder masks a token unless its string exactly equals the next expected terminal. Output quality is poor and some legal outputs are impossible to produce. What is the flaw?
options: Tokens are not grammar terminals: a legal token may cover part of a terminal or several at once, so the mask must track which tokens advance the grammar's automaton, not which equal a terminal

The mask must be applied after sampling rather than before, since the softmax needs the full vocabulary to remain properly normalized at every step; drawing a token and resampling if it is illegal is the only way to keep the distribution unbiased

The tokenizer must be retrained so that every terminal of the grammar is exactly one token, with the merges that produce 'trueish' removed; no other alignment between grammar and vocabulary is possible
The grammar must be translated into token ids by hand, since byte-pair tokenizers cannot represent terminals that begin with whitespace
explain: The same string has many tokenizations and many tokens straddle grammar symbols. Constrained decoders compile the grammar into an automaton over characters or bytes and precompute, for each state, which vocabulary tokens are valid prefixes of some legal continuation.

q: In speculative decoding, the large target model verifies 5 draft tokens in one forward pass, and at batch size 1 this pass takes about as long as generating a single token. Why is verification nearly free?
options: The draft model has already computed the target model's KV cache for the drafted tokens, so the target can skip its attention layers and only runs the feed-forward blocks during verification
At small batch each decoding pass is limited by reading the model's weights from memory once; feeding 5 positions instead of 1 reuses those reads and adds little time
The target model processes the 5 tokens one at a time but at lower numerical precision, which makes each of them about five times faster
Verification only compares the drafted token ids against the target's vocabulary, which does not require running a forward pass at all
explain: Decode at low batch is memory-bandwidth bound: the time goes to streaming the weights, not to arithmetic. Five positions per pass turn idle compute into verified tokens; the same accounting explains why batching requests raises throughput.

q: Contrastive decoding scores each token by log p_expert - log p_amateur, where the amateur is a much smaller model, and only tokens with p_expert >= alpha x max p_expert are eligible. Token A: p_expert 0.6, p_amateur 0.5. Token B: p_expert 0.001, p_amateur 0.00001. Without the eligibility rule, which token wins, and what does the rule prevent?
options: A wins (0.6 against 0.001), so the rule is only a speed optimization that prunes the vocabulary before the two models are compared
They tie, since both differences are positive and the method only looks at the sign of the contrast, and the rule breaks the tie in favor of the expert's most probable token
B wins by a wide margin (log 100 against log 1.2), so the rule exists to stop implausible tokens that the amateur finds even less plausible from being promoted
B wins, and the rule prevents the expert's top token from dominating every step, which would collapse the method to greedy decoding and reduce the diversity of the output
explain: The score is a ratio: the amateur dislikes B even more than the expert does, so B looks like a brilliant idea. The plausibility constraint keeps the contrast within tokens the expert itself considers reasonable, so the method sharpens the expert's judgment instead of amplifying noise.

q: You use an LLM as a zero-shot classifier by comparing the probabilities of full answer strings. For the description 'a thin device with a keyboard and a folding screen', 'a laptop' gets 0.30, 'a notebook' 0.20, 'a portable computer' 0.10 and 'a dog' 0.35, so 'a dog' wins. Which methodological issue is this, and what addresses it?
options: Exposure bias: the model's own earlier tokens mislead it during scoring; teacher forcing with the reference answer at test time fixes it
Tokenization leakage: the longer strings pay a per-token penalty that the short one escapes; decoding a single token greedily fixes it
Miscalibration: the probabilities do not sum to 1 over the four candidates, so the comparison is meaningless; a temperature sweep on a dev set followed by renormalization fixes it
Surface form competition: synonymous answers split the probability of one concept; restrict to one canonical label per class, or score each string relative to its probability without the input
explain: The three computer answers together carry 0.60, and any one of them alone loses to the dog. Scoring against the unconditional probability of each string (a PMI-style correction) or forcing a single canonical label per class removes the split.

q: Two ways to adapt the same pretrained transformer to answer customer questions about returns. Method 1 adds a small classification head over the final hidden state and fine-tunes it to pick one of 12 canned replies. Method 2 instruction-tunes the model to generate the reply as text. Which statement about the trade-off is correct?
options: Method 1 needs far more labelled data than Method 2, since a freshly added head starts from random weights and must be trained from nothing, while Method 2 reuses the pretrained head and converges from a handful of examples
Method 2 cannot be evaluated with accuracy, since generated text is never identical to a reference reply
Method 1 adds new parameters and can only choose among its 12 classes; Method 2 keeps the language-model head and can produce replies outside the list, including wrong ones
Method 1 trains only the head and leaves the transformer untouched, while Method 2 must retrain the token embeddings from scratch
explain: A head turns the model into a closed-set classifier: cheap, checkable, limited. Generation reuses what the model already does and opens the output space, which is where both the flexibility and the hallucinations come from.

q: A reward model is trained on human choices between two answers. The humans see only the two texts, not the model and not its reasoning, and have no time to check facts. What does the policy optimized against this reward model end up being optimized toward?
options: Toward whatever reads as better to a quick human judge, which includes confident mistakes and flattery as well as genuine quality
Toward factual correctness, since humans prefer true statements over false ones and the reward model inherits that preference exactly, whatever the raters' time budget
Toward the reference answers of the SFT stage, since the reward model is trained to recognize and reproduce them
Toward shorter answers, since judges with little time systematically prefer brevity over detail
explain: A behavioral criterion rewards appearance, and the imitation game's judge can be fooled by a good performance. Reward models inherit every bias of the raters who labelled the pairs, and a policy optimized against them finds those biases faster than the raters did.

q: A large base model, prompted with a few examples, solves translation, arithmetic and classification without any fine-tuning. Yet an instruction-tuned version of the same model was still built. Which need did prompting alone fail to cover reliably?
options: Access to facts learned after pretraining, which instruction tuning injects into the weights from the demonstrations and which no prompt could supply at inference time
Consistent instruction following, output format and refusals: a base model continues text in the prompt's style rather than doing what was asked
A larger vocabulary, since base models cannot emit tokens that were absent from their few-shot examples
Longer context windows, which only a dedicated fine-tuning stage on long documents can extend
explain: Few-shot prompting showed the capability was there; post-training made it the default behavior. Format, obedience and declining bad requests are behaviors, not knowledge, and knowledge is the one thing post-training adds least.

q: LoRA replaces the update of a 1,000 x 1,000 weight matrix by the product B A, with A of size r x 1,000 and B of size 1,000 x r. At which rank r does the adapter stop having fewer parameters than the matrix it adapts?
explain: 2 x 1,000 x r equals a million at r = 500; beyond that the adapter is bigger than a full update of the matrix. In practice ranks of 8 to 64 do most of the work, which is the finding that makes LoRA worth the trouble.

q: A reward model is built from a decoder-only LLM by replacing the language-model head with a layer that outputs one scalar. The scalar is read from the hidden state at the last token of the answer. Why the last token rather than, say, the first?
options: The last token is always the end-of-sequence token, whose embedding is trained during pretraining to store a quality score
The first token's hidden state is reserved for the positional encoding and carries no information about the content
With causal attention only the final position has attended to the whole prompt and answer, so only its state can summarize the complete text
Any position would do, since the residual stream is identical at every position after the final layer of a decoder, and the choice of the last token is only a convention
explain: In a decoder each position sees only its past. The scalar needs the whole answer in view, so it is read where the past is longest; an encoder-style model could read a dedicated first token instead.

q: You have a reward model but no time for RL. For each prompt you sample 8 answers and keep the one the reward model scores highest. Suppose each sample independently meets your quality bar with probability 0.3 and the reward model reliably recognizes that. What is the probability the returned answer meets the bar, and what did it cost?
options: About 0.94, at eight times the generation cost and with no change to the weights
About 0.30, since selection cannot change the per-sample probability of a good answer
Exactly 1.0, since eight samples always guarantee at least one good answer
About 0.94, and the policy improves permanently after a few hundred such prompts
explain: 1 - 0.7^8 is about 0.94. Best-of-n is alignment at inference time: it works immediately, scales with the compute you pay per query and teaches the model nothing; the same samples can later become training data.

q: A project team compares its fine-tuned model with the hosted model it is meant to replace by asking a judge model which of two answers is better. The tuned answer is always placed first, and it wins 70% of pairs. The night before the roadshow someone swaps the order, and now the hosted model wins 65%. What should the team conclude?
options: The two runs average to a tie, so the models are equivalent and either number can be reported as long as the ordering is mentioned in a footnote
The judge has a position bias; each pair must be judged in both orders and the verdicts combined before any win rate is reported
The judge is broken and should be replaced by exact-match comparison against the hosted model's outputs
Swapping the order changes the prompts the judge sees, so the second run is invalid and the 70% stands
explain: Judges favor a position, often the first, and a fixed order turns that into a result. Judging both orders and counting only consistent wins, or averaging, is the minimum; checking agreement with a few dozen human labels is the rest.

q: An old fine-tuning recipe adds the language-modeling loss on the training text itself to the task loss, with weight 0.5. A modern team instead mixes 10% general instruction data into a domain-specific SFT set. What do the two practices share, and what does neither of them do?
options: Both speed up convergence by doubling the gradient signal per example, so the same accuracy is reached in about half the steps; neither has any effect on what the model forgets
Both regularize by shrinking the weights toward their pretrained values, in the manner of an L2 penalty on the parameter delta; neither interacts with the learning rate or the number of epochs
Both are forms of knowledge distillation from a larger model; neither applies when the model is trained with a small learning rate
Both keep the model exercising its general next-token skill during adaptation so it drifts less from pretraining; neither adds domain knowledge beyond the fine-tuning text
explain: An auxiliary LM loss and replay of general data are two ways of reminding the model what it already knew. They slow forgetting, cost compute and change nothing about the model's facts, which come from pretraining and from the fine-tuning text itself.

q: One network learns five tasks from a shared representation. Task A has 500,000 examples; tasks B, C, D and E have 10,000 each. Training examples are sampled in proportion to dataset size. What share of training steps goes to task A, and what is the usual remedy in modern instruction mixtures?
options: About 20%; each task gets equal steps by construction, so no remedy is needed
About 50%; mixture weights are set per task family rather than per dataset, which halves the share of A
About 93%; cap or down-weight large tasks, for example by sampling proportional to size raised to a power below 1
About 93%; add a separate output head per task so that the small tasks are shielded from A and the shared representation is not distorted by it
explain: 500 / 540 is about 0.93: four tasks share the remaining 7%. Shared representations are the easy part; deciding how much of each task the model sees is the part that still gets tuned by hand, in instruction mixtures as in the old multitask nets.

q: For SFT a team adds two new special tokens for the user and assistant roles to the tokenizer, then trains LoRA adapters on the attention projections only. The model never learns to respect turn boundaries, and the embeddings of the new tokens are identical before and after training. Why?
options: The new token ids map to freshly initialized rows of the embedding matrix and the output layer, which were frozen, so nothing about them could be learned
LoRA cannot change the model's behavior on tokens that were absent from pretraining, since the adapters only act on existing directions; only full fine-tuning can introduce new tokens
The special tokens must be registered with the tokenizer's normalizer, otherwise they are split into bytes before the model sees them
Attention projections do not see embeddings directly, so the adapters never receive gradients from the positions of these tokens
explain: A new token is only a row of random numbers until something trains it. Either make the embedding and unembedding rows trainable, at least for the new ids, or reuse existing tokens for the template.

q: A team runs LoRA on a 7B model, adapting only the query and value projections at rank 8. Raising the rank to 64 barely changes the result. Adding adapters to all linear layers, including the MLP blocks, at rank 8 improves it clearly. What is the most plausible reading?
options: Rank 64 violates the low-rank assumption behind the method, so an adapter must stay at rank 8 or below to train at all
The MLP blocks hold most of each layer's parameters and were receiving no adaptation at all; coverage of matrices mattered more than capacity per adapted matrix
Query and value projections are frozen by default in common PEFT libraries unless the target modules are named explicitly, so the first two runs trained nothing and the result is noise

The MLP adapters act as a regularizer that lowers the effective learning rate of the attention adapters and stabilizes them, which is why the gain appears although the MLP blocks themselves need no adaptation
explain: Two thirds of a transformer layer is the feed-forward block, and an adapter that never touches it leaves most of the model's function fixed. Rank is capacity per matrix; which matrices you adapt decides where that capacity can act.

q: Your SFT set has 20,000 examples averaging 600 tokens, of which about 200 per example are the assistant's answer. You train 3 epochs, and the GPU processes 2,000 tokens per second for forward plus backward. A colleague says the loss mask on the prompt tokens will cut the time by two thirds. How long does training take?
options: About 1.7 hours; masked tokens are skipped entirely by the forward and backward passes, so only the 200 answer tokens per example cost any compute
About 15 hours; the mask forces a second pass over the answer tokens in every epoch
About 5 hours per epoch, so 15 hours; the mask changes nothing about the compute and each epoch reprocesses all 36 million tokens
About 5 hours; the mask zeroes the prompt tokens' loss, but they still pass through the forward and backward computation
explain: 20,000 x 600 x 3 = 36 million tokens at 2,000 per second is 18,000 seconds, five hours. Masking decides what is learned from, not what is computed; the prompt tokens are the context the answer attends to, so they cannot be dropped.

q: You train with group-normalized advantages: 8 samples per prompt, each reward minus the group mean, divided by the group's standard deviation (population form). Correctness gives 1.0, but early on no sample is ever correct, so you add a format reward of 0.1 for using the required answer tags. In one group, 2 of 8 samples use the tags. What advantages result?
options: About +0.1 for the two formatted samples and 0 for the rest, since the reward is tiny
About +0.075 and -0.025, the raw deviations from the group mean of 0.025, since the standard deviation is only used once correctness rewards are present
About +1.7 for the two formatted samples and about -0.6 for the other six, the same as if the format reward had been 1.0
Zero for all eight, since the correctness reward is zero everywhere in the group
explain: Mean 0.025, standard deviation about 0.043, so +0.075 / 0.043 is about 1.7 and -0.025 / 0.043 about -0.6. Normalization throws away the reward's scale and keeps only its ranking within the group, which is why a small shaping reward moves the policy and a group with identical rewards moves nothing.

q: A draft-and-improve tool logs how users edit generated reply emails and turns each edit into a preference pair: the draft is rejected, the edited version is chosen. Many edits insert details only the user knew, such as an order number or a delivery date, that were nowhere in the prompt. What does training on these pairs teach the model?
options: To produce such specifics without any basis, since the chosen answers contain information the model could not have had; those details belong in the prompt or the pairs must be dropped
Nothing harmful: DPO only compares the two answers, so content that appears in the chosen answer but is absent from the prompt cancels out of the loss against the reference model's log-ratio
To refuse when details are missing, since the model learns that the drafts lacking them were the rejected ones and that asking the user for the missing facts is the chosen behaviour
To copy the user's writing style, which is the only property a preference pair can transmit to the policy
explain: The pair says 'the answer with the order number was better', not 'the order number was known'. A model rewarded for unverifiable specifics learns to invent them; put the facts in the context, or cut edits that add information rather than improve wording.

q: A policy is optimized against human approval of its answers. On a hard task two directions raise approval: making answers more often correct, or making wrong answers harder for the judge to detect. Suppose the second is cheaper for the optimizer. What should you expect, and what is the methodological lesson?
options: Approval and accuracy rise together, since persuasiveness without correctness cannot be learned from pairwise labels alone; the judge's ratings are consistent only when the content is right
Approval rises while accuracy stalls and the judges' error detection gets worse; approval must be anchored by checks the judge cannot be talked out of, such as verifiable outcomes
Approval falls, because the KL penalty keeps the policy near the reference and blocks any change in presentation
Accuracy rises faster than approval, since the judge's confusion adds label noise that regularizes the policy and keeps it from overfitting to presentation
explain: An imitation-game criterion rewards convincing the judge, and optimization follows the cheapest gradient toward that. Ground-truth checks are the only thing that separates being right from sounding right, so they belong in the training signal or at least in the evaluation.

q: A Bradley-Terry reward model, P(i beats j) = sigmoid(r_i - r_j), is trained on pairwise human labels. Annotators preferred A over B 75% of the time and B over C 75% of the time, and the model fits both exactly. What does the model imply for P(A beats C), and what does this reveal about the model class?
options: 0.75: the model assigns the same confidence to every comparison it has seen or inferred
0.56: the probabilities multiply, 0.75 x 0.75, since the two comparisons are independent events and the model has no other way to combine them
Undefined: the model has no information about A against C until such a pair is labelled
0.90: scalar rewards force a transitive, additive structure, so cyclic or context-dependent human preferences cannot be represented
explain: Two gaps of ln 3 add to ln 9, and sigmoid(ln 9) = 0.9. A single scalar per answer makes every preference transitive by construction, which is a convenience when humans are consistent and a model error when they are not.

q: A team fine-tunes a small model on 1,000 examples of a tagging task and reports that it beats the zero-shot base model by 20 points. Reviewer #2 asks for the base model with 5 in-context examples: the gap shrinks to 3 points, and five training seeds of the tuned model spread over 4 points. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Fine-tuning has failed, since the prompted model is equivalent and cheaper per query than the tuned one
The 20-point gain stands, since zero-shot is the standard baseline for fine-tuned models in the literature and in-context examples are a different method altogether
The fair baseline is the prompted base model; the measured gain is within seed noise and needs more seeds or more data before it can be claimed
The few-shot run is unfair, since in-context examples count as training data that the tuned model never saw
explain: Zero-shot flatters any fine-tune; the question is what the base model does when it is told what the task is. Three points inside a four-point seed spread is not yet a result, though the tuned model may still win on cost per query, which is a different claim.

q: A team improves a math model by sampling 16 solutions per problem, keeping those with the correct final answer and running SFT on them. After several rounds the model's top-ranked solutions are good, but the probability of its typical wrong solutions has hardly moved. Why, and which family of methods fixes this directly?
options: Discarded wrong samples contribute no gradient, so their probability falls only through normalization; preference or policy-gradient methods use them as negatives and push them down explicitly

SFT on self-generated data cannot change the model at all, since the samples come from its own distribution and the gradient of the log-likelihood is zero in expectation whatever subset of samples is kept
The correct solutions are too similar to each other, so their SFT gradients cancel; sampling at a higher temperature fixes it

Correct answers were selected by string match on the final line, which teaches the model the answer format rather than the reasoning and leaves the wrong solutions untouched; a verifier that checks each step fixes it
explain: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning only ever says 'more of this'. Pushing probability toward the kept samples lowers the rest a little and indiscriminately; DPO-style pairs or RL with a reward of zero on wrong samples name the failures and penalize them.

q: With group-normalized advantages and a binary reward, each sample's advantage is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group's standard deviation (population form). In a group where exactly 2 of 10 samples are correct, what advantage does each correct sample receive, and what follows for which prompts drive learning?
options: +1 for each correct sample and 0 for each wrong one, since the normalization only rescales rewards into the unit interval; every prompt contributes in proportion to its number of correct samples
+2 for each correct sample and -0.5 for each wrong one; rare successes on hard prompts get the largest per-sample push, while prompts solved by all or none contribute nothing
+0.8 for each correct and -0.2 for each wrong; easy prompts dominate because they have more correct samples per group

+0.2 for each correct and -0.8 for each wrong, the mean and the mean minus one; the signal is strongest for prompts the model already solves most of the time, since these supply the most positive samples per group
explain: Mean 0.2, standard deviation sqrt(0.2 x 0.8) = 0.4, so (1 - 0.2) / 0.4 = 2 and (0 - 0.2) / 0.4 = -0.5. Normalization makes a lucky success on a hard prompt loud and a routine success on an easy one quiet, and prompts at 0% or 100% fall silent, so curating prompts by pass rate is part of the method.
