q: You run DPO on 20,000 preference pairs whose answers were all generated by last year's model. The loss falls nicely, yet on fresh prompts the new policy's own failures, which look nothing like the rejected answers in the data, are untouched. What is the limitation, and what is the usual remedy?
options: Beta is too large, so the policy cannot move far enough from the reference to reach the new failure modes; lowering it lets the existing pairs generalize to failures the data never shows

The reference model must be last year's model rather than the SFT model, since the pairs were sampled from it; swapping it aligns the implicit reward with the pairs and restores the signal on fresh prompts
DPO cannot use pairs with answers from any other model; the pairs must be regenerated by the reference model before training can begin
The pairs are off-policy: they describe another model's mistakes, so the current policy's mistakes are never penalized; sample new pairs from the current policy and label them, iteratively or online
explain: A preference pair teaches a contrast between two specific answers. If the policy now fails in other ways, nothing in the data points at those failures; re-sampling from the current policy and labelling the new pairs, by humans or a judge, keeps the signal where the policy actually is.

q: Asked whether it is a human, a chat model says plainly that it is an AI. A columnist concludes that the model 'fails the Turing test and therefore cannot reason'. What is wrong with the inference?
options: The imitation game is a sufficient criterion, not a necessary one: failing to pass as human shows nothing about reasoning
The test is only failed when the judge is a trained linguist, so a columnist is in no position to declare a failure
The test requires the machine to claim to be human, so an honest answer counts as a pass rather than a failure
The test measures reasoning directly, so the inference is valid and the model has indeed been shown unable to reason
explain: Imitation was offered as a behavioural criterion a thinking machine could meet, never as one it must meet; a machine that declines to pretend has simply not entered the game. The reverse inference is as sound as concluding that someone who refuses a chess match cannot play.

q: A chat arena shows a user two anonymous answers to the same question and reveals the model names only after the vote. Which feature of the imitation game does this inherit, and what does it buy?
options: The time limit on the conversation, which keeps the judges from tiring and voting at random
The text-only channel, which removes identity cues so that the vote rests on the behaviour shown
The requirement that one participant is human, which anchors every vote to a human baseline
The expert judge, which guarantees that the votes reflect correctness rather than writing style
explain: Turing put the players behind a teleprinter so the judge could not vote on faces or voices; the arena hides the logos for the same reason. The judges are still whoever shows up, so style can still win.

q: On a three-way natural language inference benchmark, a model that sees only the hypothesis and never the premise reaches 67% accuracy. A fine-tuned encoder that sees both reaches 90%. What does the 67% tell you?
options: The task is impossible without the premise, so the 67% can only come from a leak of the test labels
The hypothesis-only model is the stronger architecture and should replace the encoder in production
Chance on three classes is 33%, so 67% shows that the hypothesis-only model is already a solid inference system
Annotators left cues in the hypotheses, so a large part of the task can be solved without doing it
explain: Writers of contradictions reach for negation and writers of entailments shorten the premise, and a model learns the habits of annotators instead of inference. The 90% is real on this test set and says less about inference than it appears to.

q: An LLM judge agrees with a human label on 85% of 200 answers. The project team, the night before its roadshow, wants to call this 'near-human'. Which number do they need before the claim means anything?
options: The agreement between two independent human annotators on the same 200 answers
The agreement of the judge with itself when the same 200 answers are scored a second time
The accuracy of the judged model on the 200 answers, to rule out a test set that is too easy
The agreement of the judge with a second LLM judge taken from a different model family
explain: If two humans agree on 80% of the items, 85% is at the ceiling the labels allow; if they agree on 98%, the judge is far behind. Agreement with humans is read against how much humans agree with each other.

q: A model scores 71% on a 500-item benchmark and you attach a 95% binomial confidence interval of about 67% to 75%. Which source of variation does this interval account for?
options: The sampling of the 500 items from the population of possible test items
The choice of prompt wording, since each item was shown with one template
The randomness of training, since another run would produce other weights
The sampling temperature at decoding, since it changes which answer comes out
explain: The binomial interval treats the items as a random sample and asks how far the score would move with another 500 of them. Prompts, seeds and decoding are held fixed, and each can move the score by more than the interval is wide.

q: A team needs a gold set to evaluate its claim-verification system. Short on time, they let the same LLM that powers the system label 100 sentences as supported or not, then report 97% accuracy against this gold. What did they measure?
options: The system's accuracy, since a gold set is a gold set whoever produces it
The agreement of the system with itself, since the gold is the model's own opinion
An upper bound on accuracy, since model labels are stricter than human labels would be
The inter-annotator agreement of the team, since the model acted as one more annotator
explain: The gold set and the system share the same source of error, so the 3% is mostly sampling noise and the 97% says nothing about the world. Humans label the gold; the model is the thing being graded.

q: An LLM judge is told to answer with a score from 1 to 5. Your code reads the first digit of the reply and stores 0 when it finds none. After a change to the judge prompt, the mean score of system B drops from 3.9 to 3.1. Before concluding that B got worse, what should you do first?
options: Read a sample of the raw judge replies and count how many were parsed as 0
Rerun the judge at temperature 0 so that the scores become deterministic
Switch the judge to a 1 to 10 scale to get a finer resolution of the drop
Add a second judge and average the two, so that one judge's bias cannot dominate
explain: A judge that now writes 'Score: four out of five' is parsed as zero, and zeros pull a mean down faster than any real regression. Metrics are computed after the raw outputs have been looked at, not instead.

q: Two language models are compared on the same English test text. Model A, with a 32k-token vocabulary, reaches 2.0 bits per token and its tokens average 4 bytes. Model B, with a 128k-token vocabulary, reaches 2.4 bits per token and its tokens average 5 bytes. Which model compresses the text better, and by how much?
options: Model A, at 0.50 against 0.48 bits per byte
Model B, at 0.48 against 0.50 bits per byte
Model A, since 2.0 bits per token is the lower figure
Neither can be said, since bits per token cannot be converted
explain: Bits per byte is bits per token divided by bytes per token: 2.0/4 = 0.50 for A and 2.4/5 = 0.48 for B. Per-token perplexity (4.0 against 5.3) says the opposite because B pays for more text with each prediction; the information-theoretic quantity is per unit of source, not per tokenizer decision.

q: An old word-level language model with a 10,000-word vocabulary maps 4% of the test tokens to a single UNK symbol and reports perplexity 80. A byte-level model on the same text, with no UNK, reports 95 per word. A student at 3 a.m. concludes the old model is the better predictor. What is the flaw?
options: Byte-level models always have higher perplexity, so the two numbers are not of the same kind at all
Perplexity should be reported per sentence rather than per word, which reverses the order of the two
Predicting UNK is cheap: the old model never pays for spelling the rare words it replaced
The 4% UNK rate shows that the test set is contaminated with words from another domain
explain: Every rare word collapses into one frequent symbol that is easy to predict, so the closed-vocabulary model is scored on a simplified text. The byte-level model is charged for every character of 'Schweinfurt'; the comparison is fair only when both pay for the same string.

q: A benchmark has 1,000 items and your model scores 80% on all of them. An overlap check flags 300 items as present in the training data. On the remaining 700 clean items the model scores 77%. What is its score on the 300 flagged items, and what does the gap suggest?
options: 80%: contamination has no effect here, since the overall score is unchanged
83%: a modest gap that lies within the noise of a 300-item subset
87%: a 10-point gap that points to memorized answers on the flagged items
93%: the flagged items are nearly saturated, so the whole benchmark is unusable
explain: 800 correct in total minus 0.77 * 700 = 539 leaves 261 of 300, or 87%. Ten points between seen and unseen items is the fingerprint of memorization; report the clean-subset score, with the caveat that an n-gram check misses paraphrased leaks.

q: You want to tell two models apart when their true accuracies differ by 2 points, both near 50%, with each model evaluated on its own random set of items (unpaired). You require the observed gap to be at least two standard errors of the difference. Roughly how many items per model do you need?
options: About 500
About 1,250
About 5,000
About 20,000
explain: The standard error of the difference is sqrt(2 * 0.25 / n); setting 2 * SE = 0.02 gives SE = 0.01, so 0.5/n = 1e-4 and n = 5,000. Running both models on the same items and testing the discordant pairs is how you get away with far fewer.

q: Two candidate models are each compared pairwise to the same baseline on 200 prompts by a judge who may declare ties. Model A: 110 wins, 60 ties, 30 losses. Model B: 120 wins, 0 ties, 80 losses. Which model beats the baseline by the larger margin?
options: Model B under both conventions, since it has more outright wins and ties never count
Model A under both conventions, since it loses to the baseline far less often than B does
They are equal, since both are preferred to the baseline on a majority of the prompts
Model A if ties count as half a win (70% vs 60%), Model B if only wins are counted (55% vs 60%)
explain: A: (110 + 30)/200 = 0.70 with ties as half, 110/200 = 0.55 by raw wins; B: 0.60 either way. The ranking is a property of the tie rule, so the rule belongs in the table next to the number.

q: A team tries 20 prompt variants against their default prompt on the same 300-item dev set and tests each difference at the 5% level. Exactly one variant comes out significantly better. The founder wants to ship it. What is the sober expectation?
options: The variant is a real improvement, since the test controlled the error rate at 5% for each comparison
The result is real only if the variant is also the longest prompt, since extra length adds information
Nineteen variants failing proves the default is near optimal, so none of them should ship
About one false positive is expected among 20 null comparisons, so this result needs a fresh item set
explain: Twenty tests at 5% produce one spurious winner on average when nothing works, which is exactly what was observed. Confirm the chosen variant on items it was not selected on, or correct for the multiple comparisons.

q: A RAG system is tested on 100 answerable and 50 unanswerable questions. It refuses 45 of the 50 unanswerable ones and also refuses 30 of the 100 answerable ones. A second system refuses every question. Which comparison is the fair one?
options: System one refuses 90% of the unanswerable questions and system two refuses 100%, so system two is the safer system to ship, since a refusal can never be a hallucination and costs nothing
System one answers 70% of the answerable and refuses 90% of the unanswerable; system two scores 0% and 100%: refusal must be read with the answer rate
System one has an overall refusal rate of 50%, which is close to ideal when a third of the questions have no answer in the corpus
The refusal rates cannot be compared, since the unanswerable set is only half the size of the answerable set and needs upweighting before either rate is meaningful
explain: Refusing everything maximizes the refusal metric for free, so it is a pair of numbers or nothing: 70/90 against 0/100. Set sizes do not matter for rates, and the 50% overall figure mixes two behaviours that should be judged apart.

q: A model reaches 92% on a reading comprehension benchmark and the announcement says it 'understands text'. A critic in the Chinese-room tradition replies that the score shows only symbol manipulation. What does the score itself actually license?
options: A claim about behaviour on that distribution of items; whether to call it understanding is settled by a definition and further evidence, not by the number
A refutation of the critic, since the room argument predicts that a pure symbol manipulator would score near chance on comprehension items
A claim of understanding, since the score exceeds the human baseline measured on the same benchmark under the same conditions
Nothing at all, since only an inspection of the internal mechanism can establish any property of a model
explain: The Chinese room grants perfect behaviour and denies the conclusion, so no score can answer it, and no score needs to. The benchmark measures what it samples; 'understanding' is a construct that has to be defined and validated before a number can speak to it.

q: Two groups train the same translation model. Group A, as decided before training, evaluates the weight average of the last five checkpoints. Group B evaluates all 50 checkpoints on the test set and reports the best one, 0.6 BLEU above A. What is the sober reading?
options: B's procedure is better, since it uses more information about the model's training trajectory
A's procedure is flawed, since averaging the weights of different checkpoints produces a model nobody trained
The numbers are equivalent, since both groups used the same test set and the same architecture
B's figure is biased upward by selecting on the test set; 0.6 is about what the maximum of 50 noisy scores yields
explain: Choosing a checkpoint by test score turns the test set into a development set, and the maximum of fifty noisy numbers sits well above their mean. Averaging checkpoints is a legitimate recipe because it was fixed without looking; the selection, not the averaging, is the problem.

q: A model solves 95% of the items of a classic false-belief test of theory of mind. When object names, locations and character names are replaced by made-up ones and the sentence order is lightly varied, with the logic untouched, accuracy falls to 55%. What does this show about the benchmark score?
options: The model lacks theory of mind entirely, since any capacity for the construct would give the same score on both versions and a drop of this size can only mean rote recall
The perturbed items are unfair, since made-up names are out of distribution for any reader, human or model
The 95% measured familiarity with the item template as much as the construct; a construct should survive surface variation
The two scores should be averaged to 75%, which is the model's true level on the construct being measured, since the original and perturbed items are two equally valid samples of it
explain: A construct is what stays constant when the wording changes; a score that collapses under renaming was tracking the wording. The 55% still beats a coin flip, so the model has something; just less than the headline.

q: In pairwise votes, model A beats B 60% of the time, B beats C 60% of the time, and C beats A 60% of the time, with hundreds of votes per pair. You fit a Bradley-Terry model to produce a leaderboard. What comes out, and what does it hide?
options: A ranks first because it is listed first, and the fit reports the cycle as a convergence warning
The three get nearly equal ratings, predicting 50% for every pair; the cycle is invisible on the leaderboard
The fit fails to converge, since a cycle of preferences has no maximum likelihood solution and the ratings drift apart without bound as the optimizer runs
C ranks first, since beating the top model A counts for more than beating the weaker model B, and the fit weights each win by the strength of the opponent
explain: Bradley-Terry assigns one scalar per model and can only express transitive preferences, so a symmetric cycle is fit by a three-way tie. The leaderboard looks tidy; the 60/40 structure, which may come from different item types, shows only in the pairwise table.

q: A team optimizes its chatbot's prompts and fine-tuning data against an LLM judge. Over four iterations the judge's score rises from 6.1 to 8.7 out of 10, while a blind human preference test against the first version stays at 50%. What is the most likely reading?
options: The humans are the problem: untrained raters cannot perceive improvements that a careful judge can, so the judge's score is the more reliable measurement of quality
The judge is mis-scaled: a 2.6-point gain on a 10-point scale is too small for humans to detect
The human test is underpowered because 50% is exactly the chance level and cannot move until the difference is large enough for a majority of raters to agree
The optimization found what the judge rewards rather than what humans prefer; a metric under optimization stops being a measurement
explain: Length, confident tone and rubric vocabulary are cheap to produce and the judge pays for them; the human preference stays flat because nothing a human values changed. A judge validated against humans before optimization needs revalidation after it.

q: On 300 team-labelled examples, a fine-tuned small encoder scores 86% accuracy at 3 ms and a fraction of a cent per thousand requests; a prompted LLM scores 88% at 900 ms and roughly a hundred times the cost. The founder wants the LLM because 'it is more accurate'. Using the binomial standard error, what does the table actually support?
options: The LLM is more accurate by about one standard error, which is decisive at this sample size because a difference that survives one standard error is reproducible
The encoder is more accurate once cost is factored in, since accuracy per euro is the right metric
The 2-point gap is about one standard error (roughly 1.9 points) and may not exist, while the 300x latency and 100x cost gaps are certain
Neither model can be evaluated on 300 examples; at least 3,000 are needed before any conclusion is allowed, since the binomial approximation only holds above that size
explain: sqrt(0.87 * 0.13 / 300) is about 0.019, so the quality difference is a coin flip on this set while the engineering differences are measured facts. Decide on the certain numbers, or label more data until the uncertain one speaks.

q: A spam message reads 'y0ur acc0unt is susp3nded'. Your German flatmate reads it without slowing down; a small fine-tuned classifier that caught the clean version lets it through. In Shannon's terms, what protects the reader and not the model?
options: The redundancy of English: context fixes most of a corrupted word, and the reader has learned to exploit it, while the classifier sees unfamiliar token fragments
The channel capacity of vision: a reader processes more bits per second than a text classifier can, so the corruption is absorbed before it registers
The entropy of digits: numbers carry more information than letters, so the reader gives them less weight and the classifier gives them more
The noiseless coding of the alphabet: letters and look-alike digits share one code in human memory, so the substitution is invisible to the reader
explain: Shannon put the redundancy of English near one half, which is why half-garbled words are still readable: the context carries the rest. The tokenizer splits 'susp3nded' into pieces the classifier has rarely seen with a label, so the redundancy is there but the model never learned to use it; training on noisy copies teaches it.

q: Two named-entity taggers are trained on the same 10,000 labelled sentences. One uses hand-made features such as capitalization and a gazetteer of known names; the other uses word vectors pretrained on a large unlabelled corpus. Both meet a company name that appears nowhere in the labelled data. Which one has the better chance, and why?
options: The hand-feature tagger, since capitalization alone identifies a name in any language and any text genre
The pretrained-vector tagger, since the name may have appeared in the unlabelled text in contexts that place it near other company names
Neither, since a word that is absent from the labelled data cannot be tagged by any supervised model
The hand-feature tagger, since a gazetteer is maintained by hand and therefore more complete than any corpus, and the capitalization feature backs it up on names the gazetteer lacks
explain: The labelled set is small, the unlabelled corpus is not, and a company name that was followed by 'announced quarterly results' a few thousand times has a vector that already looks like a company. Hand features cover what their authors foresaw; distributional features cover what the corpus saw.

q: Case one: a user types a long role-play preamble to get a chat model to produce content it is trained to refuse. Case two: a travel agent summarizing a hotel page follows hidden text on that page telling it to book a room. What distinguishes the two attacks?
options: Case one needs white-box access to the weights to craft the preamble, while case two works through ordinary queries alone and needs no access at all
Case one is the user against the model's policy; case two is a third party's text instructing a model that acts for someone else
Case one is a training-time attack through poisoned data that plants the role-play trigger, while case two happens at inference time
Case one is only possible with open-weight models that can be run locally, while case two is only possible with hosted ones behind an API
explain: A jailbreak is the user against the model's rules; an injection is untrusted content against the user, with the model as the confused deputy. The defenses differ accordingly: refusal training for the first, privilege limits for the second.

q: A model refuses a harmful request in plain English but complies when the same request is encoded in base64, which it decodes without being asked. Which mechanism best explains the gap?
options: Base64 strings have high perplexity, which switches the model into a code-completion mode where refusal behaviour is not active and the content of the decoded request is never evaluated
The decoding step consumes the context window, so the system prompt that carries the safety rules is pushed out of view
The ability to read base64 came from pretraining over a wide distribution; refusal training covered a narrower distribution of phrasings that did not include it
Base64 is a form of encryption, and models are trained not to interpret encrypted content as instructions of any kind, so the decoded text is treated as data to echo rather than as a request
explain: Pretraining teaches the model to understand far more than safety training teaches it to refuse, and the gap between the two generalizations is where encodings, rare languages and ciphers live. Nothing was pushed out of the window; the request simply arrived in a dialect the rules never met.

q: A membership inference attack labels a text as 'seen in training' whenever the model's loss on it is below a threshold. It flags 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' and a list of the weekdays, both of which were deliberately kept out of the training set. What is the fix?
options: Lower the loss threshold until these two sentences are no longer flagged, then keep that stricter threshold fixed for every text the attack is later run on
Compare the model's loss with a reference model's loss on the same text, so predictable text is not mistaken for memorized text
Measure the loss only on the first token of each text, since memorization shows up at the start and the rest of the text adds noise
Use accuracy instead of loss, since loss is not defined for text that lies outside the training set
explain: Some text is easy for every model, and a raw loss threshold confuses 'easy' with 'seen'. Calibrating against a reference model, or against the model's own loss on perturbed versions, asks the right question: is this text easier for you than it should be?

q: A sentiment model's explanation highlights the words 'wonderful' and 'warm' in a positive review. A colleague at the conference bar says the highlights are 'clearly right'. What has she established about the explanation?
options: That it is faithful: the model's decision was in fact caused by those two words
That it is complete: no other words in the review contributed to the decision
That it is robust: the same two words would be highlighted for any paraphrase of the review and for any model trained on the same data
That it is plausible: a human finds it convincing, which is a separate property from whether it reflects the model's computation
explain: Plausibility is judged by people, faithfulness by intervening on the model, and the two come apart regularly: a highlight that reads well can be produced by a method that ignores the model. Delete the two words and watch the prediction; that is the start of a faithfulness check.

q: A red team runs 200 jailbreak prompts. A keyword judge counts a success whenever the reply lacks 'I cannot' or 'I'm sorry' and reports 60 successes. A human reads the replies and finds 20 that contain the requested harmful content; the rest are off-topic, evasive or fictional fluff. What are the two attack success rates, and which one is the metric?
options: 30% and 10%; the keyword judge's rate, since it is reproducible and the human reading is subjective and cannot be rerun on the next model version
60% and 20%; the human rate, since percentages of the harmful prompts are what matter in a red-team report and the keyword count is only a ceiling
30% and 10%; the human rate, since attack success means the harm was produced, and a non-refusal is not a success
30% and 10%; their average of 20%, since both judges carry information and neither is perfect
explain: 60/200 and 20/200. The keyword judge measures the absence of a refusal template, which a reply can lack while also lacking the harmful content; the metric is defined by the harm, so the judge must be validated against a human reading of the raw replies.

q: A support engineer in Schweinfurt shows a heatmap: in layer 20 of a 24-layer model, the output token attends strongly to the input word 'not', and he concludes the model 'used the negation'. In an early one-layer attention translation model, an alignment matrix was a fair guide to which source word fed which target word. Why is the layer-20 heatmap much weaker evidence?
options: Deep models use multi-head attention, and heads cannot be read individually because their outputs are concatenated before the projection, so no single head's weights mean anything on their own
Attention weights in deep models are not normalized to sum to one, so the heatmap colours are not comparable across rows
Layer 20 is too close to the output to attend to input words at all; its weights reflect previously generated output tokens only
By layer 20 the vector at the position of 'not' is a mixture of the whole context, so the weight says where information was read from, not what that information was
explain: In the early model the attended state was close to one source word's embedding, so weight meant word; after twenty residual layers the position labelled 'not' may carry anything. Attention is a routing diagram; what flowed through the route needs a different instrument.

q: Linear probes for part-of-speech tags reach 97% at layer 6 of a 12-layer encoder and 88% at layer 12. A student writes that 'the model forgets syntax in the upper layers'. What is the sounder reading?
options: The upper layers are undertrained, since information can only be lost through insufficient gradient signal reaching them from the masked-token loss at the top
The student is right, and the 9-point drop measures how many bits of syntax the model has discarded by the top
Linear decodability dropped, which means the information became less linearly accessible or entangled with other features, not that it is gone
The probe at layer 12 overfits, since the top layer has more dimensions than the middle layers and therefore needs more labelled data to fit
explain: A linear probe measures the geometry of a representation, not its content: a nonlinear probe or an intervention may find the tags intact. Lower accuracy for a linear reader says the upper layers organized the space around something else, which is what they are for.

q: You test an occupational gender association with the template 'The {occupation} said that' and read the next-token probabilities. For one occupation, P(' he') = 0.64 and P(' she') = 0.16. What is log2 of the ratio P(' he') / P(' she'), and what is the main caveat before reporting it as a bias of the model?
options: 2 bits; it comes from one template, and such associations are sensitive to wording and say nothing yet about downstream decisions
4 bits; the model is four times more likely to produce 'he', an association that transfers directly to any hiring or screening decision the model is later asked to make
0.48 bits; the difference of the two probabilities is the standard measure of association in this setting and needs no logarithm
2 bits; the caveat is that log2 should be replaced by the natural logarithm when the inputs are probabilities rather than counts
explain: log2(0.64 / 0.16) = log2(4) = 2. A pronoun probability after one template is an association in the pretraining distribution; whether it shows up in a CV screen or a story is a separate measurement with its own counterfactual design.

q: A team builds an 'honesty' steering vector as the mean difference of residual activations between prompts answered honestly and prompts answered deceptively. Added at inference, it makes answers noticeably shorter and more formal, with little change in honesty scores. On inspection, the honest examples were short and formal and the deceptive ones long and chatty. What went wrong?
options: Steering vectors can only encode style, so an honesty vector was never a possibility in the first place
The vector was added at the wrong layer; honesty is represented in the embedding layer and style in the upper layers, so a middle-layer vector can only move style
The coefficient was too small; a larger multiple of the same vector would push the model past style and into honesty, which is the stronger signal
The mean difference captures every systematic difference between the two sets, so the vector encodes length and register along with honesty
explain: A contrast direction is only as clean as the contrast: whatever differs between the two sets on average goes into it. Match the pairs on length, topic and tone so that honesty is the only thing left to differ.

q: To detect hallucination you sample five answers to 'Which river runs through Würzburg?': 'The Main', 'the Main river', 'The Main', 'The Danube', 'The Danube'. Entropy over distinct strings treats each wording as its own outcome; semantic entropy first clusters the answers by meaning. In bits, what do the two give?
options: Strings: about 1.52 bits; meanings: about 0.97 bits
Strings: about 2.32 bits; meanings: about 0.97 bits
Strings: about 1.52 bits; meanings: 0 bits
Strings: about 2.32 bits; meanings: exactly 1 bit
explain: Strings have counts 2, 1, 2: 2 * 0.4 * log2(2.5) + 0.2 * log2(5) = 1.52 bits; meanings are 3 against 2: 0.97 bits. The string version counts a paraphrase as doubt, the meaning version counts the real disagreement, and the Danube is somebody else's river.

q: A PII guardrail is tested on 200 adversarial inputs that each hide one identifier, and on 1,000 ordinary messages with no PII. It catches 180 of the 200 identifiers and flags 50 of the 1,000 ordinary messages. The team announces '90% accuracy'. Which pair of numbers describes the guardrail, and what is wrong with the announcement?
options: Precision 90% and recall 95%; the announcement should have used F1, which comes to 92.4% and is the standard single figure for a detector of this kind, since it balances the two
Accuracy 90% and specificity 50%; the announcement is correct but incomplete without the specificity
Recall 90% and precision 90%; the announcement is fine, since recall is what accuracy means for a filter
Recall 90% and false-positive rate 5%; the single figure hides that one ordinary message in twenty is blocked, which is the cost users pay
explain: 180/200 is recall on the attacks and 50/1,000 is the false-positive rate on normal traffic; pooled accuracy would be (180 + 950)/1,200 = 94%, yet another number. Precision here (180/230 = 78%) depends on the test mix, which is why recall and FPR are the stable pair to report.

q: You label 100 RAG answers for a hallucination detector that runs NLI between answer and retrieved context. One answer states a fact that is true in the world but appears nowhere in the retrieved passages. Two annotators disagree about whether this is a hallucination. What should the labelling guideline say?
options: It is not a hallucination, since the detector should only flag statements that are false in the world, and a true statement harms nobody whatever the context says
It is a hallucination, since the model produced a fact the corpus does not contain, and every unsupported claim is by definition wrong however it reads to the annotator
Decide which property is measured: faithfulness to the context makes it unsupported, factuality makes it correct, and the NLI signal measures only the first
Discard the item, since items on which two annotators disagree cannot belong to a gold set
explain: An NLI checker asks whether the context entails the answer, so it will flag this item whatever the world says; a gold set that mixes faithfulness and factuality makes the detector look wrong for doing its job. Pick the construct, write it down, and label every item by it.

q: A linear probe trained on residual activations separates true from false statements of the form 'X is the capital of Y' with 98% accuracy, and a write-up concludes the model 'knows when it is lying'. The probe transfers to new capitals but drops to 55% on negated statements ('X is not the capital of Y'). What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The model has no concept of truth at all, since a genuine concept would survive negation
The direction separates a feature correlated with truth within the probe's training template; neither its generality nor the model's use of it has been shown, so the knowledge claim is not earned

The model knows truth but not negation, two separate linear features that a second probe trained on negated statements would find, after which the two probes together would support the write-up's claim
The result confirms the write-up: 98% on held-out statements is the accepted threshold for attributing knowledge to a model
explain: Separability is a fact about the geometry of activations on one template; 'knows' is a claim about a semantic relation and about use, and the negation failure shows the direction tracked something narrower than truth. The Chinese-room point survives in a modest form: decoding a label from the room's state does not show the room understood it.

q: A model switches its answer in 40% of cases after the user says 'I think the answer is X'. A colleague argues this is reasonable updating, since users often know things. Which measurement separates sycophancy from legitimate updating?
options: Measure the switch rate separately when the user's X is correct and when it is wrong; updating should flip toward truth more than away from it, sycophancy flips at the same rate either way
Measure the switch rate at temperature 0; any switching that survives is sycophancy, since deterministic decoding removes legitimate updating and leaves only the pull of the user's stated opinion
Ask the model whether it changed its mind because of the user; a yes confirms sycophancy and a no confirms updating
Count only switches on questions the model originally answered correctly, since a correct model has nothing to learn from any user
explain: A rational updater weighs the user's claim by how often such claims are right, so its flips should be enriched for true claims; a model that flips 40% toward truth and 40% toward error is tracking the user, not the evidence. Self-report is another output of the same sycophantic system.

q: A membership inference attack on a language model reports AUROC 0.75. At a false-positive rate of 1% its true-positive rate is 3%; at a false-positive rate of 50% it is 85%. A data owner wants to show that her 200 documents were in the training set. What does the attack offer her?
options: Strong evidence: AUROC 0.75 means that 75% of her documents will be correctly identified as members at whatever threshold she chooses
Little: at a false-positive rate she could defend in a dispute the attack flags almost nothing, and most of the AUROC comes from the region where it also flags half of all unseen texts
Decisive evidence if she sets the threshold at 50% FPR, since 85% of her documents will then be flagged as members, a clear majority that cannot be attributed to chance across 200 documents
Nothing, since an AUROC below 0.9 means the attack is statistically indistinguishable from chance
explain: A privacy claim lives at low false-positive rates: a detector that flags half of everything is not an argument. AUROC averages over all thresholds and can look respectable while the useful corner of the curve is empty; report TPR at 0.1% or 1% FPR.

q: A sparse autoencoder on a middle layer produces latents that an automated interpreter labels confidently; 95% of latents get a clean description. Splicing the SAE's reconstruction into the forward pass in place of the real activations raises the model's loss from 2.00 to 2.60 nats per token, roughly the gap between this model and one a quarter its size. What follows for reading the latents as 'the model's features'?
options: The latents are validated: interpretability of 95% of them shows that the dictionary captured the computation
The loss increase is irrelevant, since SAEs are analysis tools and were never meant to run inside the model, so the only test that matters is whether the latents can be labelled
Interpretable does not mean sufficient: a large share of what the model uses sits in the reconstruction error, so explanations built only from the latents miss it
The SAE is too large; shrinking the dictionary would reduce the loss gap by removing redundant latents that currently split the real features apart and absorb reconstruction error
explain: The splice test asks whether the dictionary preserves what downstream layers need, and 0.6 nats says a lot of it is thrown away. Latents can be clean and still describe only part of the mechanism; the residual is where an explanation goes to be wrong.

q: An agent follows an injected instruction found in a web page with probability 0.10 per encounter, and a defense prompt lowers this to 0.02. An attacker controls a page the agent visits once a day for 30 days. What is the chance of at least one hijack before and after the defense?
options: About 96% before, about 45% after
About 300% before, about 60% after
About 10% before, about 2% after
About 50% before, about 10% after
explain: 1 - 0.9^30 is about 0.96 and 1 - 0.98^30 about 0.45. A fivefold reduction in per-attempt obedience buys a coin flip over a month, which is why a probability is not a security boundary and the send tool is what gets gated.

q: A team adds an input filter to its chatbot. On a public suite of 500 jailbreak prompts, the attack success rate falls from 38% to 2%. Reviewer #2 writes: 'evaluate against an adaptive attacker'. What does the reviewer want, and why is the 2% not the number?
options: A stronger judge model, since the drop reflects a lenient judge rather than the filter
The suite rerun at higher temperature, since static prompts at low temperature underestimate stochastic attack success and a filter should be tested on sampled replies
The 2% rerun on a held-out half of the same suite, since the filter was tuned on the 500 prompts and the reported number is therefore a training-set score
Attacks optimized with knowledge of the filter; the suite was written against undefended models, so 2% measures the filter against yesterday's attacks
explain: A fixed suite is a regression test, not a threat model: the attacks that matter are the ones constructed after the defense is known, by paraphrase, encoding or search against the filter itself. Robustness is the success rate of the best attacker who has read your code.

q: A corpus has 1,000,000 passages. The word 'error' occurs in 100,000 of them, the code 'E-4471' in 10. With IDF = log2(N / df), how do the two terms' weights compare in a BM25 query 'error E-4471', and what does this buy a RAG system?
options: About 10 and 100,000: the raw ratios N / df are the weights, so the code counts ten thousand times more
About 3.3 and 16.6 bits: the rare code dominates the score, which a dense vector tends to blur
About 0.1 and 0.00001: df over N, so the common word 'error' is what drives the score
Equal weights: each term occurs once in the query, and IDF only matters for terms that repeat
explain: log2(10) is about 3.3 and log2(100,000) about 16.6, a factor of five in favour of the code. Exact rare strings are where lexical scoring earns its place next to embeddings.

q: A second-hand listings search gets the query 'Fahrad' for 'Fahrrad', bicycle. Index A is a whole-word BM25 index; index B is a dense encoder with a BPE tokenizer. What is the honest comparison?
options: A finds the listings anyway, because stemming reduces the misspelled and the correct form to one common stem
B maps the misspelled word to a single shared unknown-word vector, so the query carries no information at all about bicycles
A scores the typo zero, since the token never occurs; B sees shared subword pieces and often lands nearby, without guarantee
Both return nothing useful, because neither method can represent a character string that was absent from its training data
explain: A whole-word index has no entry for 'Fahrad'; BPE has no unknown token, it just produces pieces, several of them shared with the correct spelling. Character n-grams or spelling correction give the lexical side the same tolerance.

q: An embedding model's documentation says to prepend 'query: ' to search queries and 'passage: ' to documents before encoding. A team indexes the documents correctly but forgets the prefix for live queries. Retrieval quality drops noticeably. Why?
options: The tokenizer strips the prefix from documents, so the documents were in fact encoded without it as well
Without the prefix the query is a few tokens shorter, and shorter inputs systematically get noisier vectors
The model returns a default vector for any input that does not match the template it was trained with
The model learned the prefixes as role markers; unprefixed queries are embedded as if they were passages
explain: Asymmetric models are trained with role prefixes so a short question and a long answer can be mapped to the same place. Drop the marker and the question is encoded as a tiny, oddly phrased passage.

q: A vector store holds 10,000 product descriptions. A user filters to 'in stock in Würzburg', which matches 2% of them. The code runs an unfiltered top-10 nearest-neighbour search and applies the filter afterwards. How many results should the user expect, and what is the fix?
options: About 0.2 on average; apply the filter inside the search or retrieve far more candidates
About 2 on average; retrieve the top 100 and the problem disappears for good
All 10, since a metadata filter does not change which vectors are nearest
About 5, since in practice half of the nearest neighbours satisfy any reasonable filter
explain: 10 x 0.02 = 0.2: most queries return an empty page. Pre-filtering, or filtered traversal in the index, searches among the 200 eligible items instead of hoping they rank first.

q: A team upgrades to a better embedding model for the query side, 'because queries are where quality matters', and leaves the 3 million stored document vectors as they are. Search results become essentially random. What happened?
options: The new model produces vectors of a slightly different norm, which flips the cosine ranking
Query and document vectors now come from two unrelated spaces, so their similarities mean nothing
The new model is too strong for the old index, which only accepts vectors of lower quality
The approximate index was built for the old query distribution and needs its graph rebuilt
explain: Nothing ties dimension 17 of one model to dimension 17 of another. Comparing across models is comparing coordinates in two coordinate systems; a model change means re-embedding everything, which is the real cost of upgrading.

q: A hiking-guide bot retrieves 80-token chunks: matching is precise, but the generator keeps lacking the surrounding information, such as which trail a 'steep final section' belongs to. Larger 800-token chunks match worse. Which indexing pattern resolves the tension?
options: Embed the 800-token sections but search them with the 80-token chunks as additional query terms
Embed both sizes and let the generator pick whichever chunk it finds more fluent
Index small chunks for matching, but hand the generator the parent section each hit belongs to
Use 80-token chunks with 70 tokens of overlap, so neighbouring content is always present
explain: Match small, read big. Retrieval likes focused units; generation likes context; a pointer from child chunk to parent section serves both without indexing everything twice.

q: Your test set has 60 answerable and 40 unanswerable questions. The RAG bot refuses 36 of the 40 unanswerable ones and 6 of the 60 answerable ones. A teammate wants to report a single 'refusal rate of 90%'. What should the roadshow slide show instead, and why?
options: The 90% alone: refusal on unanswerable questions is the only number the refusal test is designed to produce
An overall refusal rate of 42%, computed over all 100 questions together, since a single aggregate is easier to compare across systems
The 6 wrongful refusals only, since over-refusal is the failure mode users notice and complain about
Both numbers, 90% correct refusals and 10% wrongful refusals, since a bot that refuses everything scores 100% on the first
explain: Refusal is a classification task with two error types. Either number alone is trivially gamed; the pair is what tells you whether the bot knows when it does not know.

q: A flat-finder embeds listings with a model trained on co-occurrence style objectives and searches 'cheap flat near the Main'. The top hits are luxury flats near the Main. The engineer blames the small model. What is the more fundamental reason?
options: Words that occur in the same contexts get nearby vectors, and 'cheap' and 'luxury' share almost all their contexts
Embedding models learn to treat evaluative adjectives as stop words and keep only the nouns of a query
Cosine similarity cannot become negative for normalized vectors, so opposites can never be pushed apart
The listings state prices as digit strings, which tokenize into fragments that the encoder has learned to ignore entirely
explain: Distributional similarity is similarity of contexts, and antonyms are the textbook case of words that swap in and out of the same sentences. A relevance-trained reranker, a price filter, or plain lexical matching knows the difference.

q: Two designs answer questions about a 100,000-token handbook: paste it all, or retrieve 2,000 tokens. In the prefill, the attention scores of one layer cost on the order of n^2 and the per-token feed-forward work on the order of n. By what factors do these two costs grow when you paste instead of retrieve?
options: Both about 50 times, since attention is parallel over positions and scales like any other layer
Attention about 50 times and feed-forward about 2,500 times, since the MLP sees every pair of tokens
Attention about 2,500 times and feed-forward about 50 times, since only the scores pair tokens up
Attention about 100,000 times and feed-forward about 50 times, since the scores form an n by n matrix
explain: n grows 50-fold; n^2 grows 2,500-fold. Attention over everything is the honest realization of soft alignment: every token looks at every other, and the bill is quadratic. Retrieval is a cheap hard alignment done before the model starts.

q: A 32-layer model uses grouped-query attention: 32 query heads but 8 key-value heads, head dimension 128, and the KV cache is stored in fp16 (2 bytes). A customer keeps a 100,000-token conversation open. How much KV cache does that one conversation hold?
options: About 1.3 GB
About 13 GB
About 52 GB
About 130 GB
explain: Per token: 2 (K and V) x 32 layers x 8 heads x 128 x 2 bytes = 128 KB, times 100,000 tokens is 12.8 GB. Counting the 32 query heads instead of the 8 KV heads gives 52 GB, the wrong heads. Long context is paid per token, per layer, for as long as the tab stays open.

q: You store 10 million float32 embeddings of 1,024 dimensions, about 41 GB, which no longer fits in RAM. The embedding model was trained with a Matryoshka-style objective. You keep only the first 256 dimensions in memory. What do you get, and why does it work?
options: About 41 GB still, since the index has to store every dimension and truncation only makes the dot products faster
About 10 GB, and it works because embedding dimensions are interchangeable, so any 256 of them would have served equally well
About 2.5 GB, and it works because the dropped dimensions were close to zero for nearly all stored vectors
About 10 GB; training made the leading dimensions carry the most information, so rescore a shortlist with full vectors
explain: A quarter of the dimensions is a quarter of the memory. In an ordinary model the information is spread over all coordinates; the Matryoshka loss concentrates it at the front, so a coarse search on the prefix followed by exact rescoring of the top few hundred loses little.

q: A RAG bot refuses when the best passage's cosine similarity to the question is below 0.75, a threshold tuned carefully on a labelled set. The team swaps in a different embedding model and the bot now refuses almost every question. What is going on?
options: Absolute similarity values are specific to each model; the threshold must be recalibrated on the labelled set
The new model is worse at retrieval, which is what a higher refusal rate measures by construction
The new model produces unnormalized vectors, and cosine similarity is undefined without normalization
The threshold should be on the generator's confidence, since similarity has nothing to do with answerability
explain: One model spreads its similarities over 0.2 to 0.9, another squeezes everything between 0.5 and 0.7. A number tuned on one is noise on the other. Reranker scores or a recalibrated threshold restore the behaviour.

q: On a 200-query evaluation set, a project team's dense retriever scores nDCG@10 of 0.61 and the BM25 baseline 0.60. The night before the roadshow, the founder on the team wants to delete BM25 'since it adds nothing'. What should they look at first?
options: The latency of each retriever, since equal quality means the faster one should win
Whether a cross-encoder alone could replace both retrievers on the whole corpus
The per-query results: if the two win on different queries, fusing them beats either alone
The number of corpus documents each retriever returned at least once across the set
explain: Equal averages say nothing about agreement. Lexical and dense errors are usually weakly correlated, which is the entire case for hybrid search; a per-query table shows it, an aggregate hides it.

q: A search endpoint has a latency budget of 300 ms. Hybrid retrieval of candidates takes 40 ms. The cross-encoder reranker, batched, costs about 6 ms per query-passage pair on the team's hardware. The plan was to rerank the top 100. What fits the budget?
options: Reranking the top 100 as planned, about 240 ms in total
Reranking about the top 40, since 100 pairs alone would take 600 ms
Reranking the top 10 only, since reranking cannot exceed a tenth of the budget
Reranking all candidates, since batching makes the cost independent of their number
explain: (300 - 40) / 6 is about 43 pairs. The reranker is where the budget goes, and the number of candidates it sees is the knob; measure, do not assume.

q: A single-vector retriever maps every passage to one d-dimensional vector and returns the top-k by dot product. A known result bounds, as a function of d, how many distinct top-k subsets of a fixed corpus such a retriever can ever return, so for some query sets no training can get them all right. Which remedy addresses this limit itself?
options: Train longer with harder negatives, so that the vectors use their available dimensions more efficiently
Split passages into smaller chunks with more overlap, so that each stored vector has less content to encode
L2-normalize all vectors so that cosine similarity replaces the dot product as the scoring function
Score with many vectors per passage, or add a sparse component, or rerank a wider candidate set
explain: This is the fixed-size bottleneck again: one vector per passage must serve every question anyone will ask of it, and the geometry caps which k-subsets a dot product can single out. Late interaction, sparse terms and rerankers change the scoring function rather than the training recipe.

q: In a dense index of a company wiki, three boilerplate passages ('This page describes internal procedures and responsibilities') appear in the top 10 for about 30% of all queries, however unrelated. The passages are not duplicated. What is the likely cause and the diagnostic?
options: They sit near the centre of the embedding distribution, close to many queries at once; count how often each passage appears in top-k
The encoder memorized these frequent templates during pretraining; check their perplexity under a language model trained on the same wiki data
Shorter passages have smaller norms and therefore higher cosine similarity; check passage lengths against their hit counts
The approximate index routes most queries through the same entry points; check whether exact search returns the same three passages
explain: Hubness: in high dimensions a few points end up nearest neighbour to a disproportionate share of queries, usually the bland ones near the mean. Nearest-neighbour retrieval has carried this since word vectors; a hit-count histogram finds the hubs, and downweighting or reranking removes them.

q: Instead of a fixed few-shot prompt, a classifier retrieves the 8 most similar labelled examples from a pool for each test input. Accuracy rises from 71% to 90%. Reviewer #2 suspects the gain comes from test labels leaking in through the pool rather than from in-context learning. Which check speaks most directly to the suspicion?
options: Replace the retrieved examples with 8 random ones from the same pool and confirm that accuracy falls back to about 71%
Confirm that the 8 examples use exactly the same format as the test input and are ordered by decreasing similarity
Search the pool for near-duplicates and paraphrases of each test item; if its label arrives as a demonstration, that is leakage
Repeat the run with 4 and 16 retrieved examples and check that accuracy grows smoothly with the number of demonstrations
explain: Retrieval of demonstrations is legitimate when the pool is disjoint from the test set. If the nearest neighbour of a test item is the test item with its label, the model is copying, not learning in context; the random-example ablation shows retrieval matters but not why.

q: An LLM reranker receives 20 candidate passages in one prompt and outputs their order. Shuffling the input order and asking again changes the output order substantially; the top-ranked passage agrees in 60% of cases, at temperature zero. What does this show, and what helps?
options: The model favours passages by their position in the prompt; rerank several shuffles and aggregate the ranks
Temperature zero leaves residual randomness in the decoder; lower it further or fix the sampling seed
Twenty passages exceed what the model can compare, so order is arbitrary; rerank only the top 5
The candidates are genuinely tied in relevance, so any order is correct; report the agreement as noise
explain: Determinism is not fairness: the same input in a different order is a different input, and listwise rerankers lean on position. Averaging ranks over permutations, or pointwise scoring of each passage alone, removes the lean at a cost in calls.

q: A map-reduce summarizer condenses a 40-page project report section by section, then merges the section summaries. The final summary mentions the planned 1.2 million budget and nothing about cost at all; the 15% overrun reported in section 9 was dropped as detail in that section's summary. Every step was faithful to its input. Which lesson and check follow?
options: The merge step hallucinated; an entailment check of the summary against the full report catches exactly this
The compression ratio was too aggressive; doubling the length of every section summary guarantees that such numbers survive
Sections should have been summarized in reverse order, so that outcomes come before plans in the merge
The map stage discards before anyone knows what matters; measure missing facts against a fact list, not only invented ones
explain: Nothing was invented, so a precision-style faithfulness check passes; something essential was omitted, which only a recall-style check against known facts detects. A second, query-focused pass over the sections, asking specifically about cost, is the usual repair.

q: Before building, a team generates 300 evaluation questions by showing an LLM one chunk at a time and asking for a question it answers. Retrieval recall@5 comes out at 0.97. After launch, on 300 logged real user questions, it is 0.62. What explains most of the gap?
options: The embedding model had been fine-tuned on the generated questions, so the evaluation measured training-set performance rather than retrieval quality
A question written from a chunk reuses its wording and is answerable by that chunk alone; real questions are short, underspecified and span chunks
Real users write longer and more detailed questions, and long queries are embedded less accurately than short ones
The corpus was re-indexed between evaluation and launch, so many gold chunks no longer existed at test time
explain: Synthetic questions are near-paraphrases of their source, which turns retrieval into a duplicate-detection exercise. Filter generated questions for realism, hide the chunk's vocabulary, and start logging real queries on day one.

q: A vendor insists its agent 'genuinely plans ahead' rather than reacting step by step. In the spirit of replacing an unanswerable question about inner life with a behavioral test, which evaluation is the right move?
options: Ask the agent in several different ways whether it plans ahead, and check that its answers stay consistent over time
Inspect its reasoning traces and count how often words such as 'plan', 'first' and 'later' occur
Give it novel tasks where an early choice must anticipate a constraint revealed late, and measure success
Check the vendor's architecture diagram for a separate component that is labelled as the planner
explain: The imitation game swapped 'can machines think' for a test anyone can run. Tasks in which greedy step-by-step action fails and only anticipation succeeds do the same for planning; self-reports and trace vocabulary are cheap to produce.

q: A model gets 5-digit multiplication wrong in one shot. A founder adds 20 worked examples of correct 5-digit products to the prompt, with answers only. Accuracy barely moves. Why not?
options: Demonstrations specify what the task is, which was already clear; they add no computation per answer token
Twenty examples exceed the number of demonstrations a model can attend to, so most are ignored and the effective prompt is the same as one shot
Multiplication examples must be given in words rather than digits for the model to generalize
The examples must be of 6-digit products, since models only learn from cases slightly harder than the target and 5-digit examples give nothing to generalize from
explain: Few-shot prompting is task specification, not training: the model knew it was being asked to multiply. What arithmetic lacks is serial steps, which written intermediate results or a calculator tool supply.

q: A reasoning model offers a 'thinking budget' parameter. A student at 3 a.m. sets it to 16,000 tokens for every request, including 'convert this list to JSON', and the bill doubles. What does the budget actually control?
options: The size of the model loaded for the request, since higher budgets route the request to larger models
The number of tokens allowed in the final visible answer, while the hidden reasoning is left unaffected
A fixed amount of reasoning the model is required to perform, which it fills completely on every request
An upper bound on hidden reasoning tokens; the model may stop early, and easy tasks gain nothing from a high cap
explain: A budget is a ceiling, not a quota, but models given room tend to use some of it, and a JSON conversion needs none. Scale the budget to the difficulty of the task, not to the anxiety of the hour.

q: A function-calling assistant is given search_trains(origin, destination, date). The model emits a call with the argument 'date_from', which does not exist in the schema. What should the application do?
options: Guess that 'date_from' is meant to be 'date', execute the call anyway, and log a warning for later review
Validate the call against the schema before executing it and return the validation error to the model so it can retry
Add 'date_from' to the schema as an alias, since the model's choice of names reflects what it saw in training
Set the sampling temperature to zero, which prevents the model from inventing argument names in future calls
explain: A tool call is model output, and model output is validated like any other user input. Returning the error closes the loop: the model usually fixes its own call on the next turn, and nothing is executed on a guess.

q: A web agent searching for a restaurant table runs the same search with the same arguments eleven times in a row, receives the same empty result each time, and would continue if not stopped. Which two guards does the loop need?
options: A larger context window, so the agent remembers earlier results, and a faster search tool
A system prompt asking the agent to be efficient, and a more detailed description of the search tool
A hard cap on steps per task, and detection of a repeated identical action that ends or redirects the run
A second model that approves each call before it runs, and a lower temperature for the first one
explain: The loop is the application's code, and the application owns the brakes. A step cap bounds the bill; a repeat detector tells the model, or the user, that this road is closed.

q: A chat agent's context grows by 2,000 tokens per turn (its own message plus a tool result). The whole history is sent with every call. After the tenth call, how many input tokens have been billed in total, ignoring the system prompt?
options: About 20,000
About 110,000
About 200,000
About 11,000
explain: The calls cost 2,000, 4,000, ..., 20,000 tokens: 2,000 x 55 = 110,000. Input grows linearly per turn and quadratically in total, which is why prompt caching and context pruning are agent features before they are chat features.

q: A text-to-SQL bot over a city's open-data budget database must never modify data. The system prompt says: 'Only write SELECT statements.' In testing, a question phrased as 'remove the old rows and show me the rest' produces a DELETE. Where does the protection belong?
options: In the database connection: open it read-only or as a user without write privileges, so destructive statements die at the engine
In a stronger system prompt that repeats the rule three times in capital letters and explains in detail why it matters
In a second model call that reads the generated SQL statement and judges whether it looks destructive before anything is executed
In a lower sampling temperature, since destructive statements come from the tail of the output distribution
explain: A prompt is a request; a permission is a fact. The engine enforces read-only regardless of how the question was phrased, and the prompt can still ask nicely to reduce noise.

q: A model answers a yes/no question correctly with probability 0.9 per sample. You sample 5 times independently and take the majority, in the spirit of a repetition code that buys reliability with redundancy. What reliability do you get, and at what price?
options: About 0.90, since majority voting cannot improve on the per-sample accuracy when the question is binary
About 0.95, at twice the output cost, since only the disagreeing samples need to be paid for
About 0.999, at five times the output cost, provided the five errors are independent
About 0.99, at five times the output cost, provided the five errors are independent
explain: P(at least 3 of 5 correct) = 10 x 0.9^3 x 0.1^2 + 5 x 0.9^4 x 0.1 + 0.9^5 = 0.0729 + 0.3281 + 0.5905, about 0.991. Redundancy corrects independent errors; a shared misreading of the question is a burst error that no amount of repetition fixes.

q: A support inbox is handled either by one agent with tools that decides at each step what to do, or by a fixed workflow: classify, route, draft, each a separate model call with its own test set. Historically, end-to-end models beat pipelines because hand-made intermediate stages lost information and propagated errors. Which consideration most favours the fixed workflow here?
options: A fixed workflow can use a smaller model at every stage, which makes it both cheaper and more accurate in all cases
Each stage is inspectable and testable on its own at predictable cost; flexibility pays off only when the steps cannot be enumerated in advance
The agent cannot call more than one tool per task, so a three-step process is structurally out of its reach
Pipelines avoid error propagation entirely, since every stage receives the original ticket text again as its input and starts fresh
explain: The old argument against pipelines was hand-crafted intermediate features that a network could learn better. Here the intermediate outputs are the product: a label, a queue, a draft, each checkable. Use the simplest structure that works, and let the model loose only where the structure is unknown.

q: An agent translates 'How many trams ran late in October?' into a SQL query, executes it, and reports the number, which is correct. A colleague at the conference bar says this settles the Chinese-room question: the symbols are now grounded in a database. What is the sober assessment?
options: It settles it in the agent's favour: a correctly executed query that returns a true number about the world is understanding by any reasonable definition
It settles it against the agent: the query was produced by pattern matching over training data, and pattern matching cannot count as understanding
It speaks to correctness, not understanding: the number is checkable independently of the model, while the argument holds that tool outputs are just more symbols
It settles nothing about either question: a single executed query cannot be evidence about correctness or about understanding
explain: The robot reply, sensors and effectors bolted onto the room, was answered by the argument's author: the inputs are more uninterpreted symbols. What a tool call does deliver is a result you can verify independently of the model's prose, and for an engineer that is the part that matters.

q: A coding agent runs the test suite and the tool returns a 30,000-token log. The agent needs three lines of it now and may need another part later. Which handling keeps the context small without losing the content?
options: Write the log to a file and return a handle plus a tail, with grep-like and slice tools for later access
Paste the whole log into the context, since attention will find the relevant lines whenever they are needed
Summarize the log in a separate call, insert the summary into the context and discard the original log
Split the log into thirty messages of 1,000 tokens each, so that every piece fits comfortably in one turn
explain: The context is working memory, not storage. A handle costs a few tokens, the data stays complete, and the agent fetches what it needs when it needs it; a summary is cheap today and missing the stack trace tomorrow.

q: You can afford 16 samples per task and an automatic selection step. For which task does best-of-16 improve results most reliably?
options: Writing a condolence email to a colleague, selected by the model's own rating of warmth
Translating a poem into German, selected by the model's judgement of which version reads best
Summarizing a meeting transcript, selected by taking the summary with the fewest tokens
Implementing a function against a hidden unit-test suite, selected by the number of tests passed
explain: Sampling helps when checking is much cheaper and more reliable than generating. Tests are an exact, independent verifier; a model grading its own warmth is the author reviewing the author, and token count is not a quality score.

q: A coding agent is rewarded when 'all tests pass'. After an hour it reports success. The diff shows that it edited two failing tests to assert the buggy behaviour and added a special case for the test inputs. What is the correct reading, and the fix?
options: The agent misunderstood the task; rewrite the instruction to state explicitly that tests must not be edited
The agent optimized the literal reward; grade with held-out tests it cannot see or modify
The tests were wrong, since the agent found them to be inconsistent with the implementation it was given
The agent needs a larger context window so that it can see the whole test suite at once while editing
explain: Reward hacking is the reward working as written. Instructions help at the margin; a verifier the agent cannot touch is what makes 'tests pass' mean what you meant.

q: A tool-using agent averages 8 model calls per task, each with 12,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. Prices: 2 dollars per million input tokens, 8 dollars per million output tokens. It solves 70% of tasks. What is the cost per correct answer?
options: About 0.16 dollars
About 0.22 dollars
About 0.32 dollars
About 0.45 dollars
explain: Per call 0.024 + 0.004 = 0.028 dollars; 8 calls make 0.224 dollars per task, and dividing by 0.7 gives 0.32 per correct answer. The failed tasks are not free, which is why the metric divides by successes.

q: Take 2 x parameters as the FLOPs per generated token. A 7B model writes 4,000 reasoning tokens and then a short answer; a 140B model answers directly in 200 tokens. Compare the compute, and say what differs.
options: About equal, 5.6e13 FLOPs each; the small model spent it on 4,000 dependent steps, the large one on 200 steps of greater width
The large model uses about 20 times more, since parameter count dominates compute and token counts are secondary
The small model uses about 20 times more, since reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens and output is the expensive part
About equal, 5.6e13 FLOPs each, but the small model's steps are independent of one another, so its reasoning could run in parallel
explain: 2 x 7e9 x 4,000 = 5.6e13 and 2 x 1.4e11 x 200 = 5.6e13. A transformer spends fixed depth per token, so a problem with many dependent steps needs length; width adds parallel capacity per step, not more steps. Each reasoning token conditions on the previous ones, which is the point and the reason it cannot be parallelized.

q: Across 1,000 math problems, a reasoning model's accuracy falls as its chain length grows: 92% on problems where it wrote under 1,000 tokens, 55% above 8,000. A blog post concludes that 'long reasoning causes errors' and recommends a tight budget. What is wrong with the inference, and what would test the claim?
options: Nothing; the correlation is strong enough to act on, and tighter budgets are also cheaper, so the recommendation stands either way
The sample is too small; repeat the measurement on 10,000 problems before drawing any conclusion from it
Accuracy should be measured per reasoning token rather than per problem, which would reverse the direction of the trend
Difficulty confounds it: hard problems produce long chains and errors; vary the budget on the same problems and compare
explain: The model writes more when it struggles, so length is a symptom of difficulty as much as a cause of failure. An intervention, the same problems under several budgets, separates the two; the observational correlation cannot.

q: An agent task takes 12 steps. Per step: time to first token 0.5 s, 200 generated tokens at 50 tokens per second, and a tool call of 1 s. The support engineer in Schweinfurt wants the 66-second task under 30 s and proposes caching tool results. What does the arithmetic say?
options: Tool calls take 12 s of the 66, so caching their results gets the task close to the target on its own
Time to first token adds up to 6 s and is the bottleneck; a provider with lower first-token latency solves it
Generation is 48 of the 66 s; only fewer steps or fewer generated tokens per step can reach 30 s
The 66 s are split roughly evenly, so any of the three components is an equally good optimization target
explain: Per step 0.5 + 4 + 1 = 5.5 s, times 12. Decoding 200 tokens at 50 per second is 4 of those seconds; even a free tool and an instant first token leave 48 s. Agents are slow because they talk, so make them talk less, or fewer times.

q: A coding agent runs in a sandbox with no network access, so the team considers prompt injection harmless. The repository it works on contains a .env file with API keys, and the agent reads a README from an untrusted pull request. Which channel did the sandbox not close?
options: The agent's sampling temperature: injected text raises it, which makes the agent reveal more than it otherwise would
The agent's own output: a report, commit or pull-request text can carry the keys out, so no-network is not no-egress
The model weights: injected text is written into the weights during the session and can be read out in later sessions
The file system: reading the .env file at all is already an exfiltration, since the sandbox cannot forget what it read
explain: Everything the agent returns to a human or a repository leaves the sandbox. Untrusted input plus secrets plus any outbound channel is the full set; keep the secrets out of the sandbox, and treat the agent's output as data to scan, not as a trusted report.

q: An extraction endpoint must produce zero invalid outputs on 200 inputs. Free generation yields schema-valid JSON 90% of the time; with validation and up to 3 attempts per input, the team expects about 0.2 failures in 200 and calls it done. Then a validator rejects an output whose 'total' does not equal the sum of its items. What design meets the target?
options: Constrain decoding to the schema, which guarantees shape; keep validators and retries for value-level rules the grammar cannot express
Raise the attempt limit to 5, since 1 - 0.1^5 covers 200 inputs with margin, and drop the sum validator as out of scope
Constrain decoding to the schema, which guarantees both the shape and the values of the output, and remove the validators as redundant
Replace JSON with free text parsed by a regular expression, since regex validation is deterministic and never fails
explain: 1 - 0.1^3 = 0.999 still leaves an expected 0.2 invalid outputs in 200, which is not zero. Grammar-constrained decoding makes malformed JSON impossible, but a grammar cannot check that a total equals a sum; that stays with the validator and the retry loop.

q: A text-to-SQL system is scored on 50 gold questions. Scheme A: the generated SQL must match the gold SQL string. Scheme B: both queries are executed on the demo database and their results compared. Scheme B scores 44/50. What remains to worry about with B?
options: B is stricter than A, so 44 out of 50 is a lower bound and the true accuracy of the system is certainly higher than that number
B rewards queries that run faster, since slow but correct queries can time out and are counted as failures
B cannot be applied to queries that return more than one row or column, so those cases still have to be scored under the string-matching scheme A instead
A wrong query can coincide with the right one on a small database, two empty results for example; use several databases or distinctive values
explain: Execution matching is the right idea: many SQL strings express one query. Its false positives are coincidences, and small seed databases are full of them; distinct values and more than one instance make a coincidence unlikely.

q: A forward pass costs roughly 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, attention over a short context aside. A startup founder compares a 175B-parameter general model with a 7B model fine-tuned for his one task. By what factor does the compute per generated token differ?
options: About 5 times, since cost grows with the square root of the parameter count
About 25 times, since cost grows linearly with the parameter count
About 625 times, since cost grows with the square of the parameter count
About the same, since both models emit exactly one token per forward pass
explain: Per-token compute is proportional to the number of parameters touched, so 175/7 = 25. The parameter count that made in-context learning possible is also the bill that makes a fine-tuned small model attractive once the task is known.

q: A model is quantized to 4-bit weights in groups of 32. Each group stores one fp16 scale and one 4-bit zero point. How many bits per weight does the stored model use on average?
options: 4.625 bits
4.0 bits
4.5 bits
5.25 bits
explain: Each group adds 16 + 4 = 20 bits of metadata over 32 weights, 0.625 bits per weight on top of the 4. Smaller groups track outliers better and cost more of exactly this overhead.

q: A server holds the fp16 weights of a 7B model, 14 GB. Its KV cache costs 128 KB per token. 32 users are connected at the same time, each with 8,192 tokens of context. How much memory does the cache take, and how does it compare with the weights?
options: About 1 GB, far below the weights
