About 4 GB, below the weights
About 32 GB, more than twice the weights
About 256 GB, nearly twenty times the weights
explain: 32 x 8,192 = 262,144 cached tokens, times 128 KB is 32 GB. Weights are a fixed cost; the cache grows with users times context, which is why long-context serving is a memory problem before it is a compute problem.

q: An on-device assistant sends the same 1,500-token system instructions with every request, followed by a question of about 20 tokens. Time to first token is over two seconds, and the student at 3 a.m. has already tried lowering the temperature. Which change attacks the actual cause?
options: Quantize the weights to 4 bits, which cuts the prefill time by a factor of four
Move the instructions to the end of the prompt so they are processed last
Reduce the output length, since a long prompt is charged on every generated token
Compute the KV cache of the fixed instruction prefix once and reuse it for every request
explain: Almost all of the waiting is prefill over 1,500 tokens that never change. A cached prefix leaves about 20 tokens to process per request. Weight quantization mostly speeds up bandwidth-bound decoding, not compute-bound prefill.

q: A 7B model in fp16 uses 14 GB for weights and, at the team's context length and batch, 8 GB for the KV cache stored in fp16: 22 GB in total. The team quantizes the weights to 4 bits and expects to fit in a quarter of the memory. What does it actually get?
options: About 11.5 GB, since the cache is still in fp16
About 5.5 GB, since everything shrinks by a factor of four
About 3.5 GB, since the cache is recomputed and no longer stored
About 7.5 GB, since the cache shrinks by half along with the weights
explain: Weight-only quantization touches the weights: 3.5 GB plus the untouched 8 GB cache gives 11.5 GB. The cache is made of activations and needs its own quantization, with its own accuracy questions.

q: A team classifies 50,000 support tickets a day with a prompted LLM. Each request is 800 input tokens, mostly few-shot examples, and the output is negligible. Input tokens cost 0.50 per million. The trade-off table needs a cost column next to F1 and latency. What goes in it for the LLM, per day?
options: About 2
About 20
About 200
About 2,000
explain: 50,000 x 800 = 40 million tokens a day, at 0.50 per million is 20 a day, about 7,300 a year. The few-shot examples are paid for on every single ticket; a fine-tuned small encoder paid for them once.

q: A monitoring dashboard must price each request. One request has 2,000 input tokens at 0.50 per million and 300 output tokens at 2.00 per million. What does the request cost, and which side dominates?
options: 0.0046, since all tokens are charged at the output price
0.0016, with output the larger share because it costs four times more
0.0016, with input the larger share despite the lower price
0.00115, since all tokens are charged at the input price
explain: Input: 2,000 x 0.50 / 1,000,000 = 0.0010. Output: 300 x 2.00 / 1,000,000 = 0.0006. Prompts are long and answers short in most applications, so the cheaper token is usually the larger bill.

q: A small language model has d_model = 1,024, a vocabulary of 128,000 tokens and a transformer body (attention and FFN weights) of 150M parameters. The input embedding table and the output projection are separate matrices. Roughly what share of all parameters belongs to the vocabulary, and what if the two matrices are tied?
options: About 64% untied, about 47% tied
About 47% untied, about 24% tied
About 32% untied, about 16% tied
About 87% untied, about 64% tied
explain: 128,000 x 1,024 is about 131M per matrix: 262M of 412M untied (64%), 131M of 281M tied (47%). Tying saves memory, not compute: the output projection over the full vocabulary is still the single most expensive matmul per token in a model this small.

q: A student wants to cheapen the output layer of a 100M-parameter language model with a 256,000-token vocabulary by training it with negative sampling, five sampled negatives per position, the way word2vec avoided its softmax. What is the catch for a model meant to generate text?
options: Negative sampling needs a unigram frequency table, which a transformer language model does not have
Negative sampling only works when the context is a single word, so a long context breaks the estimator
The gradient from five negatives is too large for a deep network and the training diverges
The objective learns scores that separate observed from sampled tokens, not a normalized next-token distribution
explain: Word vectors never needed their scores to be probabilities; a sampler and a perplexity do. Modern models keep the full softmax and make it cheap differently: tied matrices, fused cross-entropy kernels that never materialize the logits, and chunking over the vocabulary.

q: A 12-layer encoder with hidden size 768 is to be distilled into a student with lower cost. Option A keeps the width and uses 6 layers. Option B keeps 12 layers and halves the width to 384. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both roughly halve the compute, but only B can be initialized from the teacher, by keeping every second hidden unit of each matrix
A roughly halves the compute and can be initialized from teacher layers; B cuts weight-matrix compute about fourfold and cannot copy teacher weights directly
A cuts the compute about fourfold and B roughly halves it, and both can be initialized from the teacher since the layer count or width is preserved
Both roughly halve the compute and both can be initialized from the teacher, A by copying layers and B by taking every second row of each matrix
explain: Weight-matrix cost per token scales with the number of layers and with d^2: half the layers is half the cost, half the width is a quarter. Same-width layers can be copied from the teacher, which is why depth pruning is the usual starting point for a distilled student.

q: Two designs for mixing a small model (cost 1 per query) and a large one (cost 10). Cascade: the small model answers everything and 30% of queries are escalated to the large model. Router: a classifier costing 0.2 looks at the query alone and sends 60% to the small model and 40% to the large one. What are the average costs, and what is the structural difference?
options: Cascade 4.0, router 4.8; the cascade decides after seeing the small model's answer, the router before
Cascade 4.0, router 4.8; the router is always cheaper because it skips the small model on hard queries
Cascade 3.0, router 4.6; the cascade pays the small model only on the queries it keeps
Cascade 4.0, router 4.2; the router pays nothing for the small model on the hard 40%
explain: Cascade: 1 + 0.3 x 10 = 4.0. Router: 0.2 + 0.6 x 1 + 0.4 x 10 = 4.8. The cascade wastes the small model's cost on escalated queries but gets to inspect its answer and confidence; the router saves that cost and must guess difficulty from the question alone.

q: A phone runs a 1B-parameter model in 4-bit weights (0.5 GB). Its chip sustains 2 TFLOP/s and 50 GB/s of memory bandwidth. A request has a 300-token prompt and a 30-token answer; the budget is one second. Take prefill as compute-bound at 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and decoding as bandwidth-bound with one weight read per token. Does it fit?
options: About 0.3 s, since decoding is negligible next to the prompt
About 3.3 s, since each of the 330 tokens reads the weights once
About 0.6 s, so it fits: 0.3 s of prefill plus 0.3 s of decoding
About 6.6 s, since each token costs both a weight read and a full prefill
explain: Prefill: 300 x 2 x 10^9 = 6 x 10^11 FLOPs at 2 x 10^12 FLOP/s is 0.3 s. Decoding: 30 reads of 0.5 GB at 50 GB/s is 0.3 s. Two different bottlenecks, one for each phase; the phone's thermal throttling is the third, uninvited.

q: A server uses continuous batching. Users decoding at 30 tokens per second see their streams freeze for about two seconds whenever someone submits a 30,000-token document. Which fix addresses the mechanism?
options: Quantize the KV cache to 8 bits so that the long prompt occupies less memory and leaves room for the decode requests
Increase the maximum batch size so that the long request no longer blocks a slot that the decoding requests need
Move the long request to the end of the batch so that the decoding requests are processed before it in every step
Split the long prefill into chunks and interleave them with the decode steps of the other requests
explain: A whole 30,000-token prefill runs inside one scheduler step, and every other request's next token waits for that step to finish. Chunked prefill bounds the step time; where the long request sits in the batch changes nothing, since the step completes as a unit.

q: A hybrid search has a latency budget of 200 ms per query. BM25 and dense retrieval together take 20 ms. The cross-encoder reranker takes 3 ms per query-document pair on the team's hardware, scored one pair at a time. The night before the roadshow it reranks the top 100 and misses the budget. How many candidates can it rerank at most?
explain: 200 - 20 = 180 ms left, at 3 ms per pair is 60 candidates. The reranker is where the budget goes; the levers are the candidate count and batching the pairs, and the retriever has to be good enough to put the answer in the top 60.

q: A model is quantized to 4 bits, 16 levels per weight. A histogram shows the levels are used very unevenly: the index distribution has an entropy of 3.2 bits, and the indices behave like independent draws from it. What follows for storing or transmitting the model?
options: A lossless code can reach about 1.6 bits per weight by exploiting correlations between neighbouring weights
The quantization wasted 0.8 bits per weight, so 3-bit quantization reproduces the same model without loss
A lossless entropy code can store the indices in about 3.2 bits per weight, and nothing lossless can go below that
An entropy of 3.2 bits means that about 9 of the 16 levels are never used and can be removed
explain: Entropy is the floor for lossless coding of independent draws: about 3.2 bits per weight with an arithmetic coder, and no further. Going below means a coarser, lossier quantization; 8 levels cannot represent 16 distinct ones, and an uneven distribution can use all 16 levels and still have low entropy.

q: Per token and per layer, a decoder's weight matmuls cost about 12 d^2 multiply-adds (4 d^2 for the Q, K, V and output projections, 8 d^2 for an FFN with hidden size 4d). Attending to a context of n tokens costs about 2 n d multiply-adds per token (scores plus the weighted sum of values). At what context length do the two costs match, and what is that for d = 4,096?
options: n = 6d, about 24,600 tokens
n = d, about 4,100 tokens
n = 12d, about 49,000 tokens
n = d^2 / 12, about 1.4 million tokens
explain: 2 n d = 12 d^2 gives n = 6d, independent of the number of layers. Below that, per-token cost is set by model width and is the same for every position; above it, the length-dependent attention term takes over, which is where KV-cache tricks and sparse attention start to pay.

q: A mixture-of-experts decoder has 8 experts per layer with top-2 routing, each expert the size of a dense model's FFN. Compare it with a dense model of the same total parameter count. What changes between decoding at batch size 1 and decoding at a batch of 256 tokens per step?
options: At batch 1 the MoE is slower because routing adds a sequential step per layer; at batch 256 routing is amortized over the whole batch and the two models run at the same speed
At batch 1 the MoE needs less memory than the dense model since only 2 experts per layer are resident; at batch 256 all experts must be loaded and memory matches
At both batch sizes the MoE reads a quarter of the FFN weights per step and does a quarter of the FFN FLOPs per token, so its advantage is constant
At batch 1 the MoE reads only 2 of 8 experts per layer per step; at batch 256 nearly every expert is hit by some token, so the whole model is read and only the per-token compute saving remains
explain: Bandwidth-bound single-stream decoding profits from reading 2 experts instead of 8. With 256 tokens routed per step the experts are all busy, the weight traffic is that of the full model, and what survives is that each token still runs through 2 experts' worth of FLOPs. Memory is the full model at any batch size.

q: A GPU sustains 1,000 TFLOP/s in fp16 and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. In decoding, each step reads every fp16 weight once (2 bytes per parameter) and spends 2 FLOPs per parameter per sequence in the batch. Ignore the KV cache. Above roughly which batch size does a decode step stop being bandwidth-bound?
options: About 50 sequences
About 500 sequences
About 2,000 sequences
About 5,000 sequences
explain: Memory time per step is 2N bytes / 2 TB/s = N / 10^12 s; compute time is 2NB / 10^15 s. They match at B = 500. Below that, adding a user costs almost no extra time per step, which is the whole economics of batching; the KV cache, which also has to be read, lowers the real number.

q: For each of a decoder's 32 layers, a team measures on calibration text how much the layer changes the residual stream (cosine similarity between a layer's input and output). Several middle layers barely change it. Removing 8 of them raises perplexity only mildly, and a short fine-tune recovers most of the loss. Why does this work for middle layers but not for the first few or the last?
options: Middle layers store mostly positional information, which is redundant once the first layers have used it, while the first and last layers carry the lexical content
Middle layers are near-duplicates of one another in their weights, so dropping half of them leaves the same function, while the first and last layers have no duplicates
The first and last layers are kept in higher precision in most checkpoints and are tied to the embedding matrix, so removing them would break the interface to the tokenizer and the unembedding
Each layer adds an update to the residual stream; middle layers add small refinements close to the identity, while early layers build the representation and late ones shape the output
explain: The residual stream is what makes a layer removable: skipping a near-identity update perturbs the stream a little. Early layers turn token embeddings into something usable and the last layers aim at the unembedding, and neither is anywhere near the identity. Weight similarity between layers is not required and is usually absent.

q: A nightly benchmark compares a 7B model in fp16 with a 4-bit weight-only quantized version. At batch size 1 the quantized model decodes about 3.5 times faster. At batch size 64 the two run at the same speed, the quantized one slightly slower. Which explanation fits?
options: At batch 64 the GPU runs out of memory and pages weights in and out of host memory, which hides the quantization gain behind the transfer time
At batch 64 the KV cache is quantized too and its dequantization at every step cancels the speedup that the smaller weights bring
Weight-only quantization cuts bytes read, not arithmetic; at batch 64 the step is compute-bound and the kernel dequantizes to fp16 and runs the same matmul
The 4-bit model has fewer parameters than the fp16 one, so it must be faster at every batch size and the harness is misreporting the large-batch runs
explain: At batch 1 a decode step is a weight read, so a quarter of the bytes gives most of a 4x. At batch 64 the matmuls dominate and they are still done in fp16 on dequantized weights. Speed at large batch needs quantized arithmetic as well, such as int8 weights and activations on int8 tensor cores.

q: A student trains a text-to-image network to output pixels directly, minimizing the mean squared error against the training image for each caption. For 'a dog on grass' every output is a washed-out, blurry greenish blob with a brown smear. What is the mechanism?
options: The caption encoder has too few tokens to describe a dog, so the network receives almost no conditioning signal and falls back on an average image
Mean squared error in pixel space cannot represent colour saturation, so the network converges to desaturated averages whatever the caption says
Minimizing squared error makes the network output the mean of all images matching the caption, and the mean of many valid dogs is a blur
The training images were downscaled before training, and a squared-error loss has no way of restoring the detail that was removed
explain: A caption has countless valid images; regression picks the single output that is closest to all of them on average, which is none of them. This is the many-valid-outputs problem that sampling-based generators, autoregressive or diffusion, exist to solve.

q: A discrete image tokenizer maps a 256 x 256 RGB image (3 bytes per pixel) to 256 tokens from a codebook of 8,192 entries. What is the most information the tokens can carry, compared with the raw image?
options: At most 416 bytes against 192 KB raw, so the tokens must discard most of the pixel detail
At most 3.3 KB against 192 KB raw, roughly the ratio of a lossless image codec
Exactly 192 KB, since a well-trained tokenizer is invertible and loses nothing
At most 2 KB against 64 KB raw, so the tokens keep about a thirtieth of the image
explain: log2 8,192 = 13 bits per token, times 256 tokens is 3,328 bits, 416 bytes. The raw image is 196,608 bytes. A factor of 470 cannot be lossless, so what survives is what the tokenizer learned to care about, and small print is rarely on that list.

q: A vision-language model spends 256 tokens per page image and has an 8,192-token context. The instructions and question take 1,000 tokens. How many pages of a scanned contract can be shown to it in one request?
explain: 8,192 - 1,000 = 7,192 tokens left; 7,192 / 256 = 28.09, so 28 pages. The 40-page contract needs retrieval, chunking or more tokens, and the answer will not be on page 29 by coincidence.

q: A museum wants text search over 100,000 photographs. Design A uses two separate encoders trained contrastively, one for images and one for text, compared by dot product. Design B feeds the query and an image together into one vision-language model that outputs a match score. What is the operational difference at query time?
options: A must re-encode all 100,000 images for every query, while B scores only the images that contain the query word
A and B both need one forward pass per image per query, and differ only in the size of the model
A cannot handle queries in a language other than the one used for the captions, while B can
A encodes the images once offline and only the query at search time, while B needs 100,000 forward passes per query
explain: Separate encoders make image embeddings query-independent, so they are computed once and stored. A joint model sees query and image together and must run for every pair, which is affordable for reranking the top 20 and ruinous for the archive.

q: An A4 page scanned at 300 dpi is 2,480 x 3,508 pixels, about 8.7 million. A document model is allowed 1,024 image tokens per page. Roughly what area of the page does one token stand for, and what does that mean for 10-point text, whose lines are about 42 pixels tall at this resolution?
options: About 92 x 92 pixels, about two line heights tall per token
About 14 x 14 pixels, a fraction of one letter per token
About 30 x 30 pixels, roughly one letter per token
About 300 x 300 pixels, roughly seven lines of text per token
explain: 8.7 million / 1,024 is about 8,500 pixels per token, a square of about 92 pixels on a side, which is about two line heights tall. One vector per two lines is why document models want many tokens per page, and why the token budget per page is a quality knob, not a billing detail.

q: A contrastively trained image-text model is used to sort photos into 'tram', 'bus' and 'bicycle' by comparing each image with the embedded class names. Accuracy improves clearly when the names are wrapped as 'a photo of a tram'. Why?
options: The text encoder needs at least four tokens before it produces a usable embedding, and a single word falls short of that minimum
The article 'a' tells the model that there is exactly one object in the picture, which rules out the crowded scenes that confuse it
The training texts were caption-like sentences, so a sentence-shaped prompt lands where image embeddings were trained to be
The template switches off the text encoder's position embeddings, which distort single words that carry no context around them
explain: The model knows an image by the captions it kept company with, and nobody captions a photo with the bare word 'tram'. A bare label is out of distribution for the text encoder; the template moves it back. Averaging several templates helps for the same reason.

q: A project team builds text-to-image search over 100,000 archive photos with a small contrastive image encoder running on a CPU at 0.1 s per image. A text query is embedded in about 20 ms. What does the index cost, and what happens if the team later switches to a different, better embedding model?
options: About 2.8 hours per query, since every image has to be re-encoded and compared with the query vector at search time
About 2.8 hours once, and a model change means doing it again, since image and text vectors must come from the same trained pair
About 17 minutes once, and the index stays valid for any other model that produces vectors of the same dimension
About 2.8 hours once, and a new model only needs to re-embed the queries, since the stored image vectors remain valid
explain: 100,000 x 0.1 s = 10,000 s, under three hours, after which each query is one 20 ms text pass plus a nearest-neighbour search. The shared space exists only between the two encoders that were trained together; a new text encoder against old image vectors is two strangers in one coordinate system.

q: A vision-language model turns a 448 x 448 image into patches of 14 x 14 pixels, one token each, without pooling. A prompt has 200 text tokens. Compared with sending one image, how do the sequence length and the attention-score computation change when four images are sent?
options: Tokens 4 times, attention-score computation 16 times
Tokens 4 times, attention-score computation 4 times
Tokens about 3.5 times, attention-score computation about 3.5 times
Tokens about 3.5 times, attention-score computation about 12 times
explain: Each image is 32 x 32 = 1,024 tokens. One image: 1,224 tokens; four images: 4,296, a factor of 3.5. Attention scores grow with the square of the length, 3.5^2 = 12.3. Self-attention does not care that the vectors came from pixels, and it charges them at the usual rate.

q: Masked language modelling hides about 15% of the tokens. Masked image modelling, the same recipe on image patches, works best when about 75% of the patches are hidden, and a 15% ratio yields poor representations. Why does the ratio differ so much?
options: Pixels are spatially redundant: at a low ratio a hidden patch is interpolated from its neighbours without understanding the scene, and only a high ratio forces inference
Image encoders are larger than text encoders, so they need more masked targets per batch to make use of the compute and to keep the gradient estimates stable
The 15% in text is set by the vocabulary size and the 80/10/10 corruption scheme; images have no vocabulary, so the ratio is a free choice tuned for speed
The 75% compensates for the missing [CLS] token in images, which would otherwise carry the global information that the masked patches need to be reconstructed
explain: A word is hard to guess from its neighbours; a patch is often just their interpolation. Masking most of the image removes the shortcut, with the bonus that the encoder processes a quarter of the patches. Masked diffusion over text pushes the same idea further by training at every ratio from near 0 to 1.

q: Two ways to give a language model eyes. Design A projects 1,024 image features per image into the sequence as extra tokens handled by self-attention. Design B inserts cross-attention layers in which text positions query the image features as keys and values, outside the sequence. A chat holds 10 images and 2,000 text tokens. Which comparison is right?
options: A keeps the sequence at 2,000 tokens, since image tokens are not stored in the KV cache; B grows it to about 12,000 because the image features are appended to the sequence as keys
B keeps the language model's sequence and KV cache at 2,000 tokens, at the price of new cross-attention parameters and image features that never see the text; A grows it to about 12,000
A and B both grow the sequence to about 12,000 tokens, and differ only in whether the image encoder is trained together with the language model or kept frozen during alignment
B needs a smaller image encoder than A, since cross-attention compresses the 1,024 features into one vector per image before the text positions can query them
explain: Cross-attention is soft alignment from the text side onto a bank of features, which may be as large as it likes without lengthening the decoder's own sequence. The costs are extra parameters to train and a one-way street: in design A, image positions also attend to text and to one another.

q: A contrastive image-text model is trained with in-batch negatives on a scraped dataset where many images share generic captions such as 'a dog'. In one batch two different dog photos both carry that caption. What happens to them in the loss?
options: The loss is undefined when two captions in a batch are identical, so such batches are skipped by the training loop and the two images are never seen together
The softmax merges identical captions into one candidate, so both images are scored against a single text and the duplicate costs nothing in the gradient
Each image is pushed away from the other's identical caption, a false negative acting as label noise; per-batch deduplication or several positives per image reduces it
The two images are pulled together since they share a caption, which is the desired behaviour for duplicates and one reason generic captions are kept in the data
explain: In-batch negatives assume every other pair is a wrong match. A duplicate caption makes the model lower a similarity that should be high. With millions of pairs the noise is tolerable; with a small curated dataset and generic captions it is a visible part of the gradient.

q: A masked diffusion language model fills 256 positions in 16 steps. Sampler 1 unmasks 16 randomly chosen positions per step. Sampler 2 unmasks, at each step, the 16 positions where the model's prediction is most confident. Sampler 2 produces noticeably more coherent text. Why?
options: Confident positions are the ones that were masked last during training, so sampler 2 replays the order the model saw and avoids unfamiliar partial states
Sampler 2 needs only one step in practice, since all positions that reach the confidence threshold are unmasked at once and the rest are copied from the prompt
Sampler 2 changes the training objective to a cross-entropy over the easy tokens only, which converges faster and leaves the hard tokens to the prompt
Committing confident tokens first lets the uncertain positions condition on them later, so fewer independent guesses are made where the model is torn
explain: Tokens unmasked in the same step are sampled independently of one another. Spending that independence on positions the model is already sure about, and deciding the hard ones later with more context, is the closest a parallel sampler gets to the chain rule.

q: A vision-language model uses 576 tokens per image. A support engineer in Schweinfurt has a chat with 20 photos of a broken machine and 1,500 tokens of text. The model's KV cache costs 0.5 MB per token (decimal megabytes). How much cache does this conversation hold?
options: About 6.5 GB, almost all of it for the image tokens
About 0.75 GB, since image tokens are not stored in the cache
About 6.5 GB, mostly text, since image tokens are compressed in the cache
About 13 GB, since image tokens store keys and values twice
explain: 20 x 576 = 11,520 image tokens plus 1,500 of text is 13,020 tokens, times 0.5 MB is about 6.5 GB. To the language model an image token is a position like any other, with the same keys and values to keep. The 'picture worth 576 words' is billed in cache.

q: A document parser extracts 10 fields per receipt with a vision-language model. On the test set each field is correct 95% of the time, independently of the others. The night before the roadshow the team wants to quote the share of receipts with every field correct. What is it?
options: About 95%
About 60%
About 50%
About 90%
explain: 0.95^10 = 0.60. Field-level accuracy is the honest metric and the document-level number is the one the customer feels, and they differ by a factor you can compute before the demo rather than during it.

q: In a contrastively trained image-text model, the cosine similarity between a photo and its own correct caption is typically about 0.3, while two unrelated photos score about 0.5 and two unrelated captions about 0.4. A team uses one cosine threshold of 0.4 for 'is this caption a match' and for 'are these two photos duplicates'. What is going on?
options: The text encoder is defective: in any properly trained model a correct caption must score above two unrelated images, so the model should be retrained before any threshold is set
The training temperature was too low, so all similarities are compressed into a narrow band; dividing the scores by the temperature restores one common scale for both uses
Image and text embeddings occupy separate regions, so cross-modal similarities live on a different scale from within-modal ones; ranking within one direction works, one shared threshold does not
The embeddings were not normalized before the comparison, so cosine similarity is not meaningful for either use and both thresholds should be set on raw dot products instead
explain: The contrastive loss only needs each caption to beat the other captions for its image; it never asks an image and its caption to coincide, and the two encoders keep their own cones. The shared space is a shared ordering, in the spirit of distributional vectors, not a shared ruler across modalities.

q: An early-fusion model predicts text tokens and discrete image tokens, codebook size 16,384, with one next-token loss. Training logs show 2.5 bits per token on text and 7.5 bits per token on image tokens. Reviewer #2 concludes that the vision side is badly undertrained. What is the right reading?
options: Reviewer #2 is right: both token streams are predicted by the same network with the same loss, so after enough training their losses should converge to about the same value
The image loss is too high because the codebook is too large for the data; halving it to 8,192 entries would take one bit off the loss and most of the gap with text
The text loss is suspiciously low and suggests contamination of the training data, since image tokens are the harder stream and set the honest baseline for both
The two numbers are not comparable: the irreducible entropy of image tokens is far higher, a uniform guess over 16,384 codes costs 14 bits, so each stream needs its own floor
explain: Bits per token measure a source as much as a model, and image tokens are nearly incompressible by design. Shannon's entropy is per source; the comparison that means something is the same stream under two models, or the loss against a known floor.

q: A plain masked diffusion language model recomputes all positions at every step and cannot reuse a KV cache, and it must fix the output length in advance. A variant generates blocks of 32 tokens from left to right: within a block the attention is bidirectional and denoising runs for several steps, while finished blocks are attended to causally and never change. What does the variant buy?
options: Finished blocks can be cached like an autoregressive model's past, and generation can stop after any block, so the length need not be fixed; parallelism survives inside each block
It makes the model fully autoregressive, so every token is sampled one at a time and the parallelism of diffusion is given up entirely in exchange for the ability to cache
It removes the need for denoising steps, since each block is emitted in one forward pass once the previous blocks are known and cached, which is where the speed comes from
It allows the model to revise finished blocks when later blocks contradict them, which a plain diffusion model cannot do within its canvas once the positions are committed
explain: The causal structure between blocks restores the two things autoregression does well, caching and stopping when done, and keeps parallel denoising where it is cheap, within a block. The price is that a finished block is final, exactly as in a left-to-right model.

q: A vision-language model keeps describing objects that are not in the picture. A fix runs the model twice, once on the real image and once on a heavily blurred copy, and samples from (1 + a) x logits_real - a x logits_blurred with a around 1. What is this subtraction meant to remove?
options: The high-frequency noise in the image: the blurred run estimates the low frequencies, so the difference sharpens the model's perception of small text and fine edges
The part of the prediction that does not depend on image content, the language prior that produces plausible but absent objects, which both runs share
The effect of the blurred image acting as a negative example that is fine-tuned into the model between the two forward passes, so the prior shifts towards the real image
The duplication of image tokens: two runs double the number of visual positions in the context, so the model attends to the image more and to its own text less
explain: Hallucinated objects are the ones the language prior expects next to the ones it sees. The blurred run keeps that prior and little else, so the difference amplifies what the actual pixels contributed. The cost is two forward passes per token and no training.

q: A masked diffusion language model is trained by drawing a mask rate t uniformly from (0, 1], masking that fraction of a sequence of length L, and multiplying the cross-entropy over the masked positions by 1/t. A student at 3 a.m. objects that at t = 0.05 the weight is 20 and nearly clean sequences will dominate. What is the weight for?
options: It compensates for the mask token being rarer in the input at low t, so that its embedding and the positions around it receive enough gradient to be learned properly
It is a learning rate schedule in disguise: low-noise steps are the more informative ones, so they should take larger optimizer steps than the nearly blank sequences
It makes the objective coincide with the 15% masking recipe exactly at t = 0.15, which anchors the model to a known good setting while the other rates add robustness
At mask rate t about tL tokens are masked, so dividing by t gives every noise level the same expected total loss instead of letting heavily masked sequences dominate
explain: The sum over masked positions has about tL terms; 1/t cancels the t, so a nearly clean sequence with 5% masked and a nearly blank one with 95% masked contribute alike in expectation. This is what makes the loss a bound on the log-likelihood rather than a BERT loss averaged over ratios.

q: A form-filling system reads a PDF form's layout with a vision-language model and fills it from a profile document. The team reports a measured hallucination rate of exactly zero on 40 synthetic profiles. Every profile happens to contain a value for every field the forms ask for. What is wrong with the measurement?
options: A rate of exactly zero is not possible for a generative model, so the scoring script must be comparing the output with itself rather than with the profile document
Forty profiles are too few: with four hundred profiles the rate would certainly become nonzero, and only a nonzero rate on a large set makes the report honest
No field was ever missing, so the model never had a chance to invent a value; the test set needs profiles with deliberately absent fields, and the rate counts values produced for them
The rate should be measured on the vision model's reading of the form layout rather than on the filled form, where the validation step has already corrected the errors
explain: Hallucination here means writing something the profile does not contain, and a test set in which the profile contains everything cannot observe it. Zero on the wrong test is the most convincing number a team can produce, and the easiest for Reviewer #2 to take apart.
